lessons.title: Tajweed: what it is, its ruling and why it matters
lessons.lede: Tajweed is giving every letter its right and its due when reciting the Quran; it keeps the recitation free of mistakes.

formula.caption: Its point of articulation and the characteristics it always has
Rules that come to it, such as ikhfa' and madd
Reciting as the Quran was revealed

idea.lead: In Arabic, tajweed means making something better. As a term, it means giving every letter its right and its due. A letter's right is its point of articulation and the characteristics that never leave it, such as being whispered or voiced. Its due is what comes to it because of where it stands, such as izhar, ikhfa', madd and tafkhim.
idea.kidsLead: Tajweed means reading the Quran well: saying every letter from its right place, the right way, as the Prophet ﷺ read it.

how.text: The words and letters of the Quran.
Learning its rules is a communal duty (fard kifayah); reciting with tajweed is required of everyone who reads the Quran, as far as they are able.
It keeps the tongue from mistakes in the words of Allah.
It is learned from a skilled teacher, by listening to them and reciting before them, not from books alone.
The lessons in this app follow the riwayah of Hafs from 'Asim, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah: the same reading as the app's Mushaf.

idea.note: Ibn al-Jazari says in his Muqaddimah: «وَالأَخْذُ بِالتَّجْوِيدِ حَتْمٌ لازِمُ ... مَنْ لَمْ يُجَوِّدِ القُرآنَ آثِمُ»: applying tajweed is a firm duty, and whoever does not recite the Quran with tajweed is sinful. Lesson 4 explains clear and hidden mistakes.

quiz.q: What does tajweed mean in Arabic?
quiz.why: Jawwadtu ash-shay' means "I made it better", so tajweed means making better.

quiz.q: What is tajweed, as a term?
options: Reciting the Quran in a beautiful voice
Giving every letter its right and its due
Knowing the meaning of the ayahs
quiz.why: Tajweed is giving every letter its right and its due. A beautiful voice adorns the recitation, but it is not tajweed.

quiz.q: What is a letter's right?
options: Its point of articulation and the characteristics it always has
The rules that come to it
How it is written in the Mushaf
quiz.why: A letter's right is what never leaves it: its point of articulation and its permanent characteristics, such as being whispered or voiced.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of a letter's due?
quiz.why: Ikhfa' comes to noon sakinah because of the letter after it, so it is part of the letter's due. Its point of articulation and being voiced or whispered are its permanent right.

quiz.q: Is reciting with tajweed required of whoever reads the Quran?
quiz.why: Reciting with tajweed is required of everyone who reads the Quran, as far as they are able. Ibn al-Jazari says: «والأخذ بالتجويد حتم لازم» (applying tajweed is a firm duty).

quiz.q: What is the ruling on learning the rules and terms of tajweed?
quiz.why: Learning the rules is a communal duty: when some Muslims do it, the rest are free of blame. Reciting correctly, though, is needed by every reader.

quiz.q: How is tajweed learned properly?
options: By reciting before a skilled teacher
quiz.why: Tajweed is learned by listening and reciting: you hear the teacher, then recite before them and they correct you. Books and apps help, but do not replace that.

lessons.title: The virtue and etiquette of recitation
lessons.lede: Reciting the Quran brings a great reward, and its etiquette joins a present heart with careful reading.

formula.caption: «The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it» (al-Bukhari)

idea.lead: Reciting the Quran is one of the best acts of worship: every letter you read earns a good deed, and each good deed is worth ten. Whoever reads it with difficulty, stumbling over it, has a double reward. Reciting has etiquette that helps the reader be humble and reflect.
idea.kidsLead: Every letter you read from the Quran earns you a good deed, and each good deed is worth ten! We read the Quran with good manners: we make wudu, seek refuge with Allah, read calmly, and think about what it means.

how.text: The Prophet ﷺ said: «Whoever reads a letter from the Book of Allah has a good deed for it, and a good deed is worth ten like it. I do not say that Alif-Laam-Meem is one letter; rather, alif is a letter, laam is a letter and meem is a letter» (at-Tirmidhi).

The Prophet ﷺ said: «The one who is skilled in the Quran is with the noble, righteous scribes (the angels), and the one who reads the Quran and stumbles over it, finding it hard, has two rewards» (Muslim).
The Prophet ﷺ said: «Read the Quran, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions» (Muslim).
It is recommended to recite in a state of purity, in a clean place, facing the qiblah when possible.

Begin by seeking refuge with Allah. Allah says: «فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ الْقُرْآنَ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ» (An-Nahl 98): when you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan. Lesson 5 covers it in detail.
Recite slowly and with tajweed. Allah says: «وَرَتِّلِ الْقُرْآنَ تَرْتِيلًا» (Al-Muzzammil 4): recite the Quran in measured recitation. Do not rush so much that letters are lost.

Think about the meaning of what you read, with a present heart. Allah says: «كِتَابٌ أَنزَلْنَاهُ إِلَيْكَ مُبَارَكٌ لِّيَدَّبَّرُوا آيَاتِهِ» (Sad 29): a blessed Book We revealed to you, so that they may reflect on its ayahs.

idea.note: Reciting the Quran from memory without wudu is allowed; touching the Mushaf requires wudu according to most scholars.

quiz.q: How many good deeds does reading one letter of the Book of Allah earn?
quiz.why: The Prophet ﷺ said: «he has a good deed for it, and a good deed is worth ten like it».

quiz.q: The Prophet ﷺ said: «I do not say that Alif-Laam-Meem is one letter». How many letters is «الم»?
quiz.why: He ﷺ said: «alif is a letter, laam is a letter and meem is a letter», so reading it earns thirty good deeds.

quiz.q: What is the reward of someone who stumbles over the Quran, finding it hard?
quiz.why: Two rewards: one for reciting and one for the effort. So do not give up because it is hard: keep trying and keep learning.

quiz.q: Who are "the best of you" in al-Bukhari's hadith?
options: Those who learn the Quran and teach it
quiz.why: The Prophet ﷺ said: «The best of you are those who learn the Quran and teach it».

quiz.q: How does the reader begin reciting?
quiz.why: Allah says: «فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ الْقُرْآنَ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ»: when you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan.

quiz.q: What does reflection (tadabbur) mean?
options: Thinking about the meaning of the ayahs
quiz.why: Reflection is thinking about the meaning of what you read; the Quran was revealed «so that they may reflect on its ayahs».

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT part of the etiquette of recitation?
options: Rushing so that letters are lost
quiz.why: Allah commands tarteel, and rushing so that letters are lost goes against it.

lessons.title: Speeds of recitation: tahqiq, tadwir and hadr
lessons.lede: Recitation has three speeds: tahqiq, tadwir and hadr. All of them are allowed, as long as the letters and the rules are kept.

formula.caption: The slowest, for learning and practice

idea.lead: Recitation has three speeds. Tahqiq is reciting calmly and unhurriedly, giving every letter its due without overdoing it; it suits learning and practice. Hadr is reciting quickly while keeping the makharij, the characteristics and the rules. Tadwir is in between. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَيُقْرَأُ القُرْآنُ بِالتَّحْقِيقِ مَعْ، حَدْرٍ وَتَدْوِيرٍ وَكُلٌّ مُتَّبَعْ» (the Quran is recited with tahqiq, hadr and tadwir, and each is followed). Tartil, commanded in «وَرَتِّلِ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ تَرۡتِيلًا», describes how to recite: slowly, with reflection and with tajweed.
idea.kidsLead: We can recite the Quran slowly, at a medium speed, or faster. At every speed, what matters is saying each letter correctly, without dropping a madd or a ghunnah.

how.text: The slowest: full madds, complete vowels and clear letters, without exaggerating or stretching. It suits the learner.
The middle speed, between tahqiq and hadr. Many reciters use it in everyday recitation.
The fastest, keeping all the rules. It suits revision and reciting a lot.
A quality of all three speeds when they are recited with tajweed and reflection; some scholars count it as a speed close to tahqiq.
Its length fits the speed: a reciter using tahqiq makes the permitted madd longer than one using hadr, within the lengths that are narrated.

idea.note: No speed may be so fast that letters drop, madds shorten or ghunnahs disappear, nor so slow that letters are stretched and vowels grow into extra letters. Learn the speed from a teacher.

ayat.legendNoon: The command to recite with tartil
ayat.findHint: Recite the ayah at the three speeds, keeping the madd and the ghunnah each time.

why: The command of tartil: reciting slowly with tajweed, a quality that goes with every speed

quiz.q: How many speeds of recitation are there?
quiz.why: Three: tahqiq, tadwir and hadr, all allowed when the rules are kept.

quiz.q: Which is the slowest speed?
quiz.why: Tahqiq is the slowest: calm, unhurried reciting that gives every letter its due.

quiz.q: What is hadr?
options: Reciting quickly while keeping the rules
quiz.why: Hadr is fast reciting that drops none of the rules.

quiz.q: What is tadwir?
options: The middle speed between tahqiq and hadr
quiz.why: Tadwir is the middle speed between tahqiq and hadr.

quiz.q: Which speed suits a beginner best?
quiz.why: Tahqiq lets the learner say the letters and apply the rules carefully, so teaching starts with it.

quiz.q: What is the ruling on speed that drops letters and shortens madds?
options: Allowed for those who know the Quran by heart
quiz.why: Every speed requires keeping the letters and the rules, so speed that spoils them is not allowed.

quiz.q: How long is the permitted madd of someone reciting with tahqiq, compared with hadr?
quiz.why: Madd length fits the speed: tahqiq is longer than hadr, without going beyond the narrated lengths.

lessons.title: Clear and hidden mistakes (lahn)
lessons.lede: Lahn is a mistake in recitation. It is of two kinds: clear, which most people notice, and hidden, which only skilled reciters notice.

formula.caption: An obvious mistake in a letter or a vowel
A mistake in the finer points of reading

idea.lead: In Arabic, lahn means turning away from what is right; as a term, it is a mistake in reciting the Quran. It is of two kinds. Clear lahn is an obvious mistake in a letter or a vowel, whether or not it changes the meaning, and most people notice it. Hidden lahn spoils the finer points of pronunciation without changing a letter or its vowel, and only skilled reciters notice it.
idea.kidsLead: Lahn is a mistake in reading. Some mistakes are big and easy to hear, like saying one letter or vowel instead of another. Some are small and hidden, like leaving out the ghunnah or cutting a madd short. We learn tajweed to avoid both.

how.text: Saying one letter instead of another, such as «الهمد» with haa instead of «الحمد»; one vowel instead of another, such as «أَنْعَمْتُ» instead of «أَنْعَمْتَ», which changes the meaning; or adding or dropping a letter.
Forbidden, by agreement of the scholars, for whoever does it on purpose or neglects learning how to avoid it.
Breaking the tajweed rules while the letter and its vowel stay the same: leaving out the ghunnah, getting a madd's length wrong, or making a light letter heavy.
Less serious than clear lahn. Scholars differ on it: some say it is forbidden, others that it is disliked.

idea.note: Some hidden lahn only experts notice, such as rolling the raa too much or overdoing the ghunnah. Lesson 74 covers common mistakes in pronouncing the letters in detail.

quiz.q: What does lahn mean in Arabic?
options: Turning away from what is right
quiz.why: In Arabic, lahn means turning away from what is right; in recitation, it is a mistake.

quiz.q: Someone read «الحمد» with haa (ه): «الهمد». What kind of mistake is this?
quiz.why: Saying one letter instead of another is clear lahn, which most people notice.

quiz.q: What kind of mistake is leaving out the ghunnah in ikhfa'?
quiz.why: The letter and its vowel stay the same, but the finer point of reading is lost: this is hidden lahn.

quiz.q: What kind of mistake is reading «أَنْعَمْتَ» with a dammah on the taa?
quiz.why: The vowel changed, and so did the meaning: the favour would belong to the reader. This is clear lahn.

quiz.q: Who notices hidden lahn?
quiz.why: Only those who have learned tajweed well, from a teacher, notice hidden lahn. That is why a reader needs a teacher.

quiz.q: What is the ruling on clear lahn done on purpose?
quiz.why: Clear lahn is forbidden, by agreement of the scholars, for whoever does it on purpose or neglects learning.

quiz.q: Does clear lahn have to change the meaning?
options: No: it may or may not change the meaning
quiz.why: Clear lahn is a mistake in a letter or a vowel, whether or not it changes the meaning.

lessons.title: Isti'adhah and basmalah
lessons.lede: The reader begins with the isti'adhah (seeking refuge with Allah), then the basmalah at the start of every surah except At-Tawbah.

idea.lead: The isti'adhah is saying «أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم» (I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan) before reciting, following Allah's words: «فَإِذَا قَرَأْتَ الْقُرْآنَ فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ» (An-Nahl 98). The basmalah is saying «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم» (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful); it is read at the start of every surah except At-Tawbah. There are several ways to join or separate them and the start of the surah, given below.
idea.kidsLead: Before we read, we say: «أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم». At the start of every surah we say: «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم», except Surah At-Tawbah, which we start without it.

how.text: Its best-known wording is «أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم». Say it aloud when reciting aloud with someone listening; say it quietly in prayer and when reciting quietly.
It is read at the start of every surah except At-Tawbah. When starting in the middle of a surah, the reader may read it or leave it.
At the start of a surah, four ways are allowed: stop after each; stop after the isti'adhah and join the basmalah to the surah; join the isti'adhah to the basmalah and stop; or join all three.

Three ways are allowed: stop after each; stop at the end of the surah and join the basmalah to the next; or join all three. Joining the end of a surah to the basmalah and then stopping is not allowed, so that the basmalah is not taken as part of the surah before it.
It is read without the basmalah. Between Al-Anfal and At-Tawbah there are three ways: stop, pause briefly (saktah), or join, all without the basmalah.

idea.note: Most scholars say the isti'adhah is recommended; some say it is required. Hafs from 'Asim reads the basmalah between every two surahs, except Al-Anfal and At-Tawbah.

quiz.q: What is the best-known wording of the isti'adhah?
quiz.why: Allah says: «فَاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ الرَّجِيمِ», so its best-known wording is «أعوذ بالله من الشيطان الرجيم».

quiz.q: Which surah does not begin with the basmalah?
quiz.why: Surah At-Tawbah alone is read without the basmalah at its start.

quiz.q: At the start of a surah, how many ways are there to join or separate the isti'adhah, the basmalah and the surah?
quiz.why: Four: stop after each; stop after the first and join the second to the third; join the first to the second and stop; or join all three.

quiz.q: Which way is NOT allowed between two surahs?
options: Joining the end of the surah to the basmalah, then stopping
Stopping at the end of the surah and joining the basmalah to the next
quiz.why: It is not allowed, so that the basmalah is not taken as the end of the surah before it.

quiz.q: When starting in the middle of a surah, what about the basmalah?
quiz.why: In the middle of a surah, the reader may read the basmalah or leave it.

quiz.q: What are the ways between Al-Anfal and At-Tawbah?
options: Stop, pause briefly or join, without the basmalah
You cannot go from one to the other
quiz.why: At-Tawbah has no basmalah at its start, so the reader may stop, pause briefly (saktah) or join.

quiz.q: When does the reader say the isti'adhah quietly?
options: When reciting aloud with someone listening
quiz.why: It is said quietly in prayer and when reciting quietly, and aloud when reciting aloud with someone listening.

lessons.title: Vowel marks, tanween and sukun
lessons.lede: There are three vowel marks: fathah, dammah and kasrah. Tanween is a noon sakinah that is said but not written, and sukun means a letter has no vowel.

idea.lead: Every letter in the Quran either has one of the three vowel marks, fathah «ـَ», dammah «ـُ» or kasrah «ـِ», or has none, which is sukun. Tanween is an extra noon sakinah at the end of a noun: it is said when joining but not written as a noon; it is marked by two vowel marks on the letter. Getting the vowels right is where tajweed starts, since saying one vowel instead of another is clear lahn.
idea.kidsLead: For fathah we open the mouth: «بَ». For dammah we round the lips: «بُ». For kasrah we lower the jaw: «بِ». Sukun means no vowel: «بْ». Tanween is two vowel marks, read with a little noon sound: «بٌ» sounds like «بُنْ».

how.text: A slanted line above the letter «ـَ»; the mouth opens.
A small waw above the letter «ـُ»; the lips round.
A slanted line below the letter «ـِ»; the jaw lowers.
In the Madinah Mushaf, a small head of khaa «ـۡ» above the letter; the letter is said without a vowel.
With fathah «ـً», dammah «ـٌ» or kasrah «ـٍ»; said as a noon sakinah at the end of a noun when joining.
Stop on tanween with fathah with an alif: «أَفۡوَاجَا»; on tanween with dammah or kasrah with sukun: «أَحَدْ», «خُسۡرْ».

idea.note: In the Madinah Mushaf, tanween is drawn as two marks side by side or stacked, depending on the letter after it: a hint of the rules of noon sakinah and tanween in level 2. The length of madd and ghunnah is measured in counts; one count is the time it takes to say one vowel.

ayat.findHint: Find the tanween and the sukun in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Sukun on the laam in «قُلۡ»
Tanween with dammah on the dal in «أَحَدٌ»
Sukun on the seen
Tanween with kasrah on the raa
Sukun on the faa
Tanween with fathah on the jeem, followed by an alif that is read when stopping

ayat.tip: In the Mushaf, sukun is a small head of khaa «ۡ» above the letter, as you can see in the ayahs above.

quiz.q: What are the three vowel marks?
quiz.why: The three vowel marks are fathah, dammah and kasrah; sukun means a letter has none of them.

quiz.q: How is tanween said?
options: As an extra noon sakinah at the end of a noun
quiz.why: Tanween is an extra noon sakinah: it is said when joining, but not written as a noon.

quiz.q: What is the sign of sukun in the Madinah Mushaf?
quiz.why: Sukun is a small head of khaa. A small circle marks an extra letter that is not said.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «أَفۡوَاجٗا»?
quiz.why: When stopping, tanween with fathah becomes an alif.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «أَحَدٌ»?
quiz.why: When stopping, tanween with dammah or kasrah becomes a sukun.

quiz.q: In «خُسۡرٍ», what does the seen have?
quiz.why: The seen has the sukun sign «ۡ», and the raa after it has tanween with kasrah.

quiz.q: Is tanween written as a noon in the Mushaf?
options: No: it is said as a noon but not written as one
It is neither written nor said
It is written but not said
quiz.why: Tanween is written as two vowel marks, and said as a noon sakinah when joining.

lessons.title: Shaddah (doubled letters)
lessons.lede: A shaddah marks two of the same letter, the first with sukun and the second with a vowel, merged into one doubled letter.

formula.caption: the same letter with a vowel

idea.lead: A letter with a shaddah is two letters: the first has sukun, the second has a vowel, and the first is merged into the second. It is said by holding the tongue or lips on the point of articulation a little, then saying the letter with its vowel. The shaddah is a small head of seen «ـّ» above the letter, with the letter's vowel. So «رَبِّ» is said «رَبْ» then «بِ», joined.
idea.kidsLead: The shaddah is a small mark like the head of a seen «ـّ». A letter with a shaddah is read twice: once with sukun and once with its vowel, like «رَبِّ» = «رَبْ» + «بِ».

how.text: «رَبِّ» = «رَبْ» + «بِ»: the first baa has sukun and the second has kasrah, making one doubled baa.
A small head of seen «ـّ» above the letter, with a fathah or dammah above it, or a kasrah below it.
Hold the tongue or lips on the point of articulation a little, then say the letter with its vowel, without a break between the two.
With a shaddah, they always have ghunnah for two counts, as in «إِنَّ» and «ثُمَّ». Lesson 36 covers this.
The letter after a sun laam has a shaddah, as in «ٱلشَّمۡسِ». Lesson 25 covers this.

idea.note: Leaving out a shaddah is clear lahn, since it drops a letter from the word. A well-known example is reading «إِيَّاكَ» without the shaddah, which changes the meaning completely.

ayat.findHint: Find the letter with a shaddah and the letter with a sukun in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: The yaa has a shaddah: two yaas, the first with sukun, the second with fathah
The 'ayn has a sukun, without a shaddah
The noon has a shaddah, with ghunnah
The 'ayn has a sukun
The baa has a shaddah: «رَبْ» then «بِ»
The laam has a sukun

ayat.tip: Compare: a letter with sukun is one letter with no vowel; a letter with a shaddah is two letters, the first with sukun.

quiz.q: What does a shaddah show?
options: Two letters: the first with sukun, the second with a vowel
A letter that is not said
quiz.why: A doubled letter is two of the same letter: the first, with sukun, is merged into the second, which has a vowel.

quiz.q: How is «رَبِّ» made up?
quiz.why: The doubled baa is two baas: the first with sukun «رَبْ», the second with kasrah «بِ».

quiz.q: What is the sign of shaddah?
quiz.why: The shaddah is a small head of seen «ـّ». The head of khaa is the sign of sukun.

quiz.q: Leaving out the shaddah in «إِيَّاكَ» is:
quiz.why: Leaving out the shaddah drops a letter and changes the meaning, so it is clear lahn.

quiz.q: When noon or meem has a shaddah, it always has:
quiz.why: Noon and meem with a shaddah are said with ghunnah for two counts.

quiz.q: In «إِيَّاكَ نَعۡبُدُ», which letter has a shaddah?
quiz.why: The yaa has a shaddah; the 'ayn has a sukun without a shaddah.

quiz.q: How is a letter with a shaddah said?
options: Holding the point of articulation a little, then with its vowel, without a break
quiz.why: The point of articulation is held a little, then the letter is said with its vowel: no break between the two, and not too light.

lessons.title: The signs of the Mushaf
lessons.lede: The signs of the Mushaf are small marks in the Madinah Mushaf that tell the reciter how to say a letter: whether it is said at all, and whether it is lengthened, merged or concealed.

idea.lead: The signs (dabt) are the marks placed on the letters to show their vowels and sukun, and any madd, merging, concealment or extra letter. The Madinah Mushaf follows the conventions of the scholars of dabt, so every mark in it means something for pronunciation. Knowing them helps the reciter read correctly, but it does not replace learning from a teacher.
idea.kidsLead: The Mushaf has small marks above and below the letters, and each one tells us something: this letter is not read, this one is lengthened, this one changes. When we know them, we recite as the Prophet ﷺ recited.

how.text: A small circle above a weak letter: it is extra and never said, joining or stopping, like the waw in «أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ».
Above an alif: it is dropped when joining and said when stopping, like the alif of «لَّٰكِنَّا۠» and «ٱلظُّنُونَا۠».
A small alif, waw or yaa shows a letter left out of the writing that is still said, like the alif in «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ» and the waw in «لَهُۥ».
Above a noon, or in place of the second tanween mark: iqlab, said as a hidden meem before baa.
Stacked marks show izhar; marks one after the other show idgham or ikhfa'.
Above a saad: it is read as seen, as in «وَيَبۡصُۜطُ».
Above a madd letter: a madd longer than the natural one, because of a hamzah or sukun after it.

idea.note: Other signs come in their own lessons: the filled dot for tas-hil and imalah, as in «ءَا۬عۡجَمِيّٞ» and «مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا», the stop signs (lesson 89) and the small seen of saktah (lesson 85). The marks for vowels, sukun and shaddah are in lessons 6 and 7.

ayat.legendNext: A sign that changes the sound
ayat.findHint: Find the sign in each ayah and learn its meaning, then bring the colours back to check.

why: The waw has a round zero: it is not said, so read «أُلَٰٓئِكَ»
The alif has an upright zero: dropped when joining, said when stopping
A small seen above the saad: read as seen
The madd sign above the alif: madd lazim, six counts

ayat.tip: Every sign in the Mushaf means something for pronunciation, so if you see one you do not know, ask your teacher.

quiz.q: What are the signs (dabt) of the Mushaf?
options: The shape of the Uthmani script
The marks that show how a letter is said
quiz.why: Dabt is the marks on the letters that show their vowels and sukun, and any madd, merging or extra letter.

quiz.q: What does a round zero above a weak letter mean?
options: It is extra and never said
quiz.why: A round zero means the letter is extra and not said either way, like the waw of «أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ».

quiz.q: How is the alif of «لَّٰكِنَّا۠ هُوَ» read when joining?
quiz.why: It has an upright zero: dropped when joining, said when stopping.

quiz.q: What does the small alif in «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ» show?
options: A letter left out of the writing that is said
quiz.why: Small letters show letters left out of the writing that are said in recitation.

quiz.q: What does a small meem above a noon sakinah mean?
quiz.why: The small meem is the sign of iqlab: the noon is said as a hidden meem before baa.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «وَيَبۡصُۜطُ»?
quiz.why: The small seen above the saad means it is read as seen.

quiz.q: What do the two tanween marks mean when one is stacked above the other?
quiz.why: Stacked marks show izhar; marks one after the other show idgham or ikhfa'.

lessons.title: Points of articulation (makharij): the main areas
lessons.lede: A makhraj is where a letter comes from. There are seventeen, grouped into five main areas.

formula.caption: A hamzah with a vowel before it

idea.lead: Makhraj means "place of exit": as a term, it is where a letter comes from, which sets it apart from other letters. Ibn al-Jazari's choice is that there are seventeen makharij, grouped into five main areas: the open space (jawf), the throat, the tongue, the lips and the nose (khayshum). To find a letter's makhraj, give it a sukun and put a hamzah with a vowel before it, as in «أَبْ» or «أَتْ»: where the sound stops is its makhraj.
idea.kidsLead: Every letter comes from a place: the open space inside the mouth and throat, the throat, the tongue, the lips or the nose. To find its place, say a hamzah with fathah before it and give it a sukun: «أَبْ», «أَتْ». Where the sound stops is its place.

how.text: The open space inside the throat and mouth: one makhraj, for the three madd letters.
Three makharij for six letters: ء ه, then ع ح, then غ خ.
Ten makharij for eighteen letters.
Two makharij for four letters: faa, then waw (when not a madd letter), baa and meem.
The back of the nose (khayshum), where ghunnah comes from.

idea.note: Scholars differ on the number: seventeen for al-Khalil and Ibn al-Jazari; sixteen for Sibawayh and ash-Shatibi, without the jawf; fourteen for al-Farra', who counts laam, noon and raa as one makhraj. The next lessons cover each main area.

quiz.q: How many makharij are there, by Ibn al-Jazari's choice?
quiz.why: Ibn al-Jazari's choice is seventeen makharij.

quiz.q: How many main areas are there?
quiz.why: Five: the jawf, the throat, the tongue, the lips and the nose.

quiz.q: Which main area do the madd letters come from?
quiz.why: The three madd letters come from the jawf, the open space inside the throat and mouth.

quiz.q: How do you find a letter's makhraj?
options: Give it a sukun and put a hamzah with a vowel before it
quiz.why: As in «أَبْ»: where the sound stops is the letter's makhraj.

quiz.q: Which main area does ghunnah come from?
quiz.why: Ghunnah comes from the khayshum, at the back of the nose.

quiz.q: How many letters come from the tongue?
quiz.why: The tongue has ten makharij for eighteen letters, more than any other area.

quiz.q: Which main area does meem come from?
quiz.why: Meem comes from the lips, with baa and waw (when not a madd letter).

lessons.title: The open space (jawf) and the madd letters
lessons.lede: The three madd letters come from the jawf: alif after fathah, waw with sukun after dammah, and yaa with sukun after kasrah.

idea.lead: The jawf is the open space inside the throat and mouth. The three madd letters come from it: alif with sukun after a fathah, waw with sukun after a dammah, and yaa with sukun after a kasrah. They are called the letters of the jawf, or of the air, because they do not stop at a fixed point like other letters: they end when the breath ends. All three come together in the word «نُوحِيهَا».
idea.kidsLead: There are three madd letters: alif after fathah «قَا», waw with sukun after dammah «قُو», and yaa with sukun after kasrah «قِي». They come from the open space inside the mouth and throat, and we stretch them for two counts.

how.text: Always has sukun, and the letter before it always has fathah, as in «قَالَ».
A madd letter when it has sukun and the letter before it has dammah, as in «يَقُولُ».
A madd letter when it has sukun and the letter before it has kasrah, as in «قِيلَ».
Two counts in natural madd; level 2 covers the other kinds of madd.
When waw or yaa has sukun after a fathah, as in «خَوۡفٍ» and «بَيۡتٍ», it is a leen letter, not a madd letter; it has its own lesson.

idea.note: A common beginner's mistake is cutting a madd letter so short that it becomes a vowel, such as reading «قَالَ» as «قَلَ»: this is clear lahn, since it drops a letter. The opposite mistake, stretching a vowel into a madd letter, is also common.

ayat.legendNext: The letter before it, with its vowel
ayat.findHint: Find the madd letters and the letter before each one, then bring the colours back to check.

why: All three madd letters in one word: waw after dammah, yaa after kasrah, alif after fathah
Alif after fathah
Waw with sukun after dammah
Waw with sukun after dammah
Two yaas with sukun, each after a kasrah

ayat.tip: Look at the vowel on the letter before the madd letter: fathah before alif, dammah before waw, kasrah before yaa.

quiz.q: How many madd letters are there?
quiz.why: Three: alif, waw and yaa, under their conditions.

quiz.q: Where do the madd letters come from?
quiz.why: They come from the jawf, the open space inside the throat and mouth.

quiz.q: When is waw a madd letter?
options: When it has sukun after a dammah
When it has sukun after a fathah
quiz.why: Waw with sukun after a dammah is a madd letter; with sukun after a fathah it is a leen letter.

quiz.q: Which word has all three madd letters?
quiz.why: In «نُوحِيهَا» there is waw after dammah, yaa after kasrah and alif after fathah.

quiz.q: In «سِينِينَ», what is the madd letter?
quiz.why: Yaa with sukun after a kasrah is a madd letter, and the word has two of them.

quiz.q: Why are the madd letters called letters of the air?
options: They end when the breath ends
quiz.why: They do not stop at a fixed point like other letters: they end when the breath ends.

quiz.q: Reading «قَالَ» as «قَلَ», cutting the alif, is:
quiz.why: Cutting a madd letter until it is gone drops a letter from the word, so it is clear lahn.

lessons.title: The deepest part of the throat
lessons.lede: Hamzah and haa (ه) come from the deepest part of the throat, the part nearest the chest.

idea.lead: The throat has three makharij. The deepest, nearest the chest, gives two letters: hamzah and haa (ه). Ibn al-Jazari says: «ثُمَّ لِأَقْصَى الحَلْقِ هَمْزٌ هَاءُ» (then from the deepest throat, hamzah and haa). Hamzah is strong and voiced, and the sound stops on it; haa is soft and whispered, and the breath flows with it. They share one makhraj, and their characteristics tell them apart.
idea.kidsLead: From the deepest part of the throat, near the chest, come two letters: hamzah «أَءْ» and haa «أَهْ». Hamzah is a strong sound that stops; haa is light, with air coming out.

how.text: The deepest part of the throat: the farthest from the mouth and nearest the chest.
Said fully and clearly, strong and voiced: «أَءْ». Hafs softens it only in a few set places.
A faint, whispered letter that must be made clear, especially with sukun or when repeated: «عَلَيۡهِمۡ», «جِبَاهُهُمۡ».
Say the letter with sukun after a hamzah with fathah, with your hand on the base of your neck: «أَءْ», «أَهْ».

idea.note: Common mistakes: softening a full hamzah until it is close to alif, pushing it until it sounds like a cough, and hiding the haa or turning it into haa (ح). In the Mushaf the hamzah may sit on an alif «أ», under it «إ», on a waw or yaa, or alone «ء»; in all of these it comes from the deepest throat.

ayat.findHint: Find the hamzah and the haa in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: The haa in «هُوَ» and «ٱللَّهُ»
The hamzah in «أَحَدٌ»
Two hamzahs from the deepest throat, in «إِنَّ» and «ٱلۡإِنسَٰنَ»
A haa with sukun: made clear with a light whisper

ayat.tip: The hamzah at the start of «ٱهۡدِنَا» is a connecting hamzah, said only when starting there; it has its own lesson in level 3.

quiz.q: Where do hamzah and haa (ه) come from?
options: The deepest part of the throat
quiz.why: From the deepest part of the throat, nearest the chest.

quiz.q: Hamzah and haa share one makhraj. What tells them apart?
quiz.why: Hamzah is strong and voiced, haa is soft and whispered: their characteristics tell them apart.

quiz.q: In «قُلۡ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدٌ», how many letters come from the deepest throat?
quiz.why: The haa in «هُوَ», the haa in «ٱللَّهُ» and the hamzah in «أَحَدٌ»; the haa (ح) comes from the middle of the throat.

quiz.q: What is the mistake in saying the haa of «عَلَيۡهِمۡ»?
options: Hiding it until it is not heard
The sukun on the meem after it
quiz.why: Haa is a faint letter, so it must be made clear; hiding or swallowing it is a mistake.

quiz.q: Which makhraj does the hamzah of «إِنَّ» come from?
quiz.why: Hamzah comes from the deepest throat, whether it is written on the alif, under it or alone.

quiz.q: Which word has a haa with sukun that must be made clear?
quiz.why: The haa in «ٱهۡدِنَا» has sukun, so it needs to be made clear most.

quiz.q: What is wrong with reading «أَحَدٌ» with a weak hamzah close to alif?
quiz.why: This hamzah is full; softening it is a mistake in the riwayah of Hafs.

lessons.title: The middle of the throat
lessons.lede: 'Ayn and haa (ح) come from the middle of the throat.

formula.caption: Between the deepest and nearest parts

idea.lead: The middle of the throat is its second makhraj, and gives 'ayn and haa (ح). Ibn al-Jazari says: «ثُمَّ لِوَسْطِهِ فَعَيْنٌ حَاءُ» (then from its middle, 'ayn and haa). 'Ayn is voiced and in between strong and soft; haa (ح) is whispered and soft, and the breath flows with it. Both are low and light.
idea.kidsLead: From the middle of the throat come two letters: 'ayn «أَعْ» and haa «أَحْ». Air comes out with haa, and 'ayn has a stronger sound. Take care not to say «الهمد» instead of «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ».

how.text: The middle of the throat, between its deepest and nearest parts.
Voiced and in between: its sound neither stops fully nor flows fully. Do not turn it into hamzah or double it.
Whispered, soft and pure: do not turn it into haa (ه) or khaa, or make it hoarse.
Make 'ayn and haa (ح) clear when they have sukun: «نَعۡبُدُ», «وَٱنۡحَرۡ».

idea.note: Turning haa (ح) into haa (ه), or 'ayn into hamzah, is a clear mistake that changes the word, as in reading «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ» as «الهمد» and «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ» as «الألمين». 'Ayn and haa (ح) are letters of izhar of the throat (lesson 27).

ayat.findHint: Find the 'ayn and the haa (ح) in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: The haa (ح) in «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ»
The 'ayn in «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ»
An 'ayn with sukun: made clear from the middle of the throat
A haa (ح) with fathah: pure, not hoarse

ayat.tip: Compare «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ» with «هُوَ»: haa (ح) is from the middle of the throat and haa (ه) from its deepest part, and mixing them up changes the meaning.

quiz.q: Which two letters come from the middle of the throat?
quiz.why: 'Ayn and haa (ح) come from the middle of the throat.

quiz.q: Someone read «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ» with haa (ه). What is wrong?
options: Clear lahn: haa (ح), from the middle of the throat, became haa (ه), from its deepest part
quiz.why: One letter was said instead of another, from a different makhraj: this is clear lahn.

quiz.q: In «أَحَدٌ», where does the haa (ح) come from?
options: The deepest part of the throat
quiz.why: Haa (ح) comes from the middle of the throat; the hamzah before it comes from the deepest part.

quiz.q: Where does 'ayn stand between strong and soft letters?
quiz.why: 'Ayn is one of the in-between letters «لِنْ عُمَرْ»: its sound neither stops fully nor flows fully.

quiz.q: What is the 'ayn in «نَعۡبُدُ»?
options: It has sukun, made clear from the middle of the throat
quiz.why: The 'ayn has sukun, so it is made clear from its makhraj without turning into hamzah or being doubled.

quiz.q: Which of the two middle-throat letters is whispered?
quiz.why: Haa (ح) is whispered, with the breath flowing; 'ayn is voiced.

quiz.q: In «إِنَّآ أَعۡطَيۡنَٰكَ», where does the 'ayn come from?
options: The nearest part of the throat
quiz.why: 'Ayn comes from the middle of the throat; the two hamzahs before it come from the deepest part.

lessons.title: The nearest part of the throat
lessons.lede: Ghayn and khaa come from the nearest part of the throat, the part closest to the mouth.

idea.lead: The nearest part of the throat is its third makhraj and the closest to the mouth, and gives ghayn and khaa. Ibn al-Jazari says: «أَدْنَاهُ غَيْنٌ خَاؤُهَا» (its nearest part, ghayn and khaa). Both are elevated letters, so they are heavy; ghayn is voiced and khaa whispered, and both are soft.
idea.kidsLead: From the top of the throat, near the mouth, come two full letters: ghayn «أَغْ» and khaa «أَخْ». We say them with a full sound and never make them light.

how.text: The nearest part of the throat, the closest to the mouth.
Voiced, soft, elevated and heavy: «غَيۡرِ», «ٱلۡمَغۡضُوبِ».
Whispered, soft, elevated and heavy: «خُسۡرٍ», «خَلَقَ».
They are among «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ», so they are heavy in every case, least heavy with kasrah.

idea.note: Ghayn and khaa are the throat letters nearest the tongue, so some reciters hide the noon sakinah before them; Hafs says the noon clearly, as before the other throat letters: «مِنۡ غِلّٖ», «مِنۡ خَيۡرٖ». It is a mistake to say them so roughly that they sound like gargling.

ayat.findHint: Find the ghayn and the khaa in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: A ghayn with a vowel, then a ghayn with sukun, both heavy
Khaa from the nearest part of the throat, heavy
Ghayn with fathah followed by alif: the heaviest degree

ayat.tip: The alif after the ghayn in «غَاسِقٍ» follows it in heaviness; lesson 67 explains this.

quiz.q: Which throat letters are nearest the mouth?
quiz.why: Ghayn and khaa come from the top of the throat, nearest the mouth.

quiz.q: Which characteristic makes ghayn and khaa heavy?
quiz.why: They are elevated letters, and elevation makes a letter heavy.

quiz.q: Which of the two nearest-throat letters is voiced?
quiz.why: Ghayn is voiced; khaa is whispered, with the breath flowing.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read a noon sakinah before ghayn and khaa?
quiz.why: Hafs says it clearly before them, as before the other throat letters; some other reciters hide it.

quiz.q: How many ghayns are in «غَيۡرِ ٱلۡمَغۡضُوبِ»?
quiz.why: A ghayn with a vowel in «غَيۡرِ», and a ghayn with sukun in «ٱلۡمَغۡضُوبِ».

quiz.q: Where does the khaa of «خُسۡرٍ» come from?
options: The nearest part of the throat
quiz.why: Khaa comes from the nearest part of the throat, the closest to the mouth.

quiz.q: What is wrong with saying khaa light?
options: It drops the heaviness an elevated letter must have
quiz.why: Khaa is an elevated letter, so making it light is a mistake.

lessons.title: The back of the tongue
lessons.lede: Qaaf comes from the back of the tongue with the palate above it, and kaaf a little lower.

formula.caption: Back of the tongue with the palate

idea.lead: The back of the tongue, the part nearest the throat, has two neighbouring makharij: qaaf, from the back of the tongue with the palate above it, and kaaf, a little lower towards the mouth. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَالقَافُ أَقْصَى اللِّسَانِ فَوْقُ ثُمَّ الكَافُ، أَسْفَلُ» (qaaf is the back of the tongue, above, then kaaf, lower). They are called the uvular letters because they are near the uvula. Qaaf is elevated, voiced and has qalqalah; kaaf is low and whispered.
idea.kidsLead: Qaaf and kaaf come from the back of the tongue, near the throat. Qaaf is deeper and we say it full «أَقْ»; kaaf is nearer the mouth and we say it light, with a little air «أَكْ».

how.text: The back of the tongue with the palate above it. Heavy, with qalqalah when it has sukun: «ٱقۡرَأۡ».
A little lower than qaaf. Light, whispered and strong: a little breath comes out with it.
So called because they come from near the uvula, the flesh hanging at the back of the mouth.
«أَقْ» then «أَكْ»: you feel that kaaf is nearer the mouth.

idea.note: Common mistakes: saying qaaf as kaaf or hamzah, as in some dialects, or like the Cairene jeem; making qaaf light or kaaf heavy. Telling them apart changes the meaning: «قَلۡبٌ» (heart) is not «كَلۡبٌ» (dog).

ayat.findHint: Find the qaaf and the kaaf in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Qaaf from the back of the tongue with the palate
Kaaf a little lower than qaaf, light
A heavy qaaf, then a light kaaf, in one ayah

ayat.tip: Compare the qaaf in «قُلۡ» with the kaaf in «ٱلۡكَٰفِرُونَ»: both come from the back of the tongue, but qaaf is deeper and heavier.

quiz.q: Where does qaaf come from?
options: The back of the tongue, against the roof of the mouth
quiz.why: Qaaf comes from the back of the tongue; kaaf comes from a little lower.

quiz.q: Which letter comes a little lower than qaaf?
quiz.why: Kaaf is a little lower than qaaf, towards the mouth.

quiz.q: Why are qaaf and kaaf called the uvular letters?
options: Because they are near the uvula
Because they come from the throat
quiz.why: They come from the back of the tongue near the uvula.

quiz.q: Which of the two is heavy?
quiz.why: Qaaf is an elevated letter, so it is heavy; kaaf is low and light.

quiz.q: What is saying «قُلۡ» with a hamzah, «ؤُل»?
options: A clear mistake: one letter for another
quiz.why: Turning qaaf into hamzah replaces one letter with another, which is a clear mistake.

quiz.q: In «ٱلۡكَوۡثَرَ», where does the kaaf come from?
options: The back of the tongue, below qaaf
quiz.why: Kaaf comes from the back of the tongue, a little lower than qaaf.

quiz.q: In «ٱقۡرَأۡ», what happens to the qaaf with sukun?
quiz.why: Qaaf is a qalqalah letter, so it echoes when it has sukun.

lessons.title: The middle of the tongue
lessons.lede: Jeem, sheen and the non-madd yaa come from the middle of the tongue with the palate above it.

idea.lead: The middle of the tongue with the palate opposite it is the makhraj of three letters: jeem, sheen and the non-madd yaa. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَالوَسْطُ فَجِيمُ الشِّينُ يَا» (the middle: jeem, sheen, yaa). They are called shajariyyah, after the shajr of the mouth, its opening. Yaa comes from here when it has a vowel or has sukun after fathah; the madd yaa comes from the jawf.
idea.kidsLead: Three letters come from the middle of the tongue: jeem «أَجْ», sheen «أَشْ» and yaa «أَيْ». Raise the middle of your tongue towards the roof of your mouth and say them.

how.text: Strong, voiced, with qalqalah: the middle of the tongue presses the palate and leaves it firmly, without a soft «zh» sound or a touch of sheen.
Soft and whispered; the air spreads in the mouth, which is tafashshi.
The non-madd yaa: with a vowel «يَلِدۡ», or with sukun after fathah «قُرَيۡشٍ». Its makhraj is just after sheen.
The name of the three, because they come from the shajr of the mouth, between the jaws.

idea.note: Mistakes in jeem: saying it soft like sheen or the Levantine jeem, or like the Cairene jeem, and leaving out its qalqalah with sukun, as in «ٱلنَّجۡمِ». A mistake in sheen is losing its spreading until it sounds like seen.

ayat.findHint: Find jeem, sheen and the non-madd yaa in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Jeem from the middle of the tongue: strong, without a «zh» sound
The yaa with sukun after fathah, and the sheen, from the middle of the tongue
Sheen: the air spreads in the mouth

ayat.tip: The yaa in «لِإِيلَٰفِ» is not coloured, because it is a madd yaa from the jawf.

quiz.q: Which of these come from the middle of the tongue?
quiz.why: Jeem, sheen and yaa (when not a madd letter) come from the middle of the tongue, against the roof of the mouth.

quiz.q: In «قُرَيۡشٍ», where does the yaa come from?
quiz.why: The yaa has a sukun after a fathah, so it is not a madd letter: it comes from the middle of the tongue.

quiz.q: Why are jeem, sheen and yaa called shajariyyah?
options: Because they come from the shajr of the mouth
quiz.why: The shajr of the mouth is the space between the jaws, and these letters come from it.

quiz.q: Which of the three has qalqalah with sukun?
quiz.why: Jeem is one of «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ», so it echoes when it has sukun.

quiz.q: Which characteristic belongs to sheen?
quiz.why: Tafashshi is the air spreading in the mouth when saying sheen.

quiz.q: In «ٱلرَّحِيمِ», where does the yaa come from?
quiz.why: The yaa has sukun after kasrah, so it is a madd letter from the jawf, not from the middle of the tongue.

quiz.q: What is wrong with saying jeem soft, like sheen?
options: It loses the strength and voice of jeem
quiz.why: Jeem is strong and voiced; softening it loses this until it sounds close to sheen.

lessons.title: The sides of the tongue
lessons.lede: Daad comes from the side of the tongue with the upper molars, and laam from the front of the side to the very tip.

formula.caption: Front of the side to the tip
The two sides of the tongue

idea.lead: The tongue has two sides, and they give two makharij. Daad comes from one side of the tongue, or both, with the upper molars beside it; the left side is easier and more common. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَالضَّادُ مِنْ حَافَتِهِ إِذْ وَلِيَا، الاضْرَاسَ مِنْ أَيْسَرَ أَوْ يُمْنَاهَا» (daad from its side, next to the molars, left or right). Laam comes from the front of the side of the tongue to its very tip, with the palate beside it: «وَاللَّامُ أَدْنَاهَا لِمُنْتَهَاهَا» (and laam from its front to its end).
idea.kidsLead: Two letters come from the sides of the tongue: daad, where we put the side of the tongue on the upper molars and its sound stretches «أَضْ», and laam, from the front of the side to the tip «أَلْ».

how.text: From the side with the upper molars; the left side is easier and more common, and both sides together is allowed.
The sound of daad stretches along the side until it reaches the makhraj of laam; this sets daad apart.
From the front of the side to the very tip of the tongue, with the gums of the front teeth beside it.
In laam: the tongue leans with it towards its tip.

idea.note: Daad has the hardest makhraj of all the letters. It is a mistake to say it as a heavy dal or as dhaa (ظ); it has its own lesson with dhaa (lesson 73). Laam is light except in the name Allah after fathah or dammah (lesson 71).

ayat.findHint: Find the daad and the laam in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: The daad in «ٱلۡمَغۡضُوبِ» and «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ», from the side with the molars
The laam, from the front of the side to the tip
A light laam with sukun
Two light laams, the second with shaddah

ayat.tip: The laam of «ال» in «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ» is not said, because it is a sun laam; the daad after it is doubled.

quiz.q: Where does daad come from?
options: The tip of the tongue, with the front teeth
One or both sides of the tongue, against the upper molars
quiz.why: Daad comes from the side of the tongue; the left side is easier and more common.

quiz.q: Which side do most people find easier for daad?
quiz.why: The left side is easier and more common; the right, or both, is also allowed.

quiz.q: Where does laam come from?
options: The front of the side of the tongue to its tip
quiz.why: Laam comes from the front of the side of the tongue to its tip, with the palate beside it.

quiz.q: Which characteristic belongs to daad alone?
quiz.why: Istitalah is the sound of daad stretching along the side of the tongue.

quiz.q: What is wrong with saying «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ» with a heavy dal?
quiz.why: Daad is a letter of its own, with its makhraj and extension; saying it as a heavy dal or dhaa is a mistake.

quiz.q: Which characteristic of laam makes the tongue lean towards its tip?
quiz.why: Inhiraf is in laam and raa: the letter leans after it starts, towards the tip or the back of the tongue.

quiz.q: Is the laam in «قُلۡ» heavy or light?
quiz.why: Laam is always light, except the laam of the name Allah after fathah or dammah.

lessons.title: The tip of the tongue: laam, noon and raa
lessons.lede: The tip of the tongue has three neighbouring makharij: laam, then noon a little below it, then raa near noon, with the top of the tongue.

formula.caption: Front of the side to the tip
The tip, a little below laam
The tip with the top of the tongue

idea.lead: Laam, noon and raa are the dhalaqiyyah letters, from the dhalaq of the tongue, its tip. Laam comes from the front of the side of the tongue to its tip; noon from the tip of the tongue with the gums of the upper front teeth, a little below laam; and raa from the makhraj of noon, but a little further onto the top of the tongue. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَالنُّونُ مِنْ طَرَفِهِ تَحْتُ اجْعَلُوا، وَالرَّا يُدَانِيهِ لِظَهْرٍ أَدْخَلُ» (noon from its tip, below; and raa is near it, further onto the top). Al-Farra' and those who follow him count them as one makhraj.
idea.kidsLead: Three letters come from the tip of the tongue, close together: laam «أَلْ», noon «أَنْ» with a ghunnah from the nose, and raa «أَرْ», said without rolling the tongue much.

how.text: The widest of the three: from the front of the side to the very tip.
From the tip of the tongue with the gums of the upper front teeth, a little below laam, with ghunnah from the nose.
From the tip of the tongue, a little further onto its top; it has takrir, which is learned so it can be avoided.
The three are called dhalaqiyyah because they come from the dhalaq of the tongue, its tip.

idea.note: Because these makharij are close, noon sakinah and tanween merge into laam and raa without ghunnah (lesson 29), and a laam with sukun merges into raa, as in «قُل رَّبِّ» (lesson 78).

ayat.findHint: Find laam, noon and raa in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: A laam with sukun, then raa, then a noon with shaddah
Two laams and a noon with sukun
Two raas, the second with sukun
Two noons, the first with shaddah and ghunnah
A raa with fathah

ayat.tip: The noon with shaddah in «إِنَّآ» and «ٱلنَّاسِ» comes from the tip of the tongue with a full ghunnah from the nose.

quiz.q: Which are the dhalaqiyyah letters?
quiz.why: Laam, noon and raa come from the dhalaq of the tongue, its tip.

quiz.q: Where is the makhraj of noon compared with laam?
quiz.why: Noon comes from the tip of the tongue, a little below laam.

quiz.q: How does the makhraj of raa differ from noon?
options: The top of the tongue joins in a little
quiz.why: Raa is near the makhraj of noon, but further onto the top of the tongue.

quiz.q: Who counted laam, noon and raa as one makhraj?
quiz.why: Al-Farra' and those who follow him count them as one; Ibn al-Jazari's choice is three makharij.

quiz.q: Which characteristic of raa is learned so it can be avoided?
quiz.why: Takrir is the tip of the tongue trembling with raa; it is learned so it is not overdone.

quiz.q: What goes with noon when it is said?
quiz.why: Noon comes with a ghunnah from the nose.

quiz.q: Why do noon sakinah and tanween merge into laam and raa?
options: Because the makharij are far apart
quiz.why: The closeness of the makharij of laam, noon and raa is why they merge.

lessons.title: The tip of the tongue with the front teeth
lessons.lede: The tip of the tongue with the front teeth has three makharij: taa (ط), dal and taa; then saad, seen and zay; then dhaa (ظ), dhal and thaa.

formula.caption: Nit'iyyah: with the roots of the upper front teeth
Asaliyyah: above the lower front teeth
Lithawiyyah: with the edges of the upper front teeth

idea.lead: Nine letters come from the tip of the tongue, in three makharij. Taa (ط), dal and taa come from the tip of the tongue with the roots of the upper front teeth; they are called nit'iyyah, after the nit' of the mouth (the ridge behind the teeth). Saad, seen and zay come from the tip of the tongue just above the lower front teeth, leaving a small gap for the whistle; they are called asaliyyah. Dhaa (ظ), dhal and thaa come from the tip of the tongue with the edges of the upper front teeth; they are called lithawiyyah. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَالطَّاءُ وَالدَّالُ وَتَا مِنْهُ وَمِنْ، عُلْيَا الثَّنَايَا وَالصَّفِيرُ مُسْتَكِنْ، مِنْهُ وَمِنْ فَوْقِ الثَّنَايَا السُّفْلَى، وَالظَّاءُ وَالذَّالُ وَثَا لِلْعُلْيَا».
idea.kidsLead: Nine letters come from the tip of the tongue with the front teeth: for «ط د ت» put the tip of the tongue at the roots of the upper teeth; «ص س ز» come with a whistle; for «ظ ذ ث» the tip of the tongue shows a little under the upper teeth.

how.text: Taa (ط), dal and taa: the tip of the tongue with the roots of the upper front teeth. Taa (ط) is heavy; dal and taa are light.
Saad, seen and zay: the tip of the tongue just above the lower front teeth, with a whistle. Saad is heavy.
Dhaa (ظ), dhal and thaa: the tip of the tongue with the edges of the upper front teeth, so the tip shows a little. Dhaa (ظ) is heavy.
Taa (ط), saad and dhaa (ظ) are covered and heavy; their partners in the same makhraj are light, and their characteristics tell them apart.

idea.note: Common mistakes: saying thaa as seen or taa, dhal as zay or dal, and dhaa (ظ) as a heavy zay, as in many dialects. This replaces one letter with another and changes the meaning; lesson 21 explains the letters that sound alike.

ayat.legendNext: Dhaa, dhal, thaa; saad, seen, zay
ayat.findHint: Find the letters of the tip of the tongue with the front teeth in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

Dhal from the edges of the upper front teeth
Taa is nit'iyyah
Seen from above the lower front teeth, with a whistle

quiz.why: For dhaa (ظ), dhaal and thaa, the tip of the tongue touches the edges of the upper front teeth.

quiz.q: Which are the nit'iyyah letters?
quiz.why: Taa (ط), dal and taa come from the tip of the tongue with the roots of the upper front teeth, near the nit' of the mouth.

quiz.q: Which letters come with a whistle?
quiz.why: Saad, seen and zay are the whistling letters, from the tip of the tongue above the lower front teeth.

quiz.q: In which letters does the tip of the tongue show a little?
quiz.why: Dhaa (ظ), dhal and thaa: the tip of the tongue comes to the edges of the upper front teeth.

quiz.q: Which nit'iyyah letter is heavy?
quiz.why: Taa (ط) is elevated, covered and heavy; dal and taa (ت) are light.

quiz.q: What is wrong with saying «ذَٰلِكَ» with zay, «zalika»?

quiz.why: Dhal comes from the edges of the upper front teeth and zay from above the lower ones; mixing them is a clear mistake.

quiz.why: Taa and dal come from the tip of the tongue with the roots of the upper front teeth.

lessons.title: The lips
lessons.lede: The lips have two makharij for four letters: faa, from the inside of the lower lip with the edges of the upper front teeth, and waw, baa and meem, from between the lips.

formula.caption: The lower lip with the upper front teeth

idea.lead: The lips have two makharij. The first is the inside of the lower lip with the edges of the upper front teeth, which gives faa. The second is between the lips, which gives the non-madd waw, with the lips open, and baa and meem, with the lips closed. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَمِنْ بَطْنِ الشَّفَهْ فَالفَا مَعَ اطْرَافِ الثَّنَايَا المُشْرِفَهْ، لِلشَّفَتَيْنِ الوَاوُ بَاءٌ مِيمُ». These four are called the labial letters.
idea.kidsLead: For faa we put our upper teeth on the lower lip: «أَفْ». For baa and meem we close the lips: «أَبْ», «أَمْ». For waw we round the lips: «أَوْ».

how.text: From the inside of the lower lip with the edges of the upper front teeth: «أَفْ».
When not a madd letter: from between the lips, rounded and a little open: «أَوْ».
From between the lips, closed; baa closes them more firmly: «أَبْ», «أَمْ».
The four letters are called labial, and the rules of meem sakinah take their names from this (lessons 32–35).

idea.note: The madd waw, as in «يَقُولُ», comes from the jawf, not the lips (lesson 10). Common mistakes: saying faa from between the lips, pressing meem until it is close to baa, and rounding the lips too hard for waw.

ayat.findHint: Find the letters of the lips in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

Baa, and waw with a vowel, come from between the lips
Meem and baa come from between the lips
The faa in «كَيۡفَ» and «فَعَلَ» comes from the lower lip with the upper front teeth
Baa and meem come from between the lips: one baa and three meems

ayat.tip: The yaa in «ٱلرَّحِيمِ» is not coloured: it is a madd letter from the jawf. The waw in «وَٱنۡحَرۡ» has a vowel, so it comes from the lips.

quiz.q: How many makharij do the lips have?
quiz.why: Two: the inside of the lower lip with the front teeth for faa, and between the lips for waw, baa and meem.

quiz.q: Where does faa come from?
options: The inside of the lower lip with the edges of the upper front teeth
quiz.why: Faa comes from the inside of the lower lip with the edges of the upper front teeth.

quiz.q: Which letters come from between the lips?
quiz.why: Waw (when not a madd letter), baa and meem come from between the lips.

quiz.q: Which letter closes the lips more firmly?
quiz.why: Baa and meem both close the lips, but baa more firmly.

quiz.q: In «يَقُولُ», where does the waw come from?
quiz.why: The waw has a sukun after a dammah, so it is a madd letter from the jawf.

quiz.q: Which are the labial letters?
quiz.why: Four: faa from the inside of the lower lip, and waw, baa and meem from between the lips.

quiz.q: How does the non-madd waw come from the lips?
options: With the lips rounded and a little open
From the inside of the lower lip
quiz.why: Waw comes with the lips rounded and a little open; baa and meem with the lips closed.

lessons.title: The nose (khayshum)
lessons.lede: The khayshum is the far end of the nose. Ghunnah comes from it: a sound that goes with noon and meem.

formula.caption: The far end of the nose

idea.lead: The khayshum is the passage of the nose that opens into the back of the mouth. It is the seventeenth makhraj for Ibn al-Jazari, and ghunnah comes from it. He says: «وَغُنَّةٌ مَخْرَجُهَا الخَيْشُومُ» (and ghunnah, its makhraj is the khayshum). Ghunnah is a nasal sound built into noon and meem; the tongue plays no part in it, and if the nose is held it stops. It is clearest in noon and meem with shaddah, and in idgham with ghunnah, ikhfa' and iqlab.
idea.kidsLead: Ghunnah is a lovely sound that comes from the nose with noon and meem. Hold your nose and say «إِنَّ»: you feel that the sound needs the nose. That is the khayshum.

how.text: The far end of the nose; ghunnah comes from it alone.
A fixed characteristic of noon and meem, even with a vowel or a clear sukun, but in some places it is full and longer.
Noon comes from the tip of the tongue and meem from the lips; the ghunnah with them comes from the khayshum.
Hold your nose and say «أَمْ», then let go: you hear the difference, and so you know ghunnah comes from the khayshum.

idea.note: In ikhfa' and idgham with ghunnah, the makhraj of noon almost disappears and only its sound from the khayshum remains, so scholars say its makhraj is then the khayshum. Lessons 36 and 37 explain how long the ghunnah is and its degrees.

ayat.findHint: Find the places of ghunnah in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: A noon with shaddah: a full ghunnah from the khayshum
A meem with shaddah: a full ghunnah
A noon sakinah hidden before sheen: ghunnah from the khayshum

ayat.tip: Listen to the reciter: the ghunnah of noon and meem with shaddah lasts two counts.

quiz.q: Where does ghunnah come from?
quiz.why: Ghunnah comes from the khayshum, the back of the nose.

quiz.q: What is the khayshum?
quiz.why: The khayshum is the back of the nose, where ghunnah comes from.

quiz.q: Which two letters have ghunnah?
quiz.why: Ghunnah is a sound built into noon and meem.

quiz.q: What happens to the ghunnah if the nose is held?
quiz.why: Ghunnah comes from the khayshum, so holding the nose stops it.

quiz.q: Does the tongue play a part in ghunnah?
quiz.why: Ghunnah comes from the khayshum alone; the tongue plays no part in it.

quiz.q: Which word has a full, clear ghunnah?
quiz.why: The noon with shaddah in «إِنَّآ» has a full ghunnah from the khayshum.

quiz.q: For many scholars, what is the makhraj of noon in ikhfa'?
quiz.why: In ikhfa' the tongue's part in noon goes, and its sound remains from the khayshum.

lessons.title: Letters that sound alike
lessons.lede: Some letters are close in makhraj or in sound, so beginners mix them up. Saying one instead of another is clear lahn, and it can change the meaning.

idea.lead: A beginner's most common mistake is saying one letter instead of another that sounds like it: «عَصَى» (he disobeyed) is not «عَسَى» (perhaps), and «التِّين» (figs) is not «الطِّين» (clay). There are several kinds. A light and a heavy letter from the same or a nearby makhraj: seen and saad, taa (ت) and taa (ط), dhaal and dhaa (ظ), kaaf and qaaf. Throat letters close to each other: hamzah and 'ayn, haa (ه) and haa (ح). Letters from the tip of the tongue and the front teeth: thaa and seen, dhaal and zay. What sets them apart is their makhraj or their characteristics (sifat).
idea.kidsLead: Some letters sound alike, so we listen carefully: «س» is light and «ص» is full; «ت» is light and «ط» is full; «ك» is light and «ق» comes from the back of the tongue. If we say one instead of the other, the meaning changes: «عَصَى» is not «عَسَى».

how.text: The same makhraj: saad is heavy and covered, seen is light. «عَصَى» is not «عَسَى».
The same makhraj: taa (ط) is heavy and covered, taa (ت) is light. «التِّين» is not «الطِّين».
Dhaal is light and dhaa (ظ) is heavy, from the same makhraj. Daad comes from the side of the tongue: do not say it as dhaa (ظ) or as a heavy dal.
Qaaf comes from deeper in the back of the tongue than kaaf, and it is heavy; kaaf is light.
'Ayn and haa (ح) come from the middle of the throat; hamzah and haa (ه) from its deepest part. Do not say 'ayn as a hamzah, or haa (ح) as haa (ه).
For thaa and dhaal, the tip of the tongue touches the edges of the upper front teeth; seen and zay come from just above the lower front teeth, with a whistle.

idea.note: Two letters from the same makhraj differ in their characteristics (sifat): lesson 22 and lessons 55–63 cover them. Daad and dhaa (ظ) have their own lesson in level 3, since mistakes in them are so common.

ayat.findHint: Find the heavy letters and their light twins in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Saad, taa (ط) and qaaf are heavy
Seen and taa (ت) are light: they are the light twins of saad and taa (ط)
Saad and taa (ط) are heavy
Dhaal is the light twin of dhaa (ظ), and taa (ت) of taa (ط)
Qaaf is heavy, from the back of the tongue
Kaaf is light, a little lower than qaaf

options: Saad is heavy and seen is light, and the meanings differ
quiz.why: «عَصَى» means "he disobeyed", and «عَسَى» means "perhaps": the difference is a heavy saad and a light seen.

quiz.q: Which light letter is like taa (ط) and comes from the same makhraj?
quiz.why: Taa (ط) and taa (ت) share a makhraj: the first is heavy and the second light.

quiz.why: Dhaa (ظ), dhaal and thaa share a makhraj; only dhaa (ظ) is heavy.

quiz.q: Reading «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ» with a hamzah in place of the 'ayn is:
quiz.why: The 'ayn became a hamzah: one letter instead of another, so it is clear lahn.

quiz.q: Where do thaa and dhaal come from?
options: Just above the lower front teeth
The tip of the tongue against the edges of the upper front teeth
quiz.why: For both, the tip of the tongue touches the edges of the upper front teeth, unlike seen and zay.

lessons.title: Characteristics of the letters (sifat): an introduction
lessons.lede: A sifah is the way a letter comes out of its makhraj. The makhraj fixes where a letter comes from; its sifat set it apart from the letters that share that makhraj.

idea.lead: In Arabic, a sifah is a quality something has. As a term, it is the way a letter comes out of its makhraj: whether the breath flows or stops, whether the sound flows or stops, whether the tongue rises or stays low, and so on. Ibn al-Jazari lists seventeen in his chapter on the sifat: five with opposites, making ten, and seven without. He says: «صِفَاتُهَا جَهْرٌ وَرِخْوٌ مُسْتَفِلْ، مُنْفَتِحٌ مُصْمَتَةٌ وَالضِّدَّ قُلْ» (its sifat are jahr, rikhwah, istifal, infitah and ismat; and name their opposites).
idea.kidsLead: Every letter has a place it comes from, and qualities that make its sound different: strong or weak, with the breath flowing or held, full or light. «ت», «د» and «ط» come from the same place, but their qualities make each one a different letter.

how.text: To tell apart letters that share a makhraj: taa (ت), dal and taa (ط) come from one makhraj and differ by their sifat.
To say each letter well, and to know the strong letters from the weak, giving each its due.
Five: hams (breath flows) and jahr; shiddah (sound stops) and rikhawah, with tawassut between them; isti'la' (tongue rises) and istifal; itbaq (tongue covers) and infitah; idhlaq and ismat.
Seven: safir (whistle), qalqalah, leen, inhiraf, takrir (rolling), tafashshi (spreading) and istitalah (lengthening).
Taa (ت) is mahmus, shadid, mustafil, munfatih and musmat; taa (ط) is majhur, shadid, musta'li, mutbaq, musmat and has qalqalah. That is why taa (ط) is heavy.

idea.note: Every letter has five sifat from the pairs with opposites, one from each pair, and may have some of those without opposites too. Those who count seventeen do not count tawassut, between shiddah and rikhawah, separately; others do. Level 3 covers each sifah (lessons 55–60).

quiz.q: What is a sifah, as a term?
options: The way a letter comes out of its makhraj
quiz.why: The makhraj is where a letter comes from; its sifah is how it comes out.

quiz.q: What is the main use of knowing the sifat?
options: Telling apart letters that share a makhraj
Knowing how many letters there are
quiz.why: Only their sifat set apart letters that come from the same makhraj.

quiz.q: How many sifat does Ibn al-Jazari list?
quiz.why: Seventeen: ten in five pairs of opposites, and seven without opposites.

quiz.q: How many sifat have an opposite?
quiz.why: Five sifat have opposites: with their opposites, they make ten.

quiz.q: Which of these has no opposite?
quiz.why: Qalqalah is one of the seven sifat without an opposite.

quiz.q: What is the opposite of isti'la'?
quiz.why: Isti'la' is raising the back of the tongue; its opposite, istifal, is keeping it low.

quiz.q: Why is taa (ط) heavy and taa (ت) light?
quiz.why: They share a makhraj; the difference is in their sifat: taa (ط) is musta'li and mutbaq, taa (ت) is mustafil and munfatih.

lessons.title: Qalqalah (echo)
lessons.lede: Qalqalah is the makhraj shaking when one of the letters of «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ» is said with sukun, so that a strong bounce is heard.

idea.lead: In Arabic, qalqalah means shaking and moving. As a term, it is the makhraj shaking when a letter is said with sukun, so that a strong bounce is heard. Its letters are five, gathered in «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ». They echo because they are both voiced and strong: being voiced holds the breath, and being strong holds the sound, so a letter with sukun needs its makhraj to open for it to be heard. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَبَيِّنَنْ مُقَلْقَلًا إِنْ سَكَنَا» (make the qalqalah letter clear when it has sukun).
idea.kidsLead: The five qalqalah letters are gathered in «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ». When one of them has sukun, we say it with a sound that bounces a little, as if it jumps, as in «يَلِدْ» and «ٱقْرَأْ».

how.text: Five: qaaf, taa (ط), baa, jeem and dal, gathered in «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ».
The letter must have a sukun; with a vowel, there is no qalqalah.
They are voiced and strong: neither breath nor sound flows with them, so without qalqalah a letter with sukun would not be heard.
A short bounce, without giving the letter a vowel: add no hamzah and no full vowel after it.

idea.note: Qalqalah is a fixed characteristic of these letters, but it shows with sukun, and its strength depends on where the letter is, as lesson 24 explains. Scholars differ on how it sounds: some say it follows the vowel before it, others that it is closer to fathah.

ayat.findHint: Find the letters of «قطب جد» in each ayah: which have sukun and echo? Then bring the colours back to check.

why: The qaaf has sukun: it echoes
The dal has sukun in «يَلِدۡ» and «يُولَدۡ»: it echoes
The qaaf and baa have vowels: no qalqalah

ayat.tip: A letter with a vowel has no qalqalah, even if it is one of «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ».

letters.title: The five qalqalah letters
letters.hint: All the letters of these two words are the qalqalah letters.

quiz.q: Which two words gather the qalqalah letters?
quiz.why: The five qalqalah letters are gathered in «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ».

quiz.q: When is there qalqalah?
options: When the letter has a sukun
quiz.why: There is qalqalah only in a letter with sukun, mid-reading or when stopping.

quiz.q: Why do these letters have qalqalah?
options: They have both jahr and shiddah
quiz.why: Jahr holds the breath and shiddah holds the sound, so a letter with sukun needs its makhraj to open to be heard.

quiz.q: Does the baa in «تَبَّتۡ» have qalqalah?
quiz.why: The doubled baa in «تَبَّتۡ» has a fathah, and qalqalah is only in a letter with sukun.

quiz.q: Hamzah is voiced and strong. Is it a qalqalah letter?
options: No, because echoing it is heavy
quiz.why: Hamzah is voiced and strong, but scholars left it out of the qalqalah letters because echoing it is heavy; a few counted it.

quiz.q: What is wrong with echoing the dal of «يَلِدۡ» until it becomes «يَلِدَ»?
options: Giving a letter with sukun a full vowel
quiz.why: Qalqalah is a short bounce; if it becomes a full vowel, the word changes.

quiz.q: Which word has qalqalah?
quiz.why: The qaaf has sukun in «ٱقۡرَأۡ». The baa in «تَبَّتۡ» and «نَعۡبُدُ» has a vowel, and 'ayn is not a qalqalah letter.

lessons.title: The degrees of qalqalah
lessons.lede: Qalqalah has degrees: light for a letter with sukun inside the words, strong when stopping, and strongest for a doubled letter at a stop.

formula.caption: A doubled letter at a stop

idea.lead: Qalqalah varies in strength with where the letter is. A letter with its own sukun inside the words has a light qalqalah; a letter that takes sukun because of a stop has a strong one; and it is strongest when the letter is doubled and you stop on it. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَإِنْ يَكُنْ فِي الوَقْفِ كَانَ أَبْيَنَا» (and if it is at a stop, it is clearer). Qalqalah is also stronger in qaaf and taa (ط), because they are elevated.
idea.kidsLead: Qalqalah is not always equally strong: inside the words it is light, when stopping it is clearer, and when we stop on a doubled letter, as in «وَتَبَّ», it is the strongest.

how.text: When the letter has a sukun in the middle of the reading, as in «يَلِدۡ» and «ٱقۡرَأۡ».
When the letter takes a sukun because you stop on it, as when stopping on «ٱلۡفَلَقِ» or «خَلَقَ».
A doubled letter you stop on, as when stopping on «وَتَبَّ» or «بِٱلۡحَقِّ».
Taa (ط) echoes most, then qaaf, because they are elevated; then baa, jeem and dal.

idea.note: Scholars differ on the number of degrees: some count two, strong and light; some count three, giving the doubled letter at a stop its own degree; and some count more. At every degree, qalqalah never becomes a full vowel.

ayat.findHint: Find the letters of «قطب جد» with sukun in each ayah: mid-reading, or when stopping? Then bring the colours back to check.

why: The dal in «يَلِدۡ» has sukun and the reading goes on: minor qalqalah
The dal in «يُولَدۡ» ends the ayah: major qalqalah when stopping
The qaaf in «ٱقۡرَأۡ» has sukun: minor qalqalah
The qaaf in «خَلَقَ» takes a sukun when stopping: major qalqalah
The doubled baa in «وَتَبَّ» when stopping: the strongest qalqalah

ayat.tip: The baa in «تَبَّتۡ» has a vowel, so it has no qalqalah. When stopping on «وَتَبَّ», the baa takes a sukun: it has the strongest qalqalah, since it is doubled.

quiz.q: In «لَمۡ يَلِدۡ وَلَمۡ يُولَدۡ», what degree is the qalqalah in «يَلِدۡ»?
quiz.why: The dal has a sukun in the middle of the reading, so its qalqalah is minor.

quiz.q: When stopping on «ٱلۡفَلَقِ», the qalqalah is:
quiz.why: The qaaf takes a sukun for the stop, so its qalqalah is major.

quiz.q: Which word has the strongest qalqalah when stopping?
quiz.why: The baa is doubled and you stop on it: the strongest degree.

quiz.q: What is the degree of qalqalah in «ٱقۡرَأۡ»?
quiz.why: The qaaf has its own sukun inside the word, so its qalqalah is light.

quiz.q: When is qalqalah strong?
options: When the letter takes sukun for a stop
When the letter has a vowel
quiz.why: When a qalqalah letter takes sukun because of a stop, its qalqalah is strong.

quiz.q: Which two letters echo more strongly than the others?
quiz.why: Taa (ط) and qaaf echo most, because they are elevated as well as voiced and strong.

quiz.q: What is the degree of qalqalah when stopping on «بِٱلۡحَقِّ»?
quiz.why: The qaaf is doubled and you stop on it, so it is the strongest degree.

lessons.title: The sun and moon laam
lessons.lede: The laam of «ال» ("the") is said clearly before fourteen letters, called the moon letters, and merges into the other fourteen, called the sun letters.

idea.lead: The laam of «ال» ("the") is an extra laam with sukun added to a noun. It has two cases, depending on the letter after it. Before the moon letters, the fourteen gathered in «ابْغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ», it is said clearly, with sukun, as in «ٱلۡقَمَرِ» (the moon): this is izhar. Before the sun letters, the other fourteen, it is not said, and the letter after it is doubled, as in «ٱلشَّمۡسِ» (the sun): this is idgham. The author of Tuhfat al-Atfal says: «لِلَامِ أَلْ حَالَانِ قَبْلَ الأَحْرُفِ، أُولَاهُمَا إِظْهَارُهَا فَلْتَعْرِفِ» (the laam of al has two cases before the letters; the first is izhar, so know it).
idea.kidsLead: «ال» at the start of a word has two cases. With the moon letters, we say the laam clearly: «ٱلْقَمَر». With the sun letters, we hide the laam and double the letter after it: «ٱلشَّمْس», just as the sun's light hides the stars.

how.text: Fourteen letters, gathered in «ابْغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ»: the laam before them is said, with sukun: «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ».
The other fourteen, «ط ث ص ر ت ض ذ ن د س ظ ز ش ل»: the laam merges into them: «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ».
In the Mushaf, the moon laam has a sukun; the sun laam has no mark, and the letter after it has a shaddah.
The hamzah of «ال» is a joining hamzah: it is said with fathah when starting, and dropped when joining, as in «وَٱلشَّمۡسِ».
This rule is only for the laam of «ال»: a laam that belongs to the word is always said, as in «أَلۡسِنَتُهُمۡ» and «قُلۡ نَعَمۡ».

idea.note: The names come from the two words: the moon, «ٱلۡقَمَرِ», where the laam is said, and the sun, «ٱلشَّمۡسِ», where it merges. Laam is itself a sun letter: in «ٱللَّيۡلِ», the laam of «ال» merges into the laam after it.

ayat.findHint: Find «ال» in each ayah: is its laam said, or is the letter after it doubled? Then bring the colours back to check.

why: The laam before meem is a moon laam: it is said
The laam before daad is a sun laam: it is not said, and the daad is doubled
The laam before sheen is a sun laam: it is not said, and the sheen is doubled
The laam before meem is a moon laam: it is said
The laam before raa is a sun laam: it is not said, and the raa is doubled

ayat.tip: A sukun on the laam shows it is a moon laam and is said; a shaddah on the letter after it shows it is a sun laam.

letters.title: The moon letters
letters.hint: All the letters of this phrase are moon letters; the rest of the alphabet are sun letters. Alif here stands for hamzah.

quiz.q: How many moon letters are there?
quiz.why: Fourteen, gathered in «ابْغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ».

quiz.q: What happens to the laam of «ال» before a moon letter?
quiz.why: Before the moon letters, the laam is said clearly, with sukun.

quiz.q: What happens to the laam in «ٱلشَّمۡسِ»?
options: Idgham: it is not said, and the sheen is doubled
quiz.why: Sheen is a sun letter, so the laam merges into it.

quiz.q: Which word has a moon laam?
quiz.why: Qaaf is a moon letter, so the laam before it is said, and it has a sukun.

quiz.q: How do you spot a sun laam in the Mushaf?
options: It has no mark, and the letter after it has a shaddah
quiz.why: A sun laam has no mark, since it is not said; the letter after it has a shaddah.

quiz.q: What happens to the laam of «ال» in «ٱللَّيۡلِ»?
quiz.why: Laam is a sun letter, so the laam of «ال» merges into the laam after it.

quiz.q: Seen is a sun letter: what happens to the laam in «أَلۡسِنَتُهُمۡ»?
options: It is said: it belongs to the word, it is not the laam of «ال»
It merges, since seen is a sun letter
quiz.why: The sun and moon rule is only for the laam of «ال»; this laam belongs to the word, so it is said.
