lessons.title: Noon sakinah and tanween: an introduction
lessons.lede: A noon sakinah is a noon with no vowel; tanween is an extra noon sakinah at the end of a noun. They have four rules, depending on the letter after them.

idea.lead: A noon sakinah is a noon with no vowel. It is both said and written, and it stays when joining and when stopping. It comes in nouns, verbs and particles, in the middle or at the end of a word, as in «أَنۡعَمۡتَ» and «مِنۡ». Tanween is an extra noon sakinah at the end of a noun: it is said but not written as a noon, and it stays when joining but drops when stopping. They have four rules, depending on the letter after them. The author of Tuhfat al-Atfal says: «لِلنُّونِ إِنْ تَسْكُنْ وَلِلتَّنْوِينِ، أَرْبَعُ أَحْكَامٍ فَخُذْ تَبْيِينِي» (noon sakinah and tanween have four rules, so take my explanation).
idea.kidsLead: A noon sakinah is a noon with a sukun «نْ». Tanween is two vowel marks with a little noon sound «ـٌ». We look at the letter after them to know how to read them: say the noon clearly, merge it into the next letter, turn it into a meem, or hide it.

how.text: A noon sakinah is written and stays when stopping; it comes in nouns, verbs and particles. Tanween is not written as a noon, drops when stopping, and comes only at the end of a noun.
Before the six throat letters «ء ه ع ح غ خ». Lesson 27.
Into the six letters of «يَرْمَلُونَ»: with ghunnah into «يَنْمُو», without ghunnah into laam and raa. Lessons 28 and 29.
Before baa alone. Lesson 30.
Before the other fifteen letters. Lesson 31.

idea.note: The Mushaf's marks show the rule: a sukun on the noon, and stacked tanween marks, for izhar; no sukun and a shaddah on the next letter for full idgham; no sukun and no shaddah for partial idgham and ikhfa'; a small meem for iqlab. In ikhfa' and idgham, tanween is written as two marks one after the other.

ayat.findHint: Find the noon sakinah and the tanween in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Two noon sakinahs, in «مِّن» and «مِّنۡ»
Tanween in «جُوعٖ» and «خَوۡفِۭ»
A noon sakinah at the end of the verb «يَكُن»
Tanween in «كُفُوًا» and «أَحَدُۢ»
Tanween in «وَيۡلٞ» and «هُمَزَةٖ»

ayat.tip: Before a letter of izhar, the noon sakinah has a sukun: «مِّنۡ خَوۡفِۭ». Before other letters, it is written without one: «مِّن جُوعٖ».

quiz.q: How many rules do noon sakinah and tanween have?
quiz.why: Four: izhar, idgham, iqlab and ikhfa'.

quiz.q: How do noon sakinah and tanween differ when stopping?
options: The noon stays and the tanween drops
The noon drops and the tanween stays
quiz.why: The noon sakinah stays when stopping; the tanween drops, and after a fathah it becomes an alif.

quiz.q: Where does tanween come?
options: Only at the end of a noun
At the start of a word
quiz.why: Tanween comes only at the end of a noun; a noon sakinah comes in nouns, verbs and particles.

quiz.q: What decides the rule for noon sakinah and tanween?
quiz.why: The rule depends on the letter that comes after the noon sakinah or tanween.

quiz.q: What is the rule for noon sakinah before baa?
quiz.why: Before baa, the noon turns into a hidden meem, with ghunnah.

quiz.q: How many letters of ikhfa' are there?
quiz.why: Fifteen: the letters left after those of izhar, idgham and iqlab.

quiz.q: In the Mushaf, a sukun on the noon shows:
quiz.why: The noon has a sukun before the letters of izhar, and none with the other rules.

lessons.title: Izhar (clear)
lessons.lede: When one of the six throat letters comes after a noon sakinah or tanween, the noon is said clearly from its makhraj, without extra ghunnah.

idea.lead: In Arabic, izhar means making clear. As a term, it is saying each letter from its makhraj, with no extra ghunnah in the letter made clear. Its letters are six: hamzah, haa (ه), 'ayn, haa (ح), ghayn and khaa. It is called "of the throat" because they come from the throat. It happens because the makhraj of noon, at the tip of the tongue, is far from the throat letters. The author of the Tuhfah says: «فَالأَوَّلُ الإِظْهَارُ قَبْلَ أَحْرُفِ، لِلْحَلْقِ سِتٌّ رُتِّبَتْ فَلْتَعْرِفِ» (the first is izhar, before the six throat letters, in their order, so know them).
idea.kidsLead: When a noon sakinah or tanween comes before one of the six throat letters «ء ه ع ح غ خ», we say the noon clearly, without stretching its sound: «مَنْ أَعْطَى», «نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ».

how.text: «ء ه ع ح غ خ»: the first letters of the words in «أَخِي هَاكَ عِلْمًا حَازَهُ غَيْرُ خَاسِرِ».
The tip of the tongue touches the makhraj of noon, so the noon is clear; then move to the throat letter without a pause.
Do not stretch it: the noon keeps only its own light ghunnah.
The makhraj of noon, at the tip of the tongue, is far from the throat letters.
In one word: «يَنۡهَىٰ»; across two words: «مَنۡ أَعۡطَىٰ»; with tanween: «نَارٌ حَامِيَةُۢ».

idea.note: Common mistakes: giving the clear noon a qalqalah, pausing on it, or stretching its ghunnah. Hafs says the noon clearly before ghayn and khaa, as before the other throat letters; some other riwayahs hide it before those two.

ayat.findHint: Find the places of izhar in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Noon sakinah + hamzah, across two words
Noon sakinah + haa (ه), in one word
Tanween + haa (ح)
Noon sakinah + khaa

ayat.tip: The Mushaf marks izhar with a sukun on the noon, and with the two tanween marks stacked, as in «نَارٌ».

quiz.q: Why is the noon said clearly?

lessons.title: Idgham with ghunnah
lessons.lede: When a letter of «يَنْمُو» begins the next word after a noon sakinah or tanween, the noon merges into it, with ghunnah for two counts.

idea.lead: In Arabic, idgham means putting one thing into another. As a term, it is a letter with sukun meeting a letter with a vowel, so that the two become one doubled letter, like the second. The letters of idgham for noon sakinah and tanween are six, gathered in «يَرْمَلُونَ»; four of them, gathered in «يَنْمُو», take ghunnah. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالثَّانِ إِدْغَامٌ بِسِتَّةٍ أَتَتْ، فِي يَرْمَلُونَ عِنْدَهُمْ قَدْ ثَبَتَتْ، لَكِنَّهَا قِسْمَانِ قِسْمٌ يُدْغَمَا، فِيهِ بِغُنَّةٍ بِيَنْمُو عُلِمَا» (the second is idgham, into six letters, fixed in «يَرْمَلُونَ»; but they are of two kinds: one takes idgham with ghunnah, known as «يَنْمُو»).
idea.kidsLead: When a letter of «يَنْمُو» begins the next word after a noon sakinah or tanween, we merge the noon into that letter and keep the ghunnah sound from the nose for two counts: «مَن يَعْمَلْ» is read «مَيَّعْمَلْ».

how.text: Yaa, noon, meem and waw, gathered in «يَنْمُو».
Into noon and meem: the noon goes completely, and the ghunnah is that of the letter merged into: «مِن نِّعۡمَةٖ», «مِّن مَّسَدِۭ».
Into yaa and waw: the noon itself goes, but its ghunnah stays: «مَن يَعۡمَلۡ», «يَوۡمَئِذٖ وَاجِفَةٌ».
Two counts in all of them.
It must be across two words. When noon and yaa or waw meet in one word, the noon is said clearly: «ٱلدُّنۡيَا», «بُنۡيَٰنٞ», «صِنۡوَانٞ» and «قِنۡوَانٞ». This is called absolute izhar.

idea.note: Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, says the noon clearly in «يسٓ ۝ وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانِ» and «نٓۚ وَٱلۡقَلَمِ», even though waw comes after it. In the Mushaf, the noon has no sukun; the next letter has a shaddah in full idgham, and none in partial idgham.

ayat.tip: Compare: the meem after the noon in «مِّن مَّسَدِۭ» has a shaddah, because the idgham is full; the yaa in «مَن يَعۡمَلۡ» has none, because it is partial.

lessons.title: Idgham without ghunnah
lessons.lede: When laam or raa begins the next word after a noon sakinah or tanween, the noon merges into it completely, without ghunnah.

idea.lead: Idgham without ghunnah is merging a noon sakinah or tanween into laam or raa: the noon goes completely, with its ghunnah, and the next letter is said doubled, without ghunnah. It is called full because the noon and its ghunnah both go. It happens because the makhraj of noon is close to those of laam and raa. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالثَّانِ إِدْغَامٌ بِغَيْرِ غُنَّهْ، فِي اللَّامِ وَالرَّا ثُمَّ كَرِّرَنَّهْ» (the second is idgham without ghunnah, into laam and raa; and roll the raa).
idea.kidsLead: When laam or raa begins the next word after a noon sakinah or tanween, we do not say the noon at all, and there is no ghunnah: we double the laam or raa. «وَيْلٌ لِّكُلِّ» is read «وَيْلُلِّكُلِّ».

how.text: Laam and raa.
The noon is not said, and the next letter is doubled: «وَيۡلٞ لِّكُلِّ» is read «وَيۡلُلِّكُلِّ».
There is none: the idgham is full.
It happens only across two words, as in «مِن رَّبِّهِمۡ» and «غَفُورٞ رَّحِيمٞ».
In the Mushaf, the noon has no sukun, and the laam or raa after it has a shaddah.

idea.note: Hafs makes a short pause (saktah), without taking a breath, on the noon in «مَنۡۜ رَاقٖ» (Al-Qiyamah 27), so the noon is said clearly and does not merge into the raa. Idgham without ghunnah is how Hafs reads by way of ash-Shatibiyyah; by other ways there is also a reading with ghunnah into laam and raa.

lessons.title: Iqlab (conversion)
lessons.lede: Turning noon sakinah or tanween into a hidden meem before baa (ب), keeping the ghunnah.

idea.lead: When baa (ب) comes after noon sakinah or tanween, the noon is pronounced as a meem, though it is not written as one, and that meem is then hidden before the baa, with ghunnah.
idea.kidsLead: When baa (ب) comes after a noon sakinah or tanween, we say the noon as a meem, and keep the humming sound from the nose for two counts.

how.text: The noon or tanween is pronounced as a meem, but not written as one.
The meem is hidden before the baa: neither pronounced clearly nor merged.
The nasal sound comes from the nose, for two counts.

lessons.title: Ikhfa' (concealment)
lessons.lede: Pronouncing noon sakinah or tanween in a state between izhar and idgham, without a shaddah, keeping the ghunnah.

formula.caption: letters that may come after it

idea.lead: When one of the fifteen letters comes after noon sakinah or tanween, you neither pronounce the noon clearly nor merge it: you say it in a state between the two.
idea.kidsLead: When one of the fifteen letters comes after noon sakinah or tanween, we hide the noon: we don't say it clearly and don't merge it into the next letter, and we keep the humming sound from the nose for two counts.

how.text: It gets ready for the next letter's point of articulation, without touching the point of the noon.
The nasal sound comes from the nose, for two counts.
There is no shaddah here; this is what tells ikhfa' apart from idgham.

idea.note: The ghunnah is heavy before ص ض ط ظ ق, and light before the other ten letters.

lessons.title: Meem sakinah: an introduction
lessons.lede: A meem sakinah is a meem with no vowel. It has three rules: ikhfa' before baa, idgham into meem, and izhar before every other letter.

idea.lead: A meem sakinah is a meem with no vowel. It stays when joining and when stopping, and comes in the middle or at the end of a word, in nouns, verbs and particles. Any letter can come after it except the madd letters. It has three rules, depending on the letter after it. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالمِيمُ إِنْ تَسْكُنْ تَجِي قَبْلَ الهِجَا، لَا أَلِفٍ لَيِّنَةٍ لِذِي الحِجَا، أَحْكَامُهَا ثَلَاثَةٌ لِمَنْ ضَبَطْ، إِخْفَاءٌ ادْغَامٌ وَإِظْهَارٌ فَقَطْ» (meem sakinah comes before the letters, but not before a soft alif; its rules are three: ikhfa', idgham and izhar, no more).
idea.kidsLead: A meem sakinah is a meem with a sukun «مْ». Before baa, we hide it with ghunnah; before another meem, we merge it in with ghunnah; and before all the other letters, we say it clearly.

how.text: Before baa: ikhfa' with the lips. Lesson 33.
Into meem: idgham with the lips, also called the minor idgham of like letters. Lesson 34.
Before the other twenty-six letters: izhar with the lips. Lesson 35.
They are called "of the lips" because meem and baa come from the lips.
In the Mushaf, the meem has a sukun for izhar, and none for ikhfa' and idgham; in idgham, the meem after it has a shaddah.

idea.note: No madd letter comes after a meem sakinah, since a madd letter only follows a letter with a vowel. A meem with a shaddah is not a meem sakinah: it has a vowel, and lesson 36 covers it.

lessons.title: Ikhfa' with meem (labial)
lessons.lede: When baa comes after a meem sakinah, the meem is hidden before the baa, with ghunnah for two counts.

idea.lead: Ikhfa' with the lips is hiding a meem sakinah before baa, with ghunnah. It is called "of the lips" because meem and baa come from the lips. It happens only across two words, as in «تَرۡمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٖ». The author of the Tuhfah says: «فَالأَوَّلُ الإِخْفَاءُ عِنْدَ البَاءِ، وَسَمِّهِ الشَّفْوِيَّ لِلْقُرَّاءِ» (the first is ikhfa' before baa; call it "of the lips", for the reciters).

lessons.title: Idgham with meem (labial)
lessons.lede: When a meem with a vowel comes after a meem sakinah, the first merges into the second: one doubled meem, with ghunnah for two counts.

idea.lead: Idgham with the lips is merging a meem sakinah into the meem with a vowel after it, so that they become one doubled meem, with ghunnah for two counts. It is also called the minor idgham of like letters, since the two letters are the same and the first has a sukun. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالثَّانِ إِدْغَامٌ بِمِثْلِهَا أَتَى، وَسَمِّ إِدْغَامًا صَغِيرًا يَا فَتَى» (the second is idgham, into a letter like it; call it the minor idgham, young man).
idea.kidsLead: When another meem comes after a meem sakinah, we read them as one doubled meem, with the ghunnah sound from the nose for two counts: «أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن» is read «أَطْعَمَهُمِّن».

how.text: Meem alone.
One doubled meem: «أَطۡعَمَهُم مِّن» is read «أَطۡعَمَهُمِّن».
Two counts; it is among the fullest ghunnahs, since it is in a doubled letter.
As in «عَلَيۡهِم مُّؤۡصَدَةٞ» and «فِي قُلُوبِهِم مَّرَضٞ».
In the Mushaf, the first meem has no sukun, and the meem after it has a shaddah.

idea.note: It is also called the minor idgham of identical letters; level 3 covers identical, close and related letters in detail. When meem comes after a noon sakinah or tanween, it is idgham with ghunnah (lesson 28), not idgham with the lips.

lessons.title: Izhar with meem (labial)
lessons.lede: When any letter except baa and meem comes after a meem sakinah, the meem is said clearly from the lips, without extra ghunnah.

formula.caption: letters, all but baa and meem

idea.lead: Izhar with the lips is saying a meem sakinah clearly from its makhraj, without extra ghunnah, before twenty-six letters: the whole alphabet except baa and meem. Take extra care before waw and faa: waw comes from the same makhraj as meem and faa is close to it, so the meem could be hidden before them. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالثَّالِثُ الإِظْهَارُ فِي البَقِيَّهْ، مِنْ أَحْرُفٍ وَسَمِّهَا شَفْوِيَّهْ، وَاحْذَرْ لَدَى وَاوٍ وَفَا أَنْ تَخْتَفِي، لِقُرْبِهَا وَالِاتِّحَادِ فَاعْرِفِ» (the third is izhar, before the other letters; call it "of the lips"; and beware of hiding it before waw and faa, since one is close and the other shares its makhraj).
idea.kidsLead: When any letter except baa and meem comes after a meem sakinah, we say the meem clearly, closing the lips, without stretching its sound: «أَنْعَمْتَ», «لَكُمْ دِينُكُمْ». Take extra care before waw and faa.

how.text: Twenty-six: the whole alphabet except baa and meem.
The lips close lightly for the meem, then open for the next letter, with no pause and no qalqalah.
Take extra care before them, since waw comes from the makhraj of meem and faa is close to it: «عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَلَا», «هُمۡ فِيهَا».
Do not stretch it: the meem keeps only its own light ghunnah.
In the Mushaf, a sukun on the meem.

idea.note: Common mistakes in izhar with the lips: giving the meem a hint of a vowel, pausing on it, stretching its ghunnah, or hiding it before waw and faa.

Meem sakinah + yaa

lessons.title: Noon and meem with shaddah
lessons.lede: Noon and meem with a shaddah are said with full ghunnah for two counts; each is called a doubled letter of ghunnah.

idea.lead: Ghunnah is a nasal sound built into noon and meem. It comes from the khayshum, and the tongue plays no part in it. When noon or meem has a shaddah, its ghunnah must be said for two counts, when joining and when stopping, in the middle or at the end of a word, as in «إِنَّ» and «ثُمَّ». The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَغُنَّ مِيمًا ثُمَّ نُونًا شُدِّدَا، وَسَمِّ كُلًّا حَرْفَ غُنَّةٍ بَدَا» (give ghunnah to meem and noon with a shaddah, and call each a letter of ghunnah).
idea.kidsLead: When you see a shaddah on noon or meem, keep the ghunnah sound in your nose for two counts: «إِنَّ», «ثُمَّ». Try holding your nose: you will feel the sound needs it.

how.text: A sound from the khayshum that goes with noon and meem.
Two counts in noon and meem with a shaddah: «إِنَّ», «ثُمَّ».
The ghunnah stays full when you stop on a doubled noon or meem.
When a doubled noon comes after the laam of «ال», as in «ٱلنَّاسِ», its ghunnah is also two counts.

idea.note: One count is about the time it takes to fold or unfold a finger at an even pace. Leaving out the ghunnah in a doubled letter, or stretching it past two counts, is hidden lahn. Learn the ghunnah and its length from a teacher, by listening and repeating. Lesson 37 gives all the degrees of ghunnah.

lessons.title: Ghunnah: its length and degrees
lessons.lede: Ghunnah is a fixed characteristic of noon and meem, but it varies: fullest in a doubled letter, then a merged one, then a hidden one, then a clear one with sukun, then one with a vowel.

idea.lead: Ghunnah is a nasal sound from the khayshum. It is a fixed characteristic of noon and meem in every state, but it varies in fullness and length. In three degrees it is full and lasts two counts: noon and meem with shaddah, then noon and meem merged with ghunnah, then hidden ones, which include iqlab and labial ikhfa'. In two degrees it is incomplete and not stretched: a clear noon or meem with sukun, then one with a vowel; these have only the basic trace of ghunnah.
idea.kidsLead: The ghunnah of noon and meem is not always the same length: it lasts two counts when the letter has shaddah, is merged or is hidden, and it is very short when the noon or meem is clear or has a vowel.

how.text: The fullest: «إِنَّ», «ثُمَّ». Two counts.
In idgham with ghunnah and labial idgham: «مَن يَعۡمَلۡ», «لَهُم مَّا». Two counts.
In ikhfa', iqlab and labial ikhfa': «مِن شَرِّ», «مِنۢ بَعۡدِ», «تَرۡمِيهِم بِحِجَارَةٖ». Two counts.
In izhar of the throat and labial izhar: «أَنۡعَمۡتَ». Only the basic trace, not stretched.
The least: «نَعۡبُدُ», «مَالِكِ». Only the basic trace.
The ghunnah follows the letter after it: heavy before the elevated letters «مِن قَبۡلُ», light before the others.

idea.note: A count of ghunnah is the same as a count of madd: the time it takes to fold or unfold a finger at an even pace. Stretching the ghunnah of a clear or vowelled noon or meem, or cutting it short in a doubled, merged or hidden one, is hidden lahn. Its timing is learned by listening to a teacher.

quiz.why: Fullest in a doubled letter, then in idgham, then in ikhfa', then in a clear letter with sukun, then in a letter with a vowel.

quiz.why: The meem sakinah merged into the meem after it, so its ghunnah is of the merged degree.

quiz.q: How many degrees of ghunnah are there?
quiz.why: Five: doubled, then merged, then hidden, then clear with sukun, then with a vowel.

quiz.q: In which degrees does the ghunnah last two counts?
quiz.why: The full, stretched ghunnah is in the doubled, merged and hidden degrees; the clear and vowelled have only its trace.

quiz.q: What is the degree of ghunnah in the noon of «أَنۡعَمۡتَ»?
quiz.why: The noon has sukun with 'ayn after it, so it is clear, with only the trace of ghunnah, not stretched.

quiz.q: What is the degree of ghunnah in «مِنۢ بَعۡدِ»?
quiz.why: Iqlab is a hidden meem before baa, so its ghunnah is of the hidden degree, two counts.

quiz.q: When is the ghunnah heavy?
quiz.why: The ghunnah follows the letter after it: heavy before the elevated letters, light before the others.

lessons.title: Madd: its meaning, letters and causes
lessons.lede: Madd is stretching the sound of a madd letter. The original madd is two counts; a secondary madd is longer, because of a hamzah or a sukun.

idea.lead: In Arabic, madd means increase. As a term, it is stretching the sound of a madd letter; its opposite is qasr, saying the madd letter with no extra length. It is of two kinds. The original madd, also called natural, is needed for the letter to exist at all and does not depend on any cause; it lasts two counts. A secondary madd is longer than the natural one, because of a hamzah or a sukun. The author of the Tuhfah says: «وَالمَدُّ أَصْلِيٌّ وَفَرْعِيٌّ لَهُ، وَسَمِّ أَوَّلًا طَبِيعِيًّا وَهُو، مَا لَا تَوَقُّفٌ لَهُ عَلَى سَبَبْ، وَلَا بِدُونِهِ الحُرُوفُ تُجْتَلَبْ» (madd is original or secondary; call the first natural: it does not depend on a cause, and without it the letters cannot be said).
idea.kidsLead: Madd means stretching the sound of a madd letter: alif, waw or yaa. The shortest is two counts, as in «قَالَ». When a hamzah or a sukun comes after the madd letter, we stretch it longer, as in «جَآءَ».

how.text: Alif after fathah, waw with sukun after dammah, yaa with sukun after kasrah, as in lesson 10.
Waw and yaa with sukun after fathah, as in «خَوۡفٍ»; they are stretched only when stopping. Lesson 53.
Two counts, with no cause: «قَالَ», «يَقُولُ», «قِيلَ». Lesson 40.
A hamzah after the madd letter, in one word «جَآءَ» or the next word «إِنَّآ أَنزَلۡنَٰهُ»: lessons 45 and 46. Or a hamzah before it «ءَامَنُواْ»: lesson 42.
A fixed sukun after the madd letter «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ»: lessons 47–49. Or a sukun for stopping «ٱلرَّحِيمِ»: lesson 52.

idea.note: One count is the time it takes to say one vowel, about the time to fold or unfold a finger. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, reads the joined and separated madd for four or five counts, and the necessary madd for six; their lessons give the details.

lessons.title: Kinds of madd: original and secondary
lessons.lede: Madd has two kinds: original, which needs no cause and lasts two counts, with those madds given the same length; and secondary, caused by a hamzah or a sukun.

formula.caption: The natural madd and those like it

idea.lead: Madd is either original or secondary. The original madd is the natural madd: the madd letter cannot exist without it, it needs no cause, and it lasts two counts. Given the same length are: the 'iwad madd, the minor silah, and the five letters at the start of surahs gathered in «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ». The secondary madd is longer than the natural one because of a cause, one of two: a hamzah, giving the joined, separated, major silah and badal madds; or a sukun, giving madd lazim, the madd for stopping and the leen madd.
idea.kidsLead: Madd has two kinds: a short one of two counts that needs no cause, as in «قَالَ», and a longer one with a cause after it: a hamzah, as in «جَآءَ», or a sukun, as in «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ».

how.text: The natural madd: «قَالَ», «يَقُولُ», «قِيلَ». Two counts, no cause (lesson 40).
'Iwad (lesson 41), the minor silah (lesson 43), and the letters «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ» at the start of surahs: two counts.
Joined and separated (lessons 45 and 46), the major silah (lesson 44) and badal (lesson 42).
Lazim (lessons 47–51), for stopping (lesson 52) and leen (lesson 53).
The secondary madd has three rulings: required, the joined madd; necessary, madd lazim; and allowed, the separated, for stopping, badal and leen madds.

idea.note: The badal madd is secondary in origin, since its cause is the hamzah before it, but Hafs gives it two counts like the natural madd. When a letter has two causes, the stronger one counts, as lesson 54 explains.

ayat.findHint: Find the madd letters in each ayah: which are original and which secondary? Then bring the colours back to check.

The alif in «جَآءَ» is secondary, caused by the hamzah
The waw in «عَٰبِدُونَ» is original
The alif in «وَلَآ» and «مَآ» is secondary: separated
The alif in «وَلَا» and the yaa are original when joining
The alif after the daad is secondary, caused by the sukun

ayat.tip: The Mushaf marks a secondary madd with the madd sign «ـٓ» above the madd letter.

quiz.why: Madd has two kinds: original, and secondary with a cause.

quiz.q: Which of these has the same length as the natural madd?
quiz.why: 'Iwad lasts two counts like the natural madd, as do the minor silah and the letters «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ».

quiz.q: What makes a madd secondary?
quiz.why: A madd is secondary when its cause comes: a hamzah or a sukun.

quiz.q: Which of these madds is caused by a sukun?
quiz.why: Lazim, for stopping and leen are caused by a sukun; joined, separated and badal by a hamzah.

quiz.q: What is the ruling of madd lazim?
quiz.why: The secondary madd is required (the joined madd), necessary (madd lazim), or allowed (the others).

quiz.q: How long does Hafs make the badal madd, though its cause is a hamzah?
quiz.why: Badal is secondary in origin, but Hafs gives it two counts like the natural madd.

quiz.q: Which madd is required?
quiz.why: The joined madd is required, since all the reciters agree on stretching it beyond the natural madd.

lessons.title: Natural madd (madd tabi'i)
lessons.lede: The natural madd is stretching a madd letter for two counts, when no hamzah or sukun comes after it.

formula.caption: no hamzah or sukun after it

idea.lead: The natural madd is the original madd: a madd letter cannot be said without it, and it does not depend on a hamzah or a sukun. It lasts two counts, no more and no less. It is called natural because someone with a sound natural ear neither shortens it nor stretches it. The small alif over a letter, as in «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ», counts too: it is stretched like an alif.
idea.kidsLead: The natural madd is the shortest madd: we stretch the madd letter for just two counts, as in «قَالَ», «يَقُولُ», «قِيلَ». The small alif over a letter is also stretched for two counts: «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ».

how.text: Two counts, no more and no less: «قَالَ», «يَقُولُ», «قِيلَ».
The small alif «ـٰ» over a letter is stretched for two counts, like an alif: «ذَٰلِكَ», «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ».
The letters at the start of surahs that are said with two letters, gathered in «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ»: «ح ي ط ه ر». «طه» is read «طَا هَا».
It is two counts when you stop on the madd letter itself, as when stopping on «وَٱلضُّحَىٰ».
When a madd letter ends a word and a letter with sukun begins the next, the madd drops when joining: «قَالُواْ ٱلۡحَمۡدُ» is read «قَالُلۡحَمۡدُ».

idea.note: A common beginner's mistake is cutting the natural madd until it becomes a vowel, or stretching it past two counts. The minor silah and the 'iwad madd have the same length as the natural madd; lessons 43 and 41 cover them.

quiz.why: The natural madd is two counts, no more and no less.

quiz.q: Why is it called natural?
options: Someone with a sound ear neither shortens nor stretches it

quiz.why: Someone with a sound natural ear says it at its length, neither shorter nor longer.

quiz.q: How is the small alif in «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ» read?

quiz.why: The small alif is read as an alif and stretched for two counts, like a written alif.

quiz.q: What are the letters gathered in «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ» at the start of surahs?
quiz.why: Haa, yaa, taa, haa and raa at the start of surahs are said with two letters, as in «طَا», so they are stretched two counts.

quiz.q: How is «قَالُواْ ٱلۡحَمۡدُ» read when joining?
quiz.why: A letter with sukun comes after the waw in the next word, so the madd drops when joining: two letters with sukun cannot meet.

quiz.why: Cutting it until it is gone drops a letter from the word: clear lahn.

quiz.why: The waw has a sukun after a dammah: it is a natural madd letter.

lessons.title: The 'iwad madd
lessons.lede: The 'iwad madd is stopping on tanween with fathah with an alif instead of the tanween, stretched two counts.

idea.lead: When you stop on a word ending in tanween with fathah, the tanween is dropped and replaced by an alif, stretched two counts. It is called the 'iwad (replacement) madd because the alif replaces the tanween. Whether the alif is written after the tanween, as in «أَفۡوَاجٗا», or not, as in «جَزَآءٗ», you stop with an alif. Tanween with dammah or kasrah is stopped with sukun, with no replacement.
idea.kidsLead: When we stop on a word ending in tanween with fathah «ـًا», we do not say the noon; we read an alif for two counts: «أَفۡوَاجَا». We stop on tanween with dammah or kasrah with sukun.

how.text: Dropping tanween with fathah when stopping and replacing it with an alif: «تَوَّابَۢا» is read «تَوَّابَا».
Two counts, like the natural madd.
No 'iwad: the tanween is said as a noon sakinah with its own rule, as in «تَوَّابَۢا ۝» joined with iqlab or another rule.
No 'iwad, even with tanween with fathah: «رَحۡمَةٗ» is stopped with a haa with sukun, «رَحۡمَهۡ».
No 'iwad: «أَحَدٌ» is read «أَحَدۡ», and «خُسۡرٍ» is read «خُسۡرۡ».

idea.note: You also stop with an alif on some words that are not tanween: «إِذٗا» wherever it comes, «لَنَسۡفَعَۢا» (Al-'Alaq 15) and «وَلَيَكُونٗا» (Yusuf 32), where the light noon of emphasis is written as tanween. Lesson 91 explains stopping on taa marbutah.

Tanween with fathah: stop with «تَوَّابَا»
Taa marbutah with tanween: stop with a haa, «مَّرۡضِيَّهۡ», with no 'iwad

ayat.tip: The alif after tanween with fathah in «أَفۡوَاجٗا» is not said when joining; it is said when stopping, in place of the tanween.

quiz.q: What is the 'iwad madd?
options: A hamzah before a madd letter
Stopping on tanween with fathah with an alif
quiz.why: Tanween with fathah is dropped when stopping, and an alif replaces it.

quiz.q: How long is the 'iwad madd?
quiz.why: It lasts two counts, like the natural madd.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «عَلِيمًا»?
quiz.why: You stop on tanween with fathah with an alif: the 'iwad madd.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «رَحۡمَةً»?
quiz.why: There is no 'iwad on taa marbutah: you stop on it with a haa with sukun.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «خُسۡرٍ»?
quiz.why: Tanween with kasrah is stopped with sukun, with no 'iwad.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «إِذٗا»?
quiz.why: You stop on «إِذٗا» with an alif, like tanween with fathah.

quiz.q: Is there an 'iwad madd in «تَوَّابَۢا» when it is joined to the next word?
options: No, the tanween is said as a noon with its rule
quiz.why: 'Iwad is only when stopping; when joining, the tanween is said as a noon sakinah with its own rule.

lessons.title: The badal madd
lessons.lede: The badal madd is a hamzah before a madd letter in one word. Hafs stretches it two counts.

formula.caption: A hamzah, then a madd letter

idea.lead: The badal madd is a hamzah coming before a madd letter in one word, with no hamzah or sukun after the madd letter, as in «ءَامَنُواْ», «أُوتُواْ» and «إِيمَٰنٗا». It is called badal (replacement) because the madd letter usually replaces a hamzah: «ءَامَنَ» was «أَأْمَنَ»; two hamzahs met, and the second became a madd letter matching the vowel of the first. Hafs gives it two counts only; it is secondary in origin, since its cause is the hamzah before it.
idea.kidsLead: When a hamzah comes and then a madd letter in the same word, as in «ءَامَنُوا», we stretch it two counts only, like the natural madd.

how.text: A hamzah, then a madd letter, in one word: «ءَامَنُواْ», «أُوتُواْ», «إِيمَٰنٗا».
The madd letter usually replaces a hamzah: «ءَامَنَ» was «أَأْمَنَ».
Two counts only; four and six are for Warsh, not Hafs.
When a hamzah or a fixed sukun follows the madd letter, the stronger cause counts, as in «ءَآمِّينَ», stretched six counts (lesson 54).

idea.note: The madd letter need not really replace a hamzah: any hamzah before a madd letter counts, as in «ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ» and «مَـَٔابٗا». In the reading of Hafs, badal has the same length as the natural madd, but knowing it helps in understanding the madds.

ayat.legendNoon: A hamzah before the madd letter
ayat.findHint: Find the hamzah before the madd letter in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: A hamzah before the alif in «ءَامَنُواْ»: badal madd
A hamzah before the alif in «وَءَامَنَهُم»: badal madd
A hamzah before the yaa in «إِيمَٰنٗا»: a badal madd

ayat.tip: Every word in these examples has a hamzah then a madd letter, so it is a badal madd, read for two counts.

quiz.q: What is the badal madd?
options: A hamzah before a madd letter
A hamzah after a madd letter
A sukun after a madd letter
quiz.why: The badal madd is a hamzah coming before a madd letter, as in «ءَامَنُواْ».

quiz.q: How long does Hafs stretch the badal madd?
quiz.why: Hafs gives it two counts only.

quiz.q: What was «ءَامَنَ» originally?
quiz.why: Two hamzahs met, the second with sukun, so it became an alif matching the vowel of the first.

quiz.q: Which word has a badal madd?
quiz.why: A hamzah before the waw in «أُوتُواْ»: a badal madd.

quiz.q: Why is it called the badal madd?
options: Because it replaces the natural madd
Because its madd letter usually replaces a hamzah
quiz.why: Its madd letter usually replaces a hamzah with sukun.

quiz.q: In «ءَآمِّينَ ٱلۡبَيۡتَ» a badal and a lazim madd meet. How long is it?
quiz.why: When two causes meet, the stronger counts, and lazim is stronger than badal, so it is six counts.

quiz.q: How does badal differ from the joined madd?
options: In badal the hamzah comes before the madd letter, in the joined madd after it
The joined madd has no hamzah
quiz.why: Badal is a hamzah then a madd; the joined madd is a madd then a hamzah, in one word.

lessons.title: The minor silah madd
lessons.lede: The minor silah is joining the pronoun haa ("him", "it") to a waw or yaa when it comes between two letters with vowels and no hamzah follows; it lasts two counts.

idea.lead: The pronoun haa is the haa meaning "him" or "it", as in «إِنَّهُۥ» and «بِهِۦ». When it comes between two letters with vowels, it is joined to a waw if it has a dammah, and to a yaa if it has a kasrah; the Mushaf writes a small waw or small yaa. If no hamzah follows, it is the minor silah, lasting two counts like the natural madd. The haa of «هَٰذِهِۦ» is treated the same way.
idea.kidsLead: When you see a small waw after the haa «إِنَّهُۥ», or a small yaa «بِهِۦ», read it as a madd letter for two counts: «innahu», «bihi».

how.text: The haa comes between two letters with vowels: «إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ», «لَهُۥ كُفُوًا».
Two counts, when no hamzah follows the haa.
When the letter before it has sukun «مِنۡهُ», or the one after it «لَهُ ٱلۡمُلۡكُ», or when you stop on it.
A small waw «ۥ» after a haa with dammah, and a small yaa «ۦ» after a haa with kasrah.

idea.note: Hafs has places that differ from the rule: he joins the haa in «فِيهِۦ مُهَانًا» (Al-Furqan 69), though the letter before it has sukun; he does not join it in «يَرۡضَهُ لَكُمۡ» (Az-Zumar 7), though it is between two vowels; he gives it sukun in «أَرۡجِهۡ» (Al-A'raf 111, Ash-Shu'ara 36) and «فَأَلۡقِهۡ» (An-Naml 28); and he gives it a dammah without silah in «عَلَيۡهُ ٱللَّهَ» (Al-Fath 10) and «أَنسَىٰنِيهُ» (Al-Kahf 63).

ayat.legendNoon: The haa of the minor silah
ayat.findHint: Find the joined pronoun haa in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: The haa of «إِنَّهُۥ» is between two letters with vowels: minor silah, two counts
The haa is between two vowels with kaaf after it: minor silah
The haa ends the ayah: joined when joining, with no silah when you stop on it

ayat.tip: Silah is read only when joining; when you stop on the haa, it takes sukun with no silah.

quiz.q: When is the pronoun haa joined (silah)?
options: At the start of the surah
quiz.why: The haa is joined when it comes between two letters with vowels, never before a sukun or when stopping.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «يَرۡضَهُ لَكُمۡ» in Az-Zumar?
options: A dammah on the haa, without silah
Joining the haa to a waw
quiz.why: Hafs reads it with a dammah on the haa and no silah, though it is between two letters with vowels.

quiz.q: How long is the minor silah?
quiz.why: The minor silah lasts two counts, like the natural madd.

quiz.q: Is the haa joined in «مِنۡهُ»?
options: No, because the letter before it has sukun
quiz.why: Silah is between two vowels, and the letter before the haa here has sukun.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «فِيهِۦ مُهَانًا»?
options: Joining the haa to a yaa
With a dammah on the haa
quiz.why: Hafs joins it in this place, though the letter before it has sukun.

quiz.q: In «وَلَمۡ يَكُن لَّهُۥ كُفُوًا», what kind of silah is it?
quiz.why: The haa is between two vowels and no hamzah follows, so it is the minor silah.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «أَرۡجِهۡ» in Al-A'raf?
quiz.why: Hafs reads it with sukun on the haa, in Al-A'raf and Ash-Shu'ara.

lessons.title: The major silah madd
lessons.lede: The major silah is a joined pronoun haa followed by a cutting hamzah; it is stretched like the separated madd: four or five counts for Hafs.

idea.lead: When the pronoun haa meets the condition of silah, coming between two vowels, and a cutting hamzah follows it, it is the major silah. It takes the rule of the separated madd, since the madd letter ends one word and the hamzah begins the next. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretches it four or five counts, the same as the separated madd in that recitation. The Mushaf marks it with the madd sign above the small waw or yaa.
idea.kidsLead: When a hamzah comes after the joined haa, as in «مَالَهُۥٓ أَخۡلَدَهُۥ», we stretch the silah longer: four or five counts, like the separated madd.

how.text: A haa between two vowels, followed by a cutting hamzah: «مَالَهُۥٓ أَخۡلَدَهُۥ», «يَرَهُۥٓ أَحَدٌ».
The rule of the separated madd: four or five counts for Hafs by way of ash-Shatibiyyah.
Stretch it as long as the separated madd in the same recitation: if you give the separated madd four, give it four.
The madd sign «ـٓ» above the small waw or yaa after the haa.

idea.note: When you stop on the haa, the silah goes completely, minor or major. When a connecting hamzah follows the haa there is no silah, because the connecting hamzah drops and two letters with sukun meet: «لَهُ ٱلۡمُلۡكُ».

ayat.legendNoon: The haa of the major silah
ayat.findHint: Find the haa of silah and the hamzah after it in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: The haa of «مَالَهُۥٓ» is followed by a hamzah: major silah
The haa of «يَرَهُۥٓ» is followed by the hamzah of «أَحَدٌ»: major silah

ayat.tip: The madd sign above the small waw in «مَالَهُۥٓ» shows you it is a major silah.

quiz.q: How long is the major silah in «مَالَهُۥٓ أَخۡلَدَهُۥ»?
quiz.why: A hamzah comes after it, so it follows the separated madd: four or five counts for Hafs.

quiz.q: What makes a silah major?
options: A cutting hamzah after the haa
quiz.why: The major silah is a silah followed by a cutting hamzah.

quiz.q: What is the rule of the major silah?
options: The rule of the natural madd
The rule of the separated madd
The rule of the madd for stopping
quiz.why: The madd letter ends one word and the hamzah begins the next, so it takes the rule of the separated madd.

quiz.q: In «أَيَحۡسَبُ أَن لَّمۡ يَرَهُۥٓ أَحَدٌ», what kind of silah is it?
quiz.why: A cutting hamzah follows the haa in «أَحَدٌ», so it is the major silah.

quiz.q: If you give the separated madd five counts in your recitation, how long is the major silah?
quiz.why: The major silah is kept equal to the separated madd in one recitation.

quiz.q: Is the haa joined in «لَهُ ٱلۡمُلۡكُ»?
options: No, because a letter with sukun follows it
quiz.why: The connecting hamzah drops when joining, so a letter with sukun follows the haa, and there is no silah.

quiz.q: What happens to the major silah when you stop on the haa?
options: The silah goes and the haa takes sukun
quiz.why: There is no silah when stopping, so the haa takes sukun.

lessons.title: The joined madd (muttasil)
lessons.lede: The joined madd is a madd letter followed by a hamzah in the same word. It is required, and Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretches it four or five counts.

formula.caption: A hamzah after it in the same word

idea.lead: The joined (muttasil) madd is a madd letter followed by a hamzah joined to it in one word, as in «جَآءَ», «ٱلسَّمَآءِ», «سُوٓءَ» and «سِيٓـَٔتۡ». It is required, since all the reciters agree on stretching it beyond the natural madd, though they differ on how much. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretches it four or five counts. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَوَاجِبٌ إِنْ جَاءَ قَبْلَ هَمْزَةِ، مُتَّصِلًا إِنْ جُمِعَا بِكِلْمَةِ» (it is required when it comes before a hamzah, joined, in one word).
idea.kidsLead: When a hamzah comes after a madd letter in the same word, as in «جَآءَ» and «ٱلسَّمَآءِ», we stretch four or five counts.

how.text: The madd letter and the hamzah are in one word: «جَآءَ», «ٱلسَّمَآءِ», «سُوٓءَ».
Required. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretches it four or five counts.
When you stop on a joined madd whose hamzah ends the word, as in «ٱلسَّمَآءِ», four, five or six counts are allowed.
No reciter shortens it, so it must be stretched beyond the natural madd.

idea.note: Keep the joined and separated madds equal in one recitation (lesson 46). The madd sign «ـٓ» above the madd letter in the Mushaf marks it.

ayat.legendNext: The hamzah after it in the word
ayat.findHint: Find the madd letter and the hamzah after it in the same word, then bring the colours back to check.

why: The alif and the hamzah in «جَآءَ»: joined madd
The alif and the hamzah in «ٱلشِّتَآءِ»: joined madd

ayat.tip: The hamzah in these examples is in the same word as the madd letter, so it is joined.

quiz.q: What is the joined madd?
options: A hamzah after a madd letter in one word
A hamzah after a madd letter across two words
A hamzah before a madd letter
A sukun after a madd letter
quiz.why: The joined madd is a madd letter and a hamzah after it, in one word.

quiz.q: What is the rule for the joined madd?
quiz.why: Required, since all the reciters agree on stretching it beyond the natural madd.

quiz.q: When stopping on «ٱلسَّمَآءِ», how long may its madd be?
quiz.why: When you stop on a joined madd whose hamzah ends the word, four, five or six counts are allowed.

quiz.q: Which word has a joined madd?
quiz.why: The alif and the hamzah are in one word in «جَآءَ».

quiz.q: How long does Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretch the joined madd?
quiz.why: He stretches it four or five counts when joining.

quiz.q: Why is the joined madd called required?
options: Because it is the longest madd
Because all the reciters agree on stretching it beyond the natural madd
quiz.why: No one shortens it, so stretching it is required.

quiz.q: In «رِحۡلَةَ ٱلشِّتَآءِ», what kind of madd is it?
quiz.why: The alif and the hamzah are in the word «ٱلشِّتَآءِ», so it is joined.

lessons.title: The separated madd (munfasil)
lessons.lede: The separated madd is a madd letter ending one word and a hamzah beginning the next. It is allowed, and Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretches it four or five counts.

idea.lead: The separated (munfasil) madd is a madd letter ending one word and a hamzah beginning the next, as in «بِمَآ أُنزِلَ», «قُوٓاْ أَنفُسَكُمۡ» and «فِيٓ أَنفُسِكُمۡ». It is allowed, since some reciters shorten it. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretches it four or five counts, the same as the joined madd. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَجَائِزٌ إِذَا أَتَى مُنْفَصِلَا» (and allowed when it comes separated).
idea.kidsLead: When the madd letter ends one word and the hamzah begins the next, as in «إِنَّآ أَعۡطَيۡنَٰكَ», we stretch four or five counts.

how.text: The madd letter ends one word and the hamzah begins the next: «بِمَآ أُنزِلَ», «قُوٓاْ أَنفُسَكُمۡ», «فِيٓ أَنفُسِكُمۡ».
Allowed. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretches it four or five counts, like the joined madd.
Within one recitation, give them the same length: four for both, or five for both.
When you stop on the first word, the separated madd goes, since the hamzah is cut off from it, and it is stretched naturally: «إِنَّآ».

idea.note: Shortening the separated madd to two counts comes from Hafs by way of Tayyibat an-Nashr, not by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, which this course follows. The madd sign «ـٓ» above the madd letter in the Mushaf marks a madd longer than the natural one, joined or separated.

ayat.legendNoon: The madd letter ending the word
ayat.findHint: Find the madd letter ending a word and the hamzah starting the next, then bring the colours back to check.

why: «وَلَآ أَنتُمۡ» and «مَآ أَعۡبُدُ»: separated madd, twice
«إِنَّآ أَعۡطَيۡنَٰكَ»: separated madd

ayat.tip: If you stop on the first word, the separated madd goes, because the hamzah no longer follows it.

quiz.q: How long does Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, stretch the separated madd?
quiz.why: Four or five counts, like the joined madd.

quiz.q: Which of these has a separated madd?
quiz.why: The alif ends «بِمَآ» and the hamzah begins «أُنزِلَ»: separated. The others are joined.

quiz.q: Why is the separated madd only allowed?
quiz.why: Some reciters shorten it to two counts, so there is no agreement on stretching it.

quiz.q: If you give the joined madd four counts in a recitation, how long is the separated madd?
quiz.why: Keep them equal within one recitation: the separated madd is never longer than the joined.

quiz.q: What is the separated madd?
options: A madd letter ending a word and a hamzah starting the next
A hamzah before a madd letter
A madd letter and a hamzah in one word
A sukun after a madd letter
quiz.why: The separated madd is a madd letter ending one word and a hamzah starting the next.

quiz.q: If you stop on «إِنَّآ» in «إِنَّآ أَعۡطَيۡنَٰكَ», how long is the alif?
quiz.why: Stopping cuts the hamzah off from the madd letter, so it is stretched naturally.

quiz.q: By which way does shortening the separated madd come from Hafs?
quiz.why: Shortening comes from Hafs by way of Tayyibat an-Nashr, not ash-Shatibiyyah, which this course follows.

lessons.title: Madd lazim: its meaning and kinds
lessons.lede: Madd lazim is a madd letter followed by a fixed sukun, there both when joining and when stopping; it is stretched six counts. It has four kinds.

idea.lead: The necessary (lazim) madd is a madd letter followed by a fixed, original sukun, there both when joining and when stopping. It is called necessary because its cause is always there, and because all the reciters agree on six counts. Ibn al-Jazari says: «فَلَازِمٌ إِنْ جَاءَ بَعْدَ حَرْفِ مَدّْ، سَاكِنُ حَالَيْنِ وَبِالطُّولِ يُمَدّْ» (it is necessary when, after a madd letter, comes a sukun in both states; it is stretched long). It has four kinds: heavy in a word, light in a word, heavy in a letter, and light in a letter. The author of the Tuhfah says: «أَقْسَامُ لَازِمٍ لَدَيْهِمْ أَرْبَعَهْ، وَتِلْكَ كِلْمِيٌّ وَحَرْفِيٌّ مَعَهْ، كِلَاهُمَا مُخَفَّفٌ مُثَقَّلُ، فَهَذِهِ أَرْبَعَةٌ تُفَصَّلُ» (the necessary madd has four kinds: in a word and in a letter, each light or heavy).
idea.kidsLead: When a letter with sukun or a shaddah comes after a madd letter in the same word, we stretch it long: six counts, as in «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ». Some letters at the start of surahs too: «الٓمٓ» is read «أَلِفْ لَآمْ مِيمْ».

how.text: An original sukun after the madd letter, there both when joining and when stopping.
Six counts, necessarily, for all the reciters.
When the sukun is in a word: «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ», «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ» (lesson 48).
When it is in one of the letters at the start of surahs: «الٓمٓ», «قٓ» (lesson 49).
Heavy when its sukun is merged into a doubled letter; light when its sukun is not merged.

idea.note: The difference between madd lazim and the madd for stopping: the sukun of lazim is there both when joining and when stopping, while the sukun of the madd for stopping comes only when stopping (lesson 52). The madd of distinction is a madd lazim in a word (lesson 51).

ayat.findHint: Find the necessary madd in each ayah and the sukun after it, then bring the colours back to check.

why: An alif with a doubled laam after it: heavy, in a word
An alif with a doubled khaa after it: heavy, in a word
«لَامْ» and «مِيمْ»: necessary madd in a letter, six counts

ayat.tip: The madd sign «ـٓ» over a letter at the start of a surah marks the necessary madd, as in «الٓمٓ». Its first letter, alif, is not stretched: it is said «أَلِفْ», with no madd letter in the middle.

quiz.q: How long is the necessary madd?
quiz.why: Always six counts, by agreement of the reciters.

quiz.q: Why is it called necessary?
options: Its cause is there when joining and stopping, and its six counts are fixed
It is at the end of the surah
quiz.why: Its cause is a fixed sukun in both states, and six counts are fixed for it.

quiz.q: How many kinds of madd lazim are there?
quiz.why: Four: heavy in a word, light in a word, heavy in a letter, and light in a letter.

quiz.q: How does heavy differ from light?
options: Heavy has a doubled letter after the madd letter
quiz.why: Heavy has its sukun merged into a doubled letter; light has its sukun not merged.

quiz.q: How does madd lazim differ from the madd for stopping?
options: The sukun of lazim is there both when joining and when stopping
The madd for stopping is longer
quiz.why: The sukun of lazim is original and fixed in both states; the sukun of the madd for stopping comes only when stopping.

quiz.q: When is madd lazim "in a letter"?
options: When it is in the letters at the start of surahs
When it is across two words
quiz.why: It is in a letter in the letters at the start of surahs, as in «الٓمٓ».

quiz.q: Do the reciters differ on the length of madd lazim?
options: No, all stretch it six counts
quiz.why: The reciters agree on six counts.

lessons.title: Madd lazim in words: heavy and light
lessons.lede: Madd lazim in a word is a madd letter followed by an original sukun in a word: heavy if it is merged, light if not.

idea.lead: Madd lazim in a word has its sukun in a word, and is of two kinds. Heavy: a madd letter followed by a doubled letter, as in «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ», «ٱلصَّآخَّةُ», «دَآبَّةٖ» and «ٱلۡحَآقَّةُ», called heavy because the shaddah is heavy. Light: a madd letter followed by a sukun that is not merged, which in the Quran comes only in «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ», in its two places in Yunus (51 and 91). Both are stretched six counts.
idea.kidsLead: When a doubled letter comes after a madd letter in the same word, as in «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ», we stretch six counts. «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ» in Surah Yunus is the same.

how.text: A madd letter and a doubled letter after it, in one word: «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ», «ٱلصَّآخَّةُ», «دَآبَّةٖ».
A madd letter and a sukun without idgham after it, in one word: in the Quran, «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ», twice in Yunus (51 and 91).
The madd sign «ـٓ» above the madd letter, followed by a doubled letter or a sukun.

idea.note: There are many examples of the heavy kind, including «ٱلطَّآمَّةُ», «أَتُحَٰٓجُّوٓنِّي» and «تَأۡمُرُوٓنِّيٓ». In «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ» Hafs has two ways: changing the hamzah to a madd of six counts, or tas-hil, as in lesson 51.

ayat.findHint: Find the madd letter and the doubled letter or sukun after it, then bring the colours back to check.

why: An alif with a doubled laam after it: heavy, in a word
An alif with a doubled khaa after it: heavy, in a word
An alif followed by a laam with sukun, not merged: light, in a word

ayat.tip: The alif in «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ» replaces the hamzah of the question, and the laam after it has a fixed sukun.

quiz.q: What kind of madd is in «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ»?
quiz.why: A doubled laam comes after the alif in the same word: necessary, heavy, in a word.

quiz.why: The light kind is a madd letter followed by a sukun that is not merged, in a word.

quiz.q: In which word does the light kind in a word come in the Quran?
quiz.why: Only in «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ», in its two places in Yunus.

quiz.q: What kind of madd is in «ٱلصَّآخَّةُ»?
quiz.why: A doubled khaa follows the alif in the same word, so it is heavy, in a word.

quiz.q: Why is the heavy kind called heavy?
options: Because the shaddah after the madd letter is heavy
quiz.why: Its sukun is merged into a doubled letter, and the shaddah is heavy.

quiz.q: How long is the light kind in a word?
quiz.why: Every kind of madd lazim is six counts.

quiz.q: In which surah does «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ» come twice?
quiz.why: In Surah Yunus, ayahs 51 and 91.

lessons.title: Madd lazim in letters: heavy and light
lessons.lede: Madd lazim in a letter is in the letters at the start of surahs whose names have three letters with a madd letter in the middle: heavy if its end merges, light if not.

idea.lead: Madd lazim in a letter is in the letters at the start of surahs whose names are said with three letters, the middle one a madd letter. They are eight, gathered in «نَقَصَ عَسَلُكُمْ»: noon, qaaf, saad, 'ayn, seen, laam, kaaf and meem. If the end of the letter merges into the next, it is heavy, like the laam of «الٓمٓ», read «أَلِفۡ لَآمِّيمۡ»; if it does not, it is light, like «قٓ», «نٓ» and the meem of «الٓمٓ». All are stretched six counts, except 'ayn, which has two ways.
idea.kidsLead: At the start of some surahs are letters we read by their names, as «الٓمٓ» is read «أَلِفْ لَآمْ مِيمْ». Eight of them are stretched six counts, gathered in «نَقَصَ عَسَلُكُمْ».

how.text: At the start of surahs: each letter whose name has three letters with a madd letter in the middle, gathered in «نَقَصَ عَسَلُكُمْ»: «ن ق ص ع س ل ك م».
When the end of the letter merges into the next: «الٓمٓ» is read «لَآمِّيمْ», so the laam is heavy.
When it does not merge: «قٓ», «نٓ», «صٓ», and the meem of «الٓمٓ».
In «كٓهيعٓصٓ» and «حمٓ ۝ عٓسٓقٓ», 'ayn is stretched four or six counts, six being preferred, since its yaa is a leen letter, not a madd letter.

idea.note: In «طسٓمٓ» the noon of «سِينۡ» merges into the meem of «مِيمۡ», so the seen is heavy; it is said clearly in «طسٓ» at the start of An-Naml. The 'ayn in «كٓهيعٓصٓ» and «عٓسٓقٓ» is a leen letter, so four or six counts are allowed, and six is preferred.

The meem: «مِيمۡ» is light, in a letter

ayat.tip: The taa in «طسٓمٓ» is one of «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ», so it is stretched only two counts.

options: The meem at its end merges into the next meem
quiz.why: «لَامْ» then «مِيمْ»: the meem of «لَامْ» merges into the meem of «مِيمْ», so it is heavy.

options: Four or six, six being preferred
quiz.why: The yaa in «عَيْن» is a leen letter, so four or six counts are allowed; six is preferred.

quiz.q: How many letters are stretched as madd lazim in a letter?
quiz.why: Eight, gathered in «نَقَصَ عَسَلُكُمْ».

quiz.q: What kind of madd is in «قٓ»?
quiz.why: Qaaf is said «قَافۡ» and its end does not merge, so it is light, in a letter.

quiz.q: What kind of madd is in the meem of «الٓمٓ» when you stop on it?
quiz.why: «مِيمۡ» does not merge into anything after it, so it is light, in a letter.

lessons.title: The separate letters at the start of surahs
lessons.lede: Twenty-nine surahs begin with separate letters said by their names. In madd they are of three kinds: not stretched, two counts, and six counts.

idea.lead: The separate letters are fourteen, and twenty-nine surahs begin with them. They are read by the names of the letters, not their sounds. In madd they are of three kinds. Alif is not stretched, since there is no madd letter in the middle of its name, «أَلِفۡ». Five letters have names of two letters, the second a madd letter, gathered in «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ»: haa (ح), yaa, taa (ط), haa (ه) and raa; they are stretched naturally, two counts. Eight have names of three letters with a madd letter in the middle, gathered in «نَقَصَ عَسَلُكُمْ»; they take madd lazim, six counts, except 'ayn, which may be four or six.
idea.kidsLead: At the start of some surahs are letters we read by their names: «الٓمٓ», «يسٓ», «حمٓ». We do not stretch alif; we stretch «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ» two counts, and «نَقَصَ عَسَلُكُمْ» six counts.

how.text: Said «أَلِفۡ», with no madd.
Two counts: «طه» is read «طَا هَا», and the haa (ح) in «حمٓ» is «حَا».
Six counts, necessarily: «صٓ» is read «صَآدۡ».
In «كٓهيعٓصٓ» and «عٓسٓقٓ»: four or six counts, and six is preferred.
Hafs says the noon clearly in «يسٓ ۝ وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانِ» and «نٓ ۚ وَٱلۡقَلَمِ», before the waw after it.

idea.note: In «الٓمٓ ۝ ٱللَّهُ» at the start of Al Imran, when joining, the meem takes a fathah to avoid two letters with sukun meeting; it may be stretched six counts, counting the original sukun, or two, counting the new vowel. Hafs stops on it with six counts.

ayat.findHint: Find the opening letters in each ayah: which are stretched six counts and which two? Then bring the colours back to check.

why: 'Ayn, seen and qaaf: madd lazim in letters, with 'ayn four or six
The seen: six counts
The yaa: two counts
Kaaf and saad: six counts, and 'ayn four or six
Haa (ه) and yaa: two counts

ayat.tip: Letters with the madd sign «ـٓ» are stretched six counts; those without it, two, except alif.

quiz.q: How many surahs begin with separate letters?
quiz.why: Twenty-nine surahs; the separate letters are fourteen.

quiz.q: How is a letter of «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ» stretched?
quiz.why: These letters have names of two letters, the second a madd letter, so they are stretched naturally.

quiz.q: Why is the alif in «الٓمٓ» not stretched?
options: Because its name «أَلِفۡ» has no madd letter in the middle
quiz.why: Alif is said «أَلِفۡ», with no madd letter in it.

quiz.q: How is «طه» read?
quiz.why: Taa (ط) and haa (ه) are among «حَيٌّ طَهُرَ», so each is stretched two counts.

quiz.q: What are the two ways for the meem of «الٓمٓ ۝ ٱللَّهُ» when joining?
quiz.why: The meem takes a fathah, so it may be six counts, counting the original sukun, or two, counting the new vowel.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read the noon in «يسٓ ۝ وَٱلۡقُرۡءَانِ»?
quiz.why: Hafs says the noon clearly in «يسٓ» and «نٓ».

quiz.q: How many of the opening letters are stretched six counts?
quiz.why: Eight, gathered in «نَقَصَ عَسَلُكُمْ».

lessons.title: The madd of distinction (madd al-farq)
lessons.lede: The madd of distinction is a madd lazim in three words where the hamzah of a question comes before a connecting hamzah; it is stretched six counts to tell a question from a statement.

formula.caption: Counts, changing the hamzah to alif

idea.lead: When the hamzah of a question comes before the connecting hamzah of a word with «ال», the connecting hamzah is not dropped, so the question is not mistaken for a statement. Instead it becomes an alif stretched six counts, since a laam with sukun follows it, or it is softened (tas-hil) between hamzah and alif with no madd. It is called the madd of distinction because it tells a question from a statement. It is in three words in six places: «ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ» (Al-An'am 143 and 144), «ءَآللَّهُ» (Yunus 59 and An-Naml 59) and «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ» (Yunus 51 and 91).
idea.kidsLead: In three words in the Quran there is a question, as in «ءَآللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمۡ»: we stretch the alif six counts so the listener knows it is a question, not a statement.

how.text: The connecting hamzah becomes an alif stretched six counts; this is the preferred way.
The connecting hamzah is softened between hamzah and alif, with no madd; learn it from a teacher.
Madd lazim in a word: heavy in «ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ» and «ءَآللَّهُ», since the laam merges, and light in «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ».
Six: Al-An'am 143 and 144, Yunus 51, 59 and 91, An-Naml 59.

idea.note: Without the madd, the question would sound like a statement: «ٱللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمۡ» is a statement, and «ءَآللَّهُ أَذِنَ لَكُمۡ» a question. In «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ» there is a second, badal madd after the laam, which Hafs reads for two counts.

ayat.legendNext: The laam with sukun after it
ayat.findHint: Find the places of the madd of distinction in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Madd of distinction: six counts, or tas-hil
Madd of distinction: six counts, or tas-hil
Madd of distinction: madd lazim, light, in a word

ayat.tip: In «ءَآللَّهُ», compare the question with saying «ٱللَّهُ أَذِنَ»: the madd is what shows it is a question.

options: Turning the hamzah into an alif with six counts, or easing it
quiz.why: The second hamzah becomes an alif stretched six counts, or it is eased between hamzah and alif.

quiz.q: Why is it called the madd of distinction?
options: Because it tells a question from a statement

quiz.why: Six places, in three words.

quiz.why: A laam with a fixed sukun follows the alif, so it is stretched six counts.

quiz.q: What kind of madd is in «ءَآللَّهُ»?
quiz.why: A doubled laam follows the alif, since the laam of «ال» merges into the laam of the name Allah, so it is heavy.

quiz.why: The hamzah of a question comes before the connecting hamzah in «ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ».

quiz.why: Tas-hil between hamzah and alif, learned from a teacher.

lessons.title: The madd for stopping (al-ʿarid lis-sukun)
lessons.lede: The madd for stopping is a madd letter followed by a letter that takes sukun because you stop; it may be two, four or six counts.

idea.lead: The madd for stopping (al-'arid lis-sukun) is a madd letter followed by a letter that has a vowel when joining and takes sukun because you stop, as when stopping on «ٱلرَّحِيمِ», «نَسۡتَعِينُ» and «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ». It is called 'arid (passing) because the sukun is not original: it comes when you stop and goes when you join. It may be two counts (qasr), four (tawassut) or six (tul). Ibn al-Jazari says: «أَوْ عَرَضَ السُّكُونُ وَقْفًا مُسْجَلَا» (or when the sukun comes for stopping, in every case).
idea.kidsLead: When we stop at the end of an ayah on a word with a madd letter before its last letter, like «ٱلرَّحِيمْ», we may stretch two, four or six counts. When we join, we do not go beyond two.

how.text: A madd letter followed by a letter with sukun for the stop: «ٱلرَّحِيمۡ», «نَسۡتَعِينۡ», «يَعۡلَمُونۡ».
Two, four or six counts when stopping; when joining it goes back to the natural madd.
Whatever length you choose, keep it in the same kind of places through the recitation.
When you stop with rawm, saying part of the vowel, only two counts are allowed, since the sukun is not complete. Level 3 covers rawm.

idea.note: When a joined madd comes before the letter you stop on, as in «ٱلسَّمَآءِ», lesson 45 applies: four, five or six counts. A madd letter that is itself the last letter you stop on, as in «وَٱلضُّحَىٰ», is not stretched; it is natural.

ayat.legendNext: The letter with sukun for the stop
ayat.findHint: Look at the end of each ayah: which madd letter comes before the letter you stop on? Then bring the colours back to check.

why: A madd yaa before the meem you stop on: madd for stopping
A madd yaa before the noon you stop on: madd for stopping

ayat.tip: Listen to the reciter at the end of each ayah: he stretches the yaa before the letter he stops on.

quiz.why: Its sukun comes only from stopping; when the word is joined, it goes.

quiz.q: How long may the madd for stopping be?
quiz.why: Two counts (qasr), four (tawassut) or six (tul).

quiz.q: What kind of madd is there when stopping on:
quiz.why: The yaa is a madd letter, and the noon after it takes a sukun for the stop.

quiz.why: Rawm says part of the vowel, so the sukun is not complete: only two counts are allowed.

quiz.q: Why is it called 'arid (passing)?
options: Because its sukun comes for the stop and goes when joining
Because it is at the start of surahs
quiz.why: Its sukun is not original; it comes because of the stop.

lessons.title: The leen madd
lessons.lede: The leen madd is a waw or yaa with sukun after fathah, followed by a letter that takes sukun for the stop; it may be two, four or six counts.

idea.lead: The two leen letters are waw and yaa with sukun after fathah, as in «خَوۡفٍ» and «بَيۡتٍ». They are called leen (soft) because they come out softly, with no effort for the tongue. When a letter that takes sukun for the stop follows them, they may be two counts (qasr), four (tawassut) or six (tul); this is the leen madd. When the word is joined to the next, the leen letter is not stretched at all.
idea.kidsLead: Waw and yaa with sukun after fathah, as in «خَوْفْ» and «ٱلْبَيْتْ»: when we stop after them, we may stretch them two, four or six counts. When we join, we do not stretch them.

how.text: A waw or yaa with sukun after a fathah, followed by a letter with sukun for the stop: «خَوۡفۡ», «ٱلۡبَيۡتۡ».
No madd in a leen letter when the word is joined: «مِّنۡ خَوۡفِۭ» is joined without madd.
Do not stretch the leen letter more than the madd for stopping when both come in one recitation.
When you stop with rawm, there is no madd in the leen letter.

idea.note: Leen is one of the characteristics without opposites (lesson 61). The 'ayn in «كٓهيعٓصٓ» and «عٓسٓقٓ» is a leen letter, so four or six counts are allowed (lesson 50).

ayat.tip: The leen madd happens only when stopping, so listen to the reciter at the end of the ayah.

quiz.why: Waw and yaa with sukun after a fathah, as in «خَوۡفٍ» and «بَيۡتٍ».

quiz.why: A leen letter is stretched only when you stop with a sukun.

quiz.why: A yaa with sukun after fathah, followed by a taa that takes sukun for the stop: a leen madd.

lessons.title: The ranks of madd and the stronger cause
lessons.lede: Madds differ in strength: lazim is strongest, then joined, then for stopping, then separated, then badal. When two causes meet, the stronger counts.

idea.lead: The secondary madds, from strongest to weakest, are: lazim, then joined, then for stopping, then separated, then badal. The strongest are those whose cause is original and joined to the madd letter. When one madd letter has two causes of madd, the stronger counts and the weaker is dropped: a weak cause does not count when a strong one is there.
idea.kidsLead: When one word has two causes of madd, we follow the stronger one: lazim is stronger than all the madds, then joined, then for stopping, then separated, then badal.

how.text: Lazim, then joined, then for stopping, then separated, then badal.
When two causes meet in one madd letter, the stronger counts and the weaker is dropped.
«ءَآمِّينَ ٱلۡبَيۡتَ»: lazim counts, so it is six counts.
«رِئَآءَ ٱلنَّاسِ»: the alif has a hamzah before it and after it, so the joined madd counts: four or five.
Stopping on «ٱلسَّمَآءِ»: the joined madd and the madd for stopping meet, so four, five or six are allowed, never two.

idea.note: This rule keeps a letter with a strong cause from being shortened because of a weak one, and keeps the length right when causes meet, especially when stopping. Learn the lengths of madds together from a teacher.

ayat.findHint: Find the madd letter where two causes meet, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Badal and lazim in the alif: lazim counts, six counts
A joined madd in «ٱلشِّتَآءِ»; when stopping, the madd for stopping joins it: four, five or six, never two

ayat.tip: In «ءَآمِّينَ» there is a hamzah before the alif and a shaddah after it, so the stronger cause is lazim.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest madd?
quiz.why: Lazim is the strongest, because its cause is an original, fixed sukun joined to the madd letter.

quiz.q: Which is the weakest secondary madd?
quiz.why: Badal is the weakest, so it is dropped when a stronger cause comes with it.

quiz.q: When two causes meet in one madd letter, which counts?
quiz.why: The stronger counts and the weaker is dropped.

quiz.why: The joined madd and the madd for stopping meet, and the joined madd is never less than four, so four, five or six are allowed.

quiz.q: Which is stronger: joined or separated?
quiz.why: The joined madd is stronger, because the hamzah is joined to the madd letter in one word.

quiz.q: Which is stronger: the madd for stopping or the separated madd?
quiz.why: The order: lazim, then joined, then for stopping, then separated, then badal.

lessons.title: Hams and jahr (whispered and voiced)
lessons.lede: Hams is the breath flowing with a letter, because it presses lightly on its makhraj; its ten letters are gathered in «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ». Jahr is its opposite.

idea.lead: In Arabic, hams means quietness. As a term, it is the breath flowing as a letter is said, because the letter presses lightly on its makhraj. Its ten letters are gathered in «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ». Jahr means openness: as a term, the breath being held as a letter is said, because the letter presses firmly on its makhraj. Its letters are the other nineteen. Ibn al-Jazari says: «مَهْمُوسُهَا فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتْ» (its whispered letters are «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتْ»).
idea.kidsLead: Some letters come out with a breath, like a whisper: «سْ», «شْ», «فْ». There are ten, gathered in «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ». The other letters have a strong sound that holds the breath, like «دْ» and «عْ». Put your hand in front of your mouth and say «أَسْ», then «أَزْ»: you feel the air in the first.

how.text: Faa, haa (ح), thaa, haa (ه), sheen, khaa, saad, seen, kaaf and taa: «فَحَثَّهُ شَخْصٌ سَكَتَ».
Nineteen letters: all the others, such as dal, 'ayn and meem.
Give the letter a sukun after a hamzah: in «أَسْ» the breath flows; in «أَزْ» it is held, though both come from one makhraj.
Whispered and shadid: the sound stops, then a little breath comes out, with no exaggeration and no qalqalah: «وَٱتۡلُ», «يُدۡرِكۡكُمُ».
It tells apart letters that share a makhraj, such as whispered taa (ت) and voiced dal, or seen and zay.

idea.note: Hams is clearest in a letter with sukun. Mistakes: overdoing the hams until the letter whistles or puffs, or losing it so that taa and kaaf with sukun bounce as if they were qalqalah letters.

ayat.findHint: Find the letters with sukun in each ayah: which are whispered, and which voiced? Then bring the colours back to check.

Laam is voiced

The 'ayn in «نَعۡبُدُ» is voiced
The seen in «خُسۡرٍ» is whispered
The laam in «ٱلۡإِنسَٰنَ» is voiced

ayat.tip: Listen to the seen with sukun in «ٱلۡمُسۡتَقِيمَ» and «نَسۡتَعِينُ»: the breath flows with it, unlike 'ayn and laam.

lessons.title: Shiddah, rakhawah and tawassut
lessons.lede: Shiddah is the sound being held with a letter; its letters are «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ». Rakhawah is the sound flowing. Tawassut is in between; its letters are «لِنْ عُمَرْ».

idea.lead: In Arabic, shiddah means strength. As a term, it is the sound being held as a letter is said, because it presses on its makhraj with full strength. Its eight letters are gathered in «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ». Rakhawah means softness: the sound flowing with the letter, because it presses lightly. Tawassut is in between: the sound is neither fully held nor fully flowing. Its five letters are gathered in «لِنْ عُمَرْ». Ibn al-Jazari says: «شَدِيدُهَا لَفْظُ أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ، وَبَيْنَ رِخْوٍ وَالشَّدِيدِ لِنْ عُمَرْ» (its shadid letters are the words «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ», and between rikhw and shadid are «لِنْ عُمَرْ»).
idea.kidsLead: Some letters stop their sound suddenly, like «أَدْ» and «أَقْ»: there are eight, gathered in «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ». Some let their sound go on, like «أَسْ» and «أَشْ». Five are in the middle, their sound going on a little: «لِنْ عُمَرْ».

how.text: Eight letters: hamzah, jeem, dal, qaaf, taa (ط), baa, kaaf and taa (ت), gathered in «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ».
Five letters: laam, noon, 'ayn, meem and raa, gathered in «لِنْ عُمَرْ».
Sixteen letters: all the others, such as seen, sheen and faa.
Give the letter a sukun after a hamzah: in «أَدْ» the sound stops; in «أَسْ» it goes on; in «أَلْ» it goes on a little, then stops.
Shiddah holds the sound; jahr holds the breath. So kaaf and taa are shadid and whispered: the sound is held while the breath flows.

idea.note: The letters with both jahr and shiddah are the qalqalah letters «قُطْبُ جَدٍّ», since both breath and sound are held. Mistakes: letting the sound of a shadid letter with sukun go on, cutting off the sound of a rikhw letter, or drawing out the letters of tawassut.

ayat.findHint: Find the letters with sukun in each ayah: which are shadid, their sound stopping, and which rikhw, their sound flowing? Then bring the colours back to check.

Seen is rikhw

The seen with sukun is rikhw: the sound flows with it

ayat.tip: Compare the dal in «يَلِدۡ» with the meem in «لَمۡ»: the dal stops; the meem goes on a little, since it is a letter of tawassut.

quiz.q: How many shadid letters are there?
quiz.why: Eight, gathered in «أَجِدْ قَطٍ بَكَتْ».

quiz.q: Which of these letters is rikhw?
quiz.why: Seen is neither shadid nor in between, so it is rikhw.

quiz.q: How do shiddah and jahr differ?
options: Shiddah holds the sound; jahr holds the breath

lessons.title: Isti'la' and istifal (elevated and low)
lessons.lede: Isti'la' is the back of the tongue rising to the palate when a letter is said; its seven letters are gathered in «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ». Its opposite, istifal, is the tongue staying low, in all the other letters.

idea.lead: In Arabic, isti'la' means rising. As a term, it is the back of the tongue rising to the palate when a letter is said, so the mouth fills with its echo. Its letters are seven, gathered in «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ». Istifal means going down: the tongue staying away from the palate when a letter is said, in all the letters except the elevated ones. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَسَبْعُ عُلْوٍ خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ حَصَرْ» (and seven elevated letters, gathered in «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ»).
idea.kidsLead: For seven letters we raise the back of the tongue to the roof of the mouth, so the mouth fills with their sound: «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ». With the other letters the tongue stays low, so they come out light.

how.text: Seven letters: khaa, saad, daad, ghayn, taa (ط), qaaf and dhaa (ظ), gathered in «خُصَّ ضَغْطٍ قِظْ».
Twenty-two letters: all the others. They are light, except raa, laam and alif in some cases.
Isti'la' makes a letter heavy, and itbaq makes it heavier still: taa (ط) is heavier than qaaf.
An elevated letter stays heavy even with kasrah, though less heavy: «قِيلَ», «خِيفَةٗ», «غِشَٰوَةٞ».
A low letter is not made heavy because an elevated one is next to it: the taa in «تَطۡهِيرٗا», the seen in «يَسۡطُونَ».

idea.note: Isti'la' and istifal are opposite characteristics, and they show in heavy and light letters (lesson 65). It is a mistake to make an elevated letter light before a yaa or kasrah, or to make a low letter heavy because an elevated one is next to it.

ayat.findHint: Find the elevated letters in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

lessons.title: Itbaq and infitah (covered and open)
lessons.lede: Itbaq is part of the tongue pressing the palate, holding the sound between them, in saad, daad, taa (ط) and dhaa (ظ). Its opposite, infitah, is in all the other letters.

idea.lead: In Arabic, itbaq means sticking together. As a term, it is part of the tongue pressing the palate, so the sound is held between them, when a letter is said. Its letters are four: saad, daad, taa (ط) and dhaa (ظ). Infitah means parting: the tongue staying apart from the palate so the air comes out between them, in all the letters except the covered ones. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَصَادُ ضَادٌ طَاءُ ظَاءٌ مُطْبَقَهْ» (and saad, daad, taa and dhaa are covered).
idea.kidsLead: For four letters we press the middle of the tongue to the roof of the mouth, so their sound is very full: saad, daad, taa (ط) and dhaa (ظ). They are the heaviest letters.

how.text: Four of them: saad, daad, taa (ط) and dhaa (ظ), the heaviest letters of all.
Every covered letter is raised, but not every raised letter is covered: khaa, ghayn and qaaf are raised and open.
Twenty-five letters: all but saad, daad, taa (ط) and dhaa (ظ), including the elevated khaa, ghayn and qaaf.
Taa (ط) is the strongest covered letter, then daad, then saad, then dhaa (ظ).
When taa (ط) merges into taa (ت), its itbaq stays: «بَسَطتَ», «أَحَطتُ» (lesson 77).

idea.note: It is a mistake to lose itbaq, so that saad becomes seen, taa (ط) becomes taa (ت), dhaa (ظ) becomes dhal and daad becomes dal; the word changes, and the meaning may too.

quiz.why: Taa (ط) is raised and covered, more than any other letter.

lessons.title: Idhlaq and ismat
lessons.lede: Idhlaq is a letter being light and quick to say, because it comes from the tip of the tongue or the lips; its six letters are gathered in «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبٍّ». Ismat is its opposite.

idea.lead: In Arabic, idhlaq means a sharp, fluent tongue. As a term, it is a letter being light and quick to say, because it comes from the tip of the tongue or from the lip. Its six letters are gathered in «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبٍّ»: faa, raa, meem, noon, laam and baa. Ismat means holding back: as a term, a letter being heavier and slower to say, in the other twenty-three letters. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَفِرَّ مِنْ لُبِّ الحُرُوفِ المُذْلَقَهْ» (and «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبِّ» are the fluent letters).
idea.kidsLead: Six letters are light and quick on the tongue; they come from the tip of the tongue or the lips. We gather them in «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبٍّ». The other letters are a little heavier.

how.text: Faa, raa, meem, noon, laam and baa: «فِرَّ مِنْ لُبٍّ».
Raa, noon and laam come from the tip of the tongue; faa, baa and meem from the lips.
Twenty-three letters: all the others.
They are called "held back" because they cannot build an Arabic word of four or five root letters alone: such a word nearly always has a fluent letter.
It is a feature of the language that helps with word roots; it brings no rule in recitation, as tafkhim or qalqalah do.

idea.note: Idhlaq and ismat leave no mark on how letters sound, as hams and jahr do, so many teachers pass over them quickly. They are the last of the five pairs of opposite sifat.

ayat.tip: The fluent letters come from the tip of the tongue or the lips: they are the lightest and easiest letters to say.

lessons.title: Safir (whistling)
lessons.lede: Safir is an extra sound like a bird's whistle, from between the front teeth and the tip of the tongue; its letters are three: saad, zay and seen.

idea.lead: In Arabic, safir is a sound like a bird's. As a term, it is an extra sound from between the front teeth and the tip of the tongue when saad, zay and seen are said. It is the first of the seven characteristics without opposites: safir, qalqalah, leen, inhiraf, takrir, tafashshi and istitalah. Ibn al-Jazari says: «صَفِيرُهَا صَادٌ وَزَايٌ سِينُ» (its whistling letters are saad, zay and seen).
idea.kidsLead: Saad, zay and seen have a sharp sound like a little bird's whistle. We let it be heard clearly, without overdoing it.

how.text: An extra sound like a bird's whistle, in saad, zay and seen: «ٱلصَّمَدُ», «ٱلۡوَسۡوَاسِ».
Saad, since it is covered and elevated, then zay, since it is voiced, then seen, which is whispered and low.
Safir with itbaq tells saad from seen: «يَصۡطَرِخُونَ» and «يَسۡطُونَ»; with voice it tells zay from seen, as in the zay of «زَيَّنَّا».
Safir is clearest with sukun or shaddah: «ٱلۡوَسۡوَاسِ», «ٱلصَّمَدُ», «ٱلۡمِسۡكِينِ».

idea.note: It is a mistake to overdo safir until it is a real whistle, or to lose it so that seen comes out as thaa, as with a lisp; this is corrected by reciting to a teacher.

ayat.findHint: Find the whistling letters in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

quiz.why: Seven: safir, qalqalah, leen, inhiraf, takrir, tafashshi and istitalah.

quiz.why: Saad, zay and seen: their sound is like a bird's whistle.

quiz.why: Safir is a sharp extra sound that comes with saad, zay and seen.

quiz.q: Which whistling letter is strongest?
quiz.why: Saad is strongest, since it is covered and elevated, then zay, since it is voiced, then seen.

quiz.why: Safir gets its due, no more and no less.
