lessons.title: Leen and inhiraf
lessons.lede: Leen is waw and yaa with sukun after fathah coming out easily, with no effort; inhiraf is a letter leaning, after it starts, towards another makhraj, in laam and raa.

idea.lead: In Arabic, leen means ease. As a term, it is a letter coming from its makhraj easily, with no effort for the tongue. It has two letters: waw and yaa with sukun after fathah, as in «خَوۡفٍ» and «بَيۡتٍ». Inhiraf means leaning: a letter leaning, after it starts, until it reaches another makhraj. It has two letters: laam leans towards the tip of the tongue, and raa towards its top. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَاللِّينُ، وَاوٌ وَيَاءٌ سَكَنَا وَانْفَتَحَا، قَبْلَهُمَا وَالِانْحِرَافُ صُحِّحَا، فِي اللَّامِ وَالرَّا».
idea.kidsLead: Waw and yaa with sukun after a fathah come out easy and soft: «خَوۡفٍ», «بَيۡتٍ». The sound of laam and raa leans a little from its place, so we neither hold it nor stretch it.

how.text: Waw and yaa with sukun after fathah: «خَوۡفٍ», «بَيۡتٍ», «قُرَيۡشٍ». Leen is stretched when you stop on it (lesson 53).
A letter turning, after it comes out, away from its makhraj: laam towards the tip of the tongue, raa a little towards its back.
When the waw follows dammah or the yaa follows kasrah, they are madd letters: «يَقُولُ», «قِيلَ»; after fathah they are leen letters.
Without inhiraf the sound of laam and raa would flow like the soft letters; they are in-between letters «لِنۡ عُمَرۡ».

idea.note: A mistake in leen is stretching it when joining, or turning it into a madd letter. A mistake in inhiraf is saying laam leaning towards noon, or raa leaning towards laam or yaa, as happens with a lisp; learn them from a teacher.

The yaa in «ٱلۡبَيۡتِ» is a leen letter

quiz.q: What is leen as a term?

A letter coming from its makhraj easily, with no effort

quiz.why: A yaa with sukun after fathah is a leen letter.

lessons.title: Takrir (rolling)
lessons.lede: Takrir is raa being able to repeat, because the tip of the tongue trembles with it; it is learned so it can be avoided: raa is said with one light tap.

idea.lead: In Arabic, takrir means doing a thing again and again. As a term, it is the tip of the tongue trembling when raa is said, so it can repeat. It is a fixed characteristic of raa, but it is learned so it can be avoided: raa is said with one tap, because overdoing it adds raas that are not in the Quran. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَأَخْفِ تَكْرِيرًا إِذَا تُشَدَّدُ» (and hide the rolling when it is doubled).
idea.kidsLead: When we say raa, the tip of the tongue trembles a little. We make it one small tap, and we do not roll it «rrr».

how.text: The tip of the tongue trembling with raa. It is learned so as to avoid it: say raa with one light tremble, especially with a shaddah: «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ».
Rolling is most to be avoided in a raa with shaddah: «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ», «شَرِّ».
And in a raa with sukun, especially when stopping: «فَأَنذِرۡ», «وَٱلۡفَجۡرِ».
The tip of the tongue taps the gum once, without extra trembling, and without holding the sound so hard that the raa disappears.
Raa is voiced, in between, low, open and from the tip, with inhiraf and takrir; it is heavy or light depending on its state (lessons 68–70).

idea.note: It is a mistake to overdo the rolling until a doubled raa sounds like several raas, and also to hide it so much that the raa comes out with its sound trapped. The guide is hearing the raa from a teacher.

A raa with sukun at a stop: not rolled

quiz.q: Why learn the takrir of raa?
options: To avoid it: raa is said with one light tremble
quiz.why: Takrir is learned so as not to overdo it, especially in a doubled raa.

quiz.q: What is takrir as a term?
options: The tip of the tongue trembling when raa is said
A letter leaning to another makhraj
quiz.why: Takrir is the tip of the tongue trembling with raa, so it can repeat.

quiz.q: Which letter has takrir?
quiz.why: Takrir belongs to raa alone.

quiz.q: Where is rolling most to be avoided?
options: In a light raa with a vowel
quiz.why: A raa with shaddah is where rolling happens most, as in «ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ».

quiz.q: With how many taps is raa said?
quiz.why: Raa is said with one tap, so it does not repeat.

quiz.q: What is the mistake when stopping on «وَٱلۡفَجۡرِ»?
quiz.why: A raa with sukun at a stop must not be rolled.

quiz.q: What goes wrong when the rolling is hidden too much?
options: The raa comes out with its sound trapped and loses its character
quiz.why: Hiding the rolling does not mean holding the sound; it means leaving out the extra trembling.

lessons.title: Tafashshi and istitalah
lessons.lede: Tafashshi is the air spreading in the mouth when sheen is said; istitalah is the sound of daad stretching from the front of the side of the tongue to its end.

idea.lead: In Arabic, tafashshi means spreading. As a term, it is the air spreading in the mouth when a letter is said; its letter is sheen, by agreement, and some add faa and thaa. Istitalah means stretching: the sound stretching from the front of the side of the tongue to its end; its letter is daad, and it sets daad apart from dhaa (ظ) and dal. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَلِلتَّفَشِّي الشِّينُ ضَادًا اسْتَطِلْ» (for spreading, sheen; and stretch the daad).
idea.kidsLead: The air of sheen spreads through the whole mouth: «شَرِّ». The sound of daad stretches along the side of the tongue from its front to its end: «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ».

how.text: The air spreading through the mouth with sheen: «شَرِّ».
The sound of daad running from the front to the back of the side of the tongue: «وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ».
Istitalah is the sound stretching in the makhraj, and madd is stretching in a madd letter, so daad is not given extra time.
Tafashshi is clearest with sukun or shaddah: «ٱلۡمَشۡرِقِ», «ٱلشَّمۡسُ».
Comes from one side of the tongue, or both, with the upper molars beside it (lesson 16); lesson 73 sets it apart from dhaa (ظ).

idea.note: It is a mistake to lose the spreading so that sheen comes out weak like seen, or to lose the stretching so that daad becomes a heavy dal or dhaa (ظ). Daad is one of the hardest letters, so learn it from a teacher.

ayat.findHint: Find the sheen and daad in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Sheen: the air spreads
Daad lengthens along the side of the tongue (istitalah)
A daad with shaddah: it stretches

ayat.tip: Listen to the daad in «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ»: its sound stretches in the makhraj, then the madd comes in the alif after it.

quiz.why: Tafashshi is the air spreading through the mouth with sheen.

quiz.why: Daad lengthens: its sound runs along the side of the tongue.

quiz.why: Tafashshi is air spreading in the mouth; it is in sheen.

quiz.q: What is istitalah as a term?
options: The sound stretching from the front of the side of the tongue to its end
quiz.why: Istitalah is the sound stretching along the side of the tongue; it is in daad.

quiz.q: Which characteristic sets daad apart from dhaa (ظ)?
quiz.why: Daad and dhaa (ظ) share jahr, rakhawah, isti'la' and itbaq; only daad has istitalah.

quiz.q: Which letter spreads in «مِن شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ»?
quiz.why: Sheen is the spreading letter.

quiz.q: Is istitalah stretching daad by counts?
options: No, it is the sound stretching in its makhraj, with no madd time
quiz.why: Istitalah stretches in the makhraj; it adds no time.

lessons.title: Fixed and passing sifat, letter strength
lessons.lede: A fixed characteristic never leaves the letter, like jahr; a passing one comes in some states, like the heaviness of raa. The fixed ones make a letter strong or weak.

idea.lead: The characteristics of the letters are of two kinds. Fixed ones never leave the letter; if one were dropped, the letter would change or be spoiled; they are the characteristics with and without opposites already studied. Passing ones come to a letter in some states and leave it in others; dropping one is a mistake that does not destroy the letter, such as heavy and light raa, izhar, idgham, ikhfa' and iqlab, and madd and qasr. Some fixed characteristics are strong and some weak: a letter with many strong ones is strong, and one with many weak ones is weak.
idea.kidsLead: Some characteristics stay with a letter always, like the whisper of seen; some come and go, like the heaviness of raa: full in «رَبِّ» and light in «رِجَالٞ». A letter with many strong characteristics is strong, like taa (ط).

how.text: Jahr and hams, shiddah, rakhawah and tawassut, isti'la' and istifal, itbaq and infitah, idhlaq and ismat, safir, qalqalah, leen, inhiraf, takrir, tafashshi and istitalah.
The best known: izhar, idgham, iqlab, ikhfa', tafkhim, tarqiq, madd, qasr, a vowel, sukun and saktah.
Jahr, shiddah, isti'la', itbaq, ismat, safir, qalqalah, inhiraf, takrir, tafashshi and istitalah.
Hams, rakhawah, istifal, infitah, idhlaq and leen. Tawassut is between strong and weak.
The strongest letter is taa (ط), since all the strong characteristics meet in it; the weakest is haa (ه), and the others fall between.
A strong letter does not vanish entirely when it merges into a weak one: the itbaq of taa (ط) stays in «بَسَطتَ» (lesson 77).

idea.note: Scholars differ on whether some characteristics are strong or weak, especially idhlaq and ismat, and on the order of the letters by strength. The point of this lesson is to give a strong letter its due without weakening it, and a weak one its due without strengthening it.

ayat.findHint: Find the strong letter and the weak letter, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Taa (ط) is the strongest letter, and its itbaq stays
Taa (ت) is whispered and weaker, so taa (ط) merges into it incompletely

ayat.tip: Say «بَسَطتَ» slowly: the itbaq of taa (ط) stays, then taa (ت) is heard.

One that never leaves the letter
quiz.why: A fixed characteristic belongs to the letter itself; if it were dropped, the letter would change.

quiz.q: Which of these is a passing characteristic?
quiz.why: Raa is heavy in some states and light in others.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest letter?
quiz.why: Taa (ط) has all the strong characteristics: jahr, shiddah, isti'la', itbaq, ismat and qalqalah.

quiz.q: Which is the weakest letter?
quiz.why: Haa (ه) is whispered, soft, low and open, so it is the weakest letter.

quiz.q: Which of these is a weak characteristic?
quiz.why: Hams is weak; its opposite, jahr, is strong.

quiz.q: Which of these is a strong characteristic?
quiz.why: Jahr is a strong characteristic.

quiz.q: Why does the itbaq of taa (ط) stay in «بَسَطتَ»?
options: Because taa (ط) is stronger than taa (ت), so it does not vanish when merged
quiz.why: A strong letter does not vanish into a weak one, so the merging is incomplete.

lessons.title: Heavy and light letters: the general rules
lessons.lede: Tafkhim makes a letter heavy, so the mouth fills with its sound; tarqiq makes it light. The raised letters are always heavy; the low letters are light, except raa and laam in some cases; alif follows the letter before it.

idea.lead: In Arabic, tafkhim means fattening. As a term, it is a fullness in the sound of a letter, so that the mouth fills with its echo. Tarqiq means thinning: a lightness in the sound, so that the mouth does not fill. Letters are of three kinds. The seven raised letters are always heavy. The low letters are always light, except three: raa and the laam in the name Allah, which have their own lessons, and alif, which follows the letter before it. Ibn al-Jazari says: «فَرَقِّقَنْ مُسْتَفِلًا مِنْ أَحْرُفِ، وَحَاذِرَنْ تَفْخِيمَ لَفْظِ الأَلِفِ» (make the low letters light, and beware of making alif heavy).
idea.kidsLead: Some letters we read full, as if the mouth is filled with sound, like «ص», «ق» and «ط». Others are light and thin, like «س», «ك» and «ت». Alif takes on the letter before it: full in «قَالَ», light in «كَانَ».

how.text: They stay light even next to a heavy letter: the baa in «بَٰطِلٞ», the taa in «تَطۡهِيرٗا», the seen in «يَسۡطُونَ».
The ghunnah of a hidden noon or meem follows the letter after it: heavy before a raised letter «مِن قَبۡلُ», light before a low one.
They have their own rules: lesson 68 for raa, lesson 71 for the laam in the name Allah.

idea.note: Tafkhim has degrees (lesson 66), and alif follows the letter before it (lesson 67). It is a mistake to make a low letter heavy because a heavy letter is next to it, or to make an elevated letter with kasrah light.

quiz.why: Seen is low, so it stays light even with taa (ط) after it.

lessons.title: The degrees of tafkhim
lessons.lede: All the elevated letters are heavy, but their heaviness varies with their vowel: highest with fathah and alif after it, then fathah, then dammah, then sukun, then kasrah.

idea.lead: Tafkhim is fixed in the elevated letters, but its strength varies with the vowel of the letter. Many scholars count five degrees: fathah with alif after it «قَالَ», then fathah without alif «قَتَلَ», then dammah «قُتِلَ», then sukun «يَقۡتُلُ», then kasrah «قِيلَ». Some count three: fathah, then dammah, then kasrah, putting sukun with the vowel before it. Tafkhim also varies by letter: the covered letters are heavier than the open elevated ones.
idea.kidsLead: Heavy letters like qaaf, saad and taa (ط) are very full with fathah and alif «قَالَ», and less full with kasrah «قِيلَ», but they never become light.

how.text: Fathah with alif after it: «قَالَ», «طَآئِفَةٞ», «ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ».
Fathah without alif after it: «قَتَلَ», «صَبَرَ», «خَلَقَ».
Dammah: «قُتِلَ», «صُدُورِ», «ٱلطُّورِ».
Sukun: «يَقۡتُلُ», «أَطۡعَمَهُم», «يَخۡلُقُ». Those who count three put sukun with the vowel before it: «يَقۡطَعُونَ» like fathah, «يُخۡرِجُ» like dammah, «إِصۡلَٰحِهَا» like kasrah.
Kasrah: «قِيلَ», «خِيفَةٗ», «طِبۡتُمۡ». It is still heavy, never light.

idea.note: The difference over the number of degrees is a difference of grouping, not of recitation. What matters is that the heaviness of kasrah never reaches lightness, and that fathah is not made so heavy it sounds like dammah. Learn these differences from a teacher.

ayat.findHint: Find the elevated letter and its vowel in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

The qaaf in «قِيلَ» has kasrah: the lowest degree, and it is heavy

ayat.tip: Compare the qaaf in «قِيلَ» with the qaaf in «قَالَ» in the same ayah: both are heavy, and the second is heavier.

quiz.q: What is the lowest degree of tafkhim?
quiz.why: The lowest is kasrah, as in «قِيلَ», and it is still heavy.

quiz.why: Five: fathah with alif, then fathah, then dammah, then sukun, then kasrah.

quiz.why: The qaaf has dammah, so it is in the third degree.

lessons.title: Heavy and light alif
lessons.lede: Alif is neither heavy nor light in itself; it follows the letter before it: heavy after a heavy letter, light after a light one.

idea.lead: Alif is a madd letter made of air that rests on no part of the mouth, so it is neither heavy nor light in itself; it follows the letter before it. It is heavy after the elevated letters, after a heavy raa, and after the heavy laam of the name Allah, and light after the low letters. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَحَاذِرَنْ تَفْخِيمَ لَفْظِ الأَلِفِ» (and beware of making alif heavy), meaning after a light letter.
idea.kidsLead: Alif copies the letter before it: after qaaf, saad and taa (ط) it is full «قَالَ», and after kaaf, baa and noon it is light «كَانَ».

how.text: Heavy: «قَالَ», «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ», «طَآئِفَةٞ», «خَالِدِينَ».
Heavy after a heavy raa: «رَاقٖ», «ٱلۡأَبۡرَارَ».
Heavy after the heavy laam: «قَالَ ٱللَّهُ», «نَصۡرُ ٱللَّهِ»; light after the light laam: «بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ» (lesson 71).
Light: «كَانَ», «مَالِكِ», «ٱلنَّاسِ», «بَابَ».
Hafs has one imalah: the alif after the raa in «مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا» (Hud 41) is said towards yaa, and the raa before it is light (lesson 92).

idea.note: It is a mistake to make alif heavy after a light letter, as happens in «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ», «مَالِكِ» and «بَابَ», or light after a heavy one, as happens in «قَالَ» and «ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتِ».

The alif in «لَنَآ», after noon, is light

The alif after the jeem is light

ayat.tip: Compare the alif in «قَالَ» with the alif in «نَاقَةَ»: the first is heavy after qaaf, the second light after noon.

quiz.why: Kaaf is low, so the alif after it is light.

lessons.title: The rules of raa: when it is heavy
lessons.lede: Raa is heavy with fathah or dammah, with sukun after fathah or dammah, with sukun after a passing kasrah, or after an original kasrah with an elevated letter without kasrah after it in its word.

formula.caption: After kasrah, before an elevated letter

idea.lead: Raa is a low letter, but it is heavy in some states and light in others. It is heavy with fathah «رَبِّ», with dammah «رُزِقُواْ», with sukun after fathah «مَرۡيَمَ», with sukun after dammah «ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ», with sukun after a passing kasrah «ٱرۡجِعِيٓ», or with sukun after an original kasrah when an elevated letter without kasrah follows it in its word «مِرۡصَادٗا». At a stop it is heavy when fathah or dammah comes before it, or a letter with sukun other than yaa with fathah or dammah before that: «ٱلۡقَدۡرِ», «ٱلۡعُسۡرِ».
idea.kidsLead: We say raa full when it has fathah or dammah «رَبِّ», «رُزِقُوا», and when it has sukun with fathah or dammah before it «مَرۡيَمَ», «ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ».

how.text: With fathah «رَبِّ», dammah «رُزِقُواْ», or sukun after fathah «مَرۡيَمَ» or dammah «ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ».
With sukun after a temporary kasrah «ٱرۡجِعِيٓ», or after an original kasrah with a raised letter, without kasrah, after it in its word: «قِرۡطَاسٖ», «مِرۡصَادٗا», «فِرۡقَةٖ».
At a stop it is heavy when fathah «ٱلۡقَمَرُ» or dammah «ٱلنُّذُرُ» comes before it, or a letter with sukun other than yaa with fathah or dammah before that: «ٱلۡقَدۡرِ», «ٱلۡعُسۡرِ».
The kasrah of a connecting hamzah is passing: «ٱرۡجِعِيٓ», «ٱرۡكَبُواْ», as is the kasrah added to avoid two letters with sukun: «أَمِ ٱرۡتَابُوٓاْ»; the raa after it is heavy.

idea.note: The heaviness of raa follows the degrees of the elevated letters by its vowel (lesson 66). It is a mistake to make a heavy raa light, or to roll it (lesson 62).

A dal with sukun comes before it, with fathah before that

lessons.title: The rules of raa: when it is light
lessons.lede: Raa is light with kasrah, or with sukun after an original kasrah joined to it when no elevated letter follows in its word; at a stop it is light after a yaa with sukun or a kasrah.

formula.caption: At a stop, after a yaa with sukun

idea.lead: Raa is light with an original or passing kasrah «رِجَالٞ», «وَٱذۡكُرِ ٱسۡمَ رَبِّكَ», or with sukun after an original kasrah joined to it in its word, when no elevated letter follows in the same word «فِرۡعَوۡنَ», «مِرۡيَةٖ». At a stop it is light when a yaa with sukun comes before it «خَيۡرٞ», «قَدِيرٞ», or a kasrah «مُّنتَشِرٞ», or a low letter with sukun with kasrah before that «ٱلذِّكۡرِ». An elevated letter in another word has no effect: «أَنذِرۡ قَوۡمَكَ».
idea.kidsLead: We say raa light when it has kasrah «رِجَالٌ», or when it has sukun with kasrah before it «فِرۡعَوۡنَ». When we stop on a raa with a yaa with sukun before it, we say it light «خَيۡرۡ».

how.text: With kasrah «رِجَالٞ», or with sukun after an original kasrah and no raised letter after it: «فِرۡعَوۡنَ», «وَٱغۡفِرۡ لَنَا».

A raa you stop on is light after a yaa with sukun «خَيۡرٞ», «قَدِيرٞ», or after a kasrah «مُّنتَشِرٞ», or after a low letter with sukun that follows a kasrah «ٱلذِّكۡرِ»; otherwise it is heavy «ٱلۡقَدۡرِ».
It prevents lightness only in the same word: in «أَنذِرۡ قَوۡمَكَ» (Nuh 1) and «فَٱصۡبِرۡ صَبۡرٗا» (Al-Ma'arij 5) the raa is light.
A raa with imalah is light; for Hafs it is only in «مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا» (Hud 41) (lesson 92).

idea.note: The kasrah must be original and joined: if it is passing «ٱرۡجِعِيٓ», or in the word before «ٱلَّذِي ٱرۡتَضَىٰ», the raa is heavy (lesson 68).

lessons.title: The rules of raa: where both are allowed
lessons.lede: In some words Hafs may make the raa heavy or light: «فِرۡقٖ» when joining and stopping, and «مِصۡرَ», «ٱلۡقِطۡرِ», «يَسۡرِ», «أَسۡرِ» and «نُذُرِ» when stopping.

idea.lead: In some words the causes of heaviness and lightness pull against each other, so both are allowed. In «فِرۡقٖ» (Ash-Shu'ara 63) the raa has sukun after an original kasrah, with qaaf after it, and the qaaf has kasrah: looking at the elevation, it is heavy; looking at the qaaf's kasrah, it is light; both are correct. In «مِصۡرَ» and «ٱلۡقِطۡرِ» at a stop, an elevated letter with sukun comes before the raa after kasrah; Ibn al-Jazari chose heavy for «مِصۡرَ» and light for «ٱلۡقِطۡرِ», looking at how they are joined. In the words that lost a yaa after the raa, «يَسۡرِ», «أَسۡرِ» and «وَنُذُرِ», heavy and light are both allowed at a stop, and many reciters prefer light, looking at the missing yaa.
idea.kidsLead: In a few words we may say the raa full or light, and both are correct, such as «فِرۡقٖ» in Surah Ash-Shu'ara.

how.text: In Ash-Shu'ara 63: the raa has sukun after kasrah, with a qaaf with kasrah after it, so it may be heavy or light, joining and stopping.
When stopping on «مِصۡرَ» (Yunus 87 and elsewhere), both are allowed, and heavy is preferred, since it has fathah when joined.
When stopping on «ٱلۡقِطۡرِ» (Saba' 12), both are allowed, and light is preferred, since it has kasrah when joined.
«إِذَا يَسۡرِ» (Al-Fajr 4), «أَنۡ أَسۡرِ» (Ta Ha 77, Ash-Shu'ara 52), «فَأَسۡرِ» (Hud 81, Al-Hijr 65, Ad-Dukhan 23), «وَنُذُرِ» (Al-Qamar): both when stopping, and light is preferred.
«مِصۡرَ» is heavy, since it has fathah; «ٱلۡقِطۡرِ», «يَسۡرِ», «أَسۡرِ» and «نُذُرِ» are light, since they have kasrah. Only «فِرۡقٖ» keeps both when joining.

idea.note: All these ways are correct and recited. The preferred ones above are the choices of those who chose them, and the reciter follows what he learned from his teacher.

quiz.why: Both are allowed only when stopping; when joining it is light because of its kasrah.

lessons.title: The laam in the name Allah
lessons.lede: The laam in the name Allah is heavy after a fathah or dammah, and light after a kasrah.

idea.lead: Laam is a low letter and always light, except the laam in the name Allah, «ٱللَّه» and «ٱللَّهُمَّ». It is heavy after a fathah or dammah, as in «قَالَ ٱللَّهُ», «رُسُلُ ٱللَّهِ» and «هُوَ ٱللَّهُ», or when you start with it, since the joining hamzah then has a fathah. It is light after a kasrah, original or temporary, as in «بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ», «لِلَّهِ» and «قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ».
idea.kidsLead: In the name «ٱللَّه», we read the laam full when a fathah or dammah comes before it «قَالَ ٱللَّهُ», and light when a kasrah comes before it «بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ».

how.text: «قَالَ ٱللَّهُ», «شَهِدَ ٱللَّهُ»: heavy.
«رُسُلُ ٱللَّهِ», «هُوَ ٱللَّهُ»: heavy.
«ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ»: heavy, since the joining hamzah before it has a fathah.
«بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ», «لِلَّهِ», «بِٱللَّهِ»: light.
Light after a temporary kasrah too: «قُلِ ٱللَّهُمَّ»; and after tanween given a kasrah to join: «أَحَدٌ ۝ ٱللَّهُ ٱلصَّمَدُ», when read together.

idea.note: This rule is only for the laam in the name Allah; every other laam is light, even next to a heavy letter: «وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ», «وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ». A common mistake is making the laam heavy in «لِلَّهِ» and «بِٱللَّهِ».

lessons.title: Kinds of laam: in verbs, particles, commands and nouns
lessons.lede: A laam with sukun is of five kinds: the laam of «ال», of a verb, of a particle, of a command, and of a noun. Each has its rule of izhar or idgham.

idea.lead: A laam with sukun in the Quran is of five kinds. The laam of «ال», which has the moon izhar and the sun idgham (lesson 25). The laam of a verb, in the past «جَعَلۡنَا», the present «يَلۡتَقِطۡهُ» and the command «قُلۡ»; it is said clearly, unless laam or raa follows, when it merges: «قُل لَّهُمۡ», «قُل رَّبِّ». The laam of a particle, in «هَلۡ» and «بَلۡ»; it is clear except before laam and raa: «هَل لَّكَ», «بَل رَّفَعَهُ». The laam of a command, with sukun after waw, faa or thumma; it is always clear: «وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ». The laam of a noun, part of the word itself; it is always clear: «أَلۡسِنَتِكُمۡ», «وَأَلۡوَٰنِكُمۡ».
idea.kidsLead: We usually say a laam with sukun clearly: «قُلۡ هُوَ», «جَعَلۡنَا». But when laam or raa comes after it in «قُلۡ», «بَلۡ» and «هَلۡ», we merge it: «قُل رَّبِّ».

how.text: A moon laam is clear, a sun laam merges: «ٱلۡقَمَرُ», «ٱلشَّمۡسُ» (lesson 25).
Clear: «قُلۡ نَعَمۡ», «جَعَلۡنَا», «أَنزَلۡنَا»; merged into laam and raa: «قُل لَّهُمۡ», «وَقُل رَّبِّ».
In «هَلۡ» and «بَلۡ»: clear «هَلۡ أَتَىٰ», «بَلۡ هُمۡ»; merged into laam and raa: «هَل لَّكَ», «بَل رَّفَعَهُ».
Always clear: «وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ», «فَلۡيَعۡبُدُواْ», «ثُمَّ لۡيَقۡضُواْ».
Always clear: «أَلۡسِنَتِكُمۡ», «وَأَلۡوَٰنِكُمۡ», «سُلۡطَٰنٗا».
The laam in «بَلۡۜ رَانَ» (Al-Mutaffifin 14) does not merge, because Hafs pauses on it (lesson 85).

idea.note: The most common mistake is in the laam of a verb before noon: some reciters hide it or merge it, as in «قُلۡ نَعَمۡ», «جَعَلۡنَا», «أَنزَلۡنَا»; it must be said clearly. Every laam is light except the laam of the name Allah after fathah or dammah (lesson 71).

lessons.title: Daad and dhaa: makhraj, characteristics and telling them apart
lessons.lede: Daad and dhaa share most of their sifat, but differ in makhraj and in istitalah. Mixing them up is clear lahn and changes the meaning.

formula.caption: Side of the tongue with the molars
Tongue tip with the front teeth

idea.lead: Daad and dhaa are both voiced, rikhw, raised, covered and musmat; they differ in two things: makhraj and istitalah. Daad comes from one or both sides of the tongue against the upper molars, and its sound runs along the side: this is istitalah. Dhaa comes from the tip of the tongue against the edges of the upper front teeth. Mixing them up is clear lahn: «نَّاضِرَةٌ» means radiant, and «نَاظِرَةٞ» means looking. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَالضَّادَ بِاسْتِطَالَةٍ وَمَخْرَجِ، مَيِّزْ مِنَ الظَّاءِ وَكُلُّهَا تَجِي» (tell daad from dhaa by istitalah and makhraj).
idea.kidsLead: «ض» and «ظ» are two full letters that sound alike. «ض» comes from the side of the tongue with the back teeth, and its sound runs on. For «ظ», the tip of the tongue comes out a little between the front teeth. Careful: «نَاضِرَةٌ» means bright and beautiful, and «نَاظِرَةٌ» means looking.

how.text: From the side of the tongue against the upper molars (the left side is easier and more common), with the sound running along the side.
From the tip of the tongue against the edges of the upper front teeth; the tip comes out a little.
Jahr, rakhawah, isti'la', itbaq and ismat.
«نَّاضِرَةٌ» and «نَاظِرَةٞ» (Al-Qiyamah 22 and 23); «ضَلَّ» (went astray) and «ظَلَّ» (became).
Saying daad as a heavy dal, or as dhaa; or saying dhaa as a heavy zay.

idea.note: Hafs reads «وَمَا هُوَ عَلَى ٱلۡغَيۡبِ بِضَنِينٖ» (At-Takwir 24) with daad, meaning "stingy"; others read it with dhaa, meaning "suspected". Daad is one of the hardest letters to say: learn it from a teacher, by listening and repeating.

quiz.why: Dhaa comes from the tip of the tongue with the edges of the upper front teeth, like dhaal and thaa.

quiz.q: Which sifah does daad have and dhaa not?
quiz.why: Istitalah is the sound of daad running along the side of the tongue; dhaa does not have it.

quiz.q: What does «نَّاضِرَةٌ» mean in «وُجُوهٞ يَوۡمَئِذٖ نَّاضِرَةٌ»?
quiz.why: «نَّاضِرَةٌ» with daad means radiant; «نَاظِرَةٞ» with dhaa means looking.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «بِضَنِينٖ» in At-Takwir?
quiz.why: Hafs reads it with daad, meaning "stingy".

quiz.q: What is a common mistake with daad?
options: Saying it as a heavy dal or as dhaa
quiz.why: Among the best-known mistakes are saying daad as a heavy dal, or as dhaa.

quiz.q: Which sifat do daad and dhaa share?
quiz.why: They share jahr, rakhawah, isti'la', itbaq and ismat.

lessons.title: Common mistakes in pronouncing the letters
lessons.lede: Common mistakes in saying the letters that scholars warn about, and some words Hafs reads in his own way.

idea.lead: After the makharij, the sifat and the rules, scholars point out mistakes that often happen in saying the letters, so the reader can avoid them. Ibn al-Jazari says: «فَرَقِّقَنْ مُسْتَفِلًا مِنْ أَحْرُفِ، وَحَاذِرَنْ تَفْخِيمَ لَفْظِ الأَلِفِ، وَهَمْزَ الحَمْدُ أَعُوذُ اهْدِنَا، اللهِ ثُمَّ لَامَ لِلَّهِ لَنَا» (make the low letters light, beware of making alif heavy, and the hamzah of «الحمد», «أعوذ», «اهدنا» and «الله», and the laam of «لله» and «لنا»). The most common mistakes are swapping letters that sound alike, making light letters heavy, losing the ghunnah, and getting the madd lengths wrong.
idea.kidsLead: In this lesson we gather small mistakes many readers make, so we watch out for them: we do not turn 'ayn into a hamzah or haa (ح) into haa (ه); we do not make light letters heavy; and we keep the ghunnah and give each madd its length.

how.text: Said fully and light, not eased and not over-pressed, especially at the start of «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ», «أَعُوذُ» and «ٱهۡدِنَا» when starting.
Make it clear when it repeats or follows an alif: «جِبَاهُهُمۡ», «وُجُوهَهُمۡ», «فِيهِ هُدٗى».
Do not turn 'ayn into a hamzah or haa (ح) into haa (ه): «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ», «ٱلرَّحِيمِ».
Light, not heavy before a heavy letter, and with qalqalah when it has sukun: «بَٰطِلٞ», «بِٱلۡحَقِّ».
Keep the covering of taa (ط) in «بَسَطتَ» and «أَحَطتُ», and the whisper of taa (ت), without qalqalah: «فَتَنَّا».
Make their doubled ghunnah clear, but no longer than two counts: «ثُمَّ», «إِنَّ».
Do not roll the raa; make laam heavy only in the name Allah: «وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ», «وَلَا ٱلضَّآلِّينَ».

idea.note: These mistakes are examples, not a full list; the rule for every letter is to give it its makhraj and characteristics (lessons 9–21 and 55–64). The words where Hafs differs from the usual rule are gathered in lesson 92.

quiz.q: How is the hamzah of «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ» said when starting?
quiz.why: The hamzah is said fully and light, without easing or extra pressure.

quiz.q: How is the baa in «بَٰطِلٞ» said?
quiz.why: Baa is a low letter: it is light, even next to the heavy taa (ط).

quiz.q: What is the mistake to avoid with the haa in «جِبَاهُهُمۡ»?
options: Hiding it, or merging the two haas
quiz.why: When haa repeats, it is made clear: neither hidden nor merged.

quiz.q: What is the mistake to avoid in «بَسَطتَ»?
options: Merging the taa (ط) fully, losing its covering
Saying the seen from its makhraj
quiz.why: The idgham here is partial: the covering of taa (ط) stays.

quiz.q: How is the 'ayn in «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ» said?
options: As 'ayn from the middle of the throat, not turned into hamzah
quiz.why: 'Ayn comes from the middle of the throat, and turning it into hamzah is a mistake.

quiz.q: What is the mistake in the taa of «فَتَنَّا»?
options: Giving it qalqalah as if it were a qalqalah letter
Saying it from the tip of the tongue
quiz.why: Taa is whispered and strong, but it is not a qalqalah letter.

quiz.q: How long is the ghunnah of the noon in «إِنَّ»?
quiz.why: The ghunnah of a noon with shaddah is two counts, and it is not stretched beyond that.

lessons.title: Identical, related and close letters: the idea
lessons.lede: When two letters meet, they are identical if they share makhraj and characteristics, related if they share a makhraj but differ in characteristics, close if their makharij or characteristics are near, and far if they are apart.

idea.lead: Two letters that meet are of three kinds. Identical (mutamathilan): the same makhraj and sifat, such as baa and baa. Related (mutajanisan): the same makhraj, different sifat, such as taa and dal, taa and taa (ط), thaa and dhal, dhal and dhaa (ظ), or baa and meem. Close (mutaqariban): near in makhraj or sifat, such as laam and raa, or qaaf and kaaf. Each kind has three cases: minor, when the first has a sukun and the second a vowel; major, when both have vowels; and absolute, when the first has a vowel and the second a sukun. It is mainly the minor case that merges.
idea.kidsLead: When two letters meet, we look: are they the same letter, like taa and taa? Or from the same place, like dal and taa? Or from two places near each other, like laam and raa? That tells us whether to merge the first into the second.

how.text: Two letters that share makhraj and characteristics: baa and baa, taa and taa.
They share a makhraj but differ in characteristics: taa and dal, taa (ت) and taa (ط), thaa and dhal, dhal and dhaa (ظ), baa and meem.
Their makharij or characteristics are near: laam and raa, qaaf and kaaf.
Their makharij are far apart and their characteristics differ, like laam and haa (ح) in «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ»; they never merge.
Minor when the first has sukun and the second a vowel; major when both have vowels; absolute when the first has a vowel and the second sukun. The minor kind is the one that usually merges.

idea.note: Merging happens because the letters are identical, related or close, and the minor kind requires the first to have sukun and the second a vowel. Lessons 76–78 cover each kind; the merging of noon sakinah in «يَرۡمَلُونَ» (lessons 28 and 29) and the sun laam (lesson 25) belong here too.

ayat.findHint: Find the two letters that meet in each ayah: identical, related or close? Then bring the colours back to check.

why: Taa with sukun + taa: minor, identical
Dal with sukun + taa: minor, related
Baa with sukun + meem: related; Hafs merges them
Laam with sukun + raa: minor, close

ayat.tip: Look at the shaddah on the second letter: it is the sign of idgham in the Mushaf, and the first letter is written without sukun.

quiz.q: What are identical letters?
options: Two letters with the same makhraj and sifat
quiz.why: Identical letters share makhraj and sifat, such as taa and taa.

quiz.q: What kind of letters meet in:
quiz.why: Dal and taa share a makhraj but differ in sifat: related.

quiz.q: What kind of letters meet in:
quiz.why: Laam and raa are near in makhraj: close.

quiz.q: What are related letters?
options: Two letters sharing makhraj and characteristics
Two letters far apart in makhraj
Two letters sharing a makhraj but differing in characteristics
Two letters with near makharij or characteristics
quiz.why: Related letters share a makhraj and differ in characteristics, like dal and taa.

quiz.q: When is a meeting of two letters minor?
options: When the first has sukun and the second a vowel
When the first has a vowel and the second sukun
quiz.why: Minor is when the first has sukun and the second a vowel; this is the kind that usually merges.

quiz.q: When is a meeting of two letters major?
quiz.why: Major is when both letters have vowels.

quiz.q: What kind are the laam and haa (ح) in «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ»?
options: Far, so there is no idgham
quiz.why: Laam is from the tip of the tongue and haa (ح) from the middle of the throat, so they are far apart.

lessons.title: Merging identical letters: minor and major
lessons.lede: When two identical letters meet and the first has sukun, it must merge into the second, unless it is a madd letter. When both have vowels it is the major kind, which Hafs says clearly except in a few words.

idea.lead: Identical letters share makhraj and characteristics. When the first has sukun and the second a vowel, it is the minor kind, and it must merge, in one word or two: «رَبِحَت تِّجَٰرَتُهُمۡ», «ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ», «فَلَا يُسۡرِف فِّي ٱلۡقَتۡلِ». The exception is when the first is a madd letter: it is said clearly, so the madd is not lost: «قَالُواْ وَهُمۡ», «فِي يَوۡمٖ». When both have vowels it is the major kind, which Hafs says clearly, except in a few words such as «مَكَّنِّي» (Al-Kahf 95) and «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا» (Yusuf 11).
idea.kidsLead: When a letter with sukun is followed by the same letter with a vowel, we read them as one doubled letter: «ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ». Unless the first is a madd letter, as in «قَالُواْ وَهُمۡ»: we stretch it, then read the second.

how.text: Must merge: «رَبِحَت تِّجَٰرَتُهُمۡ», «ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ», «يُدۡرِككُّمُ».
Does not merge: «قَالُواْ وَهُمۡ», «فِي يَوۡمٖ», «ٱلَّذِي يُوَسۡوِسُ».
In «مَالِيَهۡۜ ۝ هَلَكَ» (Al-Haqqah 28 and 29) Hafs has two ways: a pause with izhar, or idgham.
Hafs says it clearly: «مَنَٰسِكَكُمۡ», «جِبَاهُهُمۡ», except «مَكَّنِّي», originally «مَكَّنَنِي», and «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا», originally «تَأۡمَنُنَا» (lesson 90).
Major merging also happens in «أَتُحَٰٓجُّوٓنِّي» (Al-An'am 80) and «تَأۡمُرُوٓنِّيٓ» (Az-Zumar 64), where one noon merges into the next.

idea.note: When identical letters merge the idgham is complete, so the letter is said doubled, and with ghunnah if it is a noon or meem: «لَهُم مَّا». Both ways in «مَالِيَهۡۜ ۝ هَلَكَ» are correct; learn them from a teacher.

ayat.findHint: Find the identical letters in each ayah: do they merge? Then bring the colours back to check.

why: A baa with sukun + baa: identical, minor
A faa with sukun + faa: identical, minor
Originally «مَكَّنَنِي»: two noons with vowels, the first merged into the second
A madd waw + waw: not merged, so the madd is not lost

ayat.tip: When the first of two identical letters is a madd letter, the second has no shaddah in the Mushaf, because it does not merge.

quiz.q: What is the rule for the minor case of identical letters?
options: Idgham, always, unless the first is a madd letter
quiz.why: Identical letters merge when the first has a sukun, unless the first is a madd letter.

quiz.q: Why is «قَالُواْ وَهُمۡ» not merged?
options: The first waw is a madd letter
quiz.why: When the first of two identical letters is a madd letter, they do not merge, so the madd is not lost.

quiz.q: What kind of idgham is in «ٱضۡرِب بِّعَصَاكَ»?
quiz.why: A baa with sukun followed by a baa with a vowel.

quiz.q: Why does «فِي يَوۡمٖ» not merge?
options: Because the first yaa is a madd letter
quiz.why: The first of the two is a madd letter, so it is said clearly and the madd is not lost.

quiz.q: What was «مَكَّنِّي» originally?
quiz.why: Two noons with vowels: the first merges into the second, so it is identical, major.

quiz.q: What is the rule of identical letters, major, for Hafs?
options: Izhar, except in a few words
quiz.why: Hafs says them clearly, except in a few words such as «مَكَّنِّي» and «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا».

quiz.q: What is allowed for the haa of «مَالِيَهۡۜ» when joined to «هَلَكَ»?
options: A pause with izhar, or idgham
quiz.why: Hafs has two ways: a pause with izhar, or idgham.

lessons.title: Merging related letters
lessons.lede: Related letters share a makhraj and differ in characteristics. Hafs merges the minor kind in seven cases: in taa, dal and taa (ط); in dhal, dhaa (ظ) and thaa; and in baa and meem.

formula.caption: Tip of the tongue with the roots of the front teeth
Tip of the tongue with the edges of the front teeth

idea.lead: Related letters, minor, is when the first of two letters sharing a makhraj but differing in characteristics has sukun. Hafs merges it in seven cases: dal into taa «قَد تَّبَيَّنَ», taa into dal «أَثۡقَلَت دَّعَوَا», taa into taa (ط) «وَدَّت طَّآئِفَةٞ», taa (ط) into taa «بَسَطتَ», dhal into dhaa (ظ) «إِذ ظَّلَمُوٓاْ», thaa into dhal «يَلۡهَث ذَّٰلِكَ», and baa into meem «ٱرۡكَب مَّعَنَا». The idgham is complete in all of them except taa (ط) into taa, which is incomplete: the itbaq stays.
idea.kidsLead: When a letter with sukun is followed by a letter from the same place, we merge the first into the second: «قَدۡ تَبَيَّنَ» is read «qattabayyana», and «ٱرۡكَب مَّعَنَا» is read «irkam-ma'ana».

how.text: Hafs merges the minor case in: «قَد تَّبَيَّنَ», «أَثۡقَلَت دَّعَوَا», «وَدَّت طَّآئِفَةٞ», «إِذ ظَّلَمُوٓاْ», «يَلۡهَث ذَّٰلِكَ», «ٱرۡكَب مَّعَنَا».
Taa (ط) into taa (ت) is a partial idgham, keeping the covering (itbaq): «بَسَطتَ», «أَحَطتُ», «فَرَّطتُ».
In Al-A'raf 176: the thaa merges completely into the dhal, for Hafs by way of ash-Shatibiyyah.
In Hud 42: the baa merges completely into the meem, with ghunnah, for Hafs by way of ash-Shatibiyyah.

idea.note: In the incomplete idgham of «بَسَطتَ», «أَحَطتُ», «فَرَّطتُمۡ» and «فَرَّطتُ», the itbaq and elevation of taa (ط) stay, so it does not become a plain taa, and its qalqalah is not heard.

ayat.findHint: Find the related letters in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: A thaa with sukun + dhal: related, merged for Hafs
Baa with sukun + meem: related; Hafs merges them
A dhal with sukun + dhaa (ظ): related
A taa with sukun + taa (ط): related
A taa (ط) with sukun + taa: incomplete idgham, the itbaq stays

ayat.tip: In «أَحَطتُ» the taa has no shaddah in the Mushaf, a sign that the idgham is incomplete.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «بَسَطتَ»?
quiz.why: Taa (ط) merges into taa (ت), but its covering stays: partial idgham.

quiz.q: In how many cases does Hafs merge related letters, minor?
quiz.why: Dal into taa, taa into dal, taa into taa (ط), taa (ط) into taa, dhal into dhaa (ظ), thaa into dhal, baa into meem.

quiz.q: What is the rule of «يَلۡهَث ذَّٰلِكَ» for Hafs by way of ash-Shatibiyyah?
options: The thaa merges completely into the dhal
quiz.why: Thaa and dhal share a makhraj, so the thaa merges into the dhal.

quiz.q: What is the rule of «ٱرۡكَب مَّعَنَا» for Hafs by way of ash-Shatibiyyah?
options: The baa merges into the meem with ghunnah
quiz.why: Baa and meem both come from the lips, so the baa merges into the meem.

quiz.q: What kind are the two letters in «إِذ ظَّلَمُوٓاْ»?
quiz.why: Dhal and dhaa (ظ) share a makhraj and differ in itbaq and isti'la'.

quiz.q: Which case of related letters has incomplete idgham?
quiz.why: Taa (ط) into taa: the itbaq of taa (ط) stays.

quiz.q: How is «وَدَّت طَّآئِفَةٞ» read?
options: The taa merges completely into taa (ط)
quiz.why: Taa and taa (ط) are related, and the taa with sukun merges into taa (ط).

lessons.title: Merging close letters
lessons.lede: Close letters have near makharij or characteristics. Hafs merges the minor kind in laam and raa «قُل رَّبِّ», and in qaaf and kaaf «نَخۡلُقكُّم».

idea.lead: Close letters have near makharij or characteristics, like laam and raa, and qaaf and kaaf. Hafs merges the minor kind in: a laam with sukun into raa «وَقُل رَّبِّ», «بَل رَّفَعَهُ», and a qaaf with sukun into kaaf in «أَلَمۡ نَخۡلُقكُّم» (Al-Mursalat 20), where complete idgham is better known and incomplete idgham, keeping the elevation of qaaf, is also allowed. Noon sakinah with laam and raa «مِن رَّبِّهِمۡ», and the sun laam, are close letters too, with their rules in lessons 25 and 29.
idea.kidsLead: When a laam with sukun has raa after it, we merge it: «قُلۡ رَبِّ» is read «qurrabbi». In «أَلَمۡ نَخۡلُقكُّم» we merge the qaaf into the kaaf.

how.text: The laam of a verb and of a particle merge into raa: «وَقُل رَّبِّ», «بَل رَّفَعَهُ».
Only in «أَلَمۡ نَخۡلُقكُّم» in the Quran: complete idgham is better known, and incomplete is allowed.
The laam does not merge into raa in «بَلۡۜ رَانَ» (Al-Mutaffifin 14), nor the noon into raa in «مَنۡۜ رَاقٖ» (Al-Qiyamah 27), because Hafs pauses on them (lesson 85).
Hafs says it clearly: in «خَلَقَكُم» the qaaf and kaaf both have vowels, so there is no idgham.

idea.note: Complete idgham in «نَخۡلُقكُّم» changes the qaaf to kaaf and merges it, leaving nothing of the qaaf; incomplete keeps its elevation. Both are correct.

ayat.findHint: Find the close letters in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Laam with sukun + raa: minor, close
A qaaf with sukun + kaaf: close; complete idgham is better known

ayat.tip: The shaddah on the kaaf in «نَخۡلُقكُّم» is the sign of idgham.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «أَلَمۡ نَخۡلُقكُّم»?
options: Full or partial idgham, full being better known
quiz.why: Qaaf merges into kaaf; full idgham is better known.

quiz.q: What kind are the two letters in «بَل رَّفَعَهُ»?
options: Close: the laam merges into the raa
quiz.why: Laam and raa have near makharij.

quiz.q: In how many places does a qaaf with sukun merge into kaaf?
quiz.why: Only in «أَلَمۡ نَخۡلُقكُّم».

quiz.q: What is incomplete idgham in «نَخۡلُقكُّم»?
options: Idgham keeping the elevation of qaaf
quiz.why: The elevation of qaaf stays as it merges.

quiz.q: What stops the noon merging into raa in «مَنۡۜ رَاقٖ»?
quiz.why: Hafs makes a short pause on «مَنۡ», so it does not merge.

quiz.q: Does the qaaf merge into kaaf in «خَلَقَكُم»?
quiz.why: Qaaf and kaaf both have vowels, so it is close, major, which Hafs says clearly.

quiz.q: Which two close letters are in «وَقُل رَّبِّ»?
quiz.why: The laam with sukun and the raa after it.

lessons.title: Two letters with sukun meeting
lessons.lede: Two letters with sukun do not meet across two words when joining: if they meet, the first is dropped if it is a madd letter, and given a vowel if it is a consonant or a leen letter.

formula.caption: The madd is dropped in speech

idea.lead: Two letters with sukun meeting means two letters with sukun one after the other. In one word, when the first is a madd letter, it is allowed and the madd is lazim, «ٱلضَّآلِّينَ», or for stopping, «نَسۡتَعِينۡ» (lessons 47 and 52). Across two words, when joining, they are avoided: if the first is a madd letter, it is dropped in speech but stays in the writing «وَقَالَا ٱلۡحَمۡدُ», «فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ», «قَالُواْ ٱتَّخَذَ». If it is a consonant or a leen letter, it takes a vowel, usually kasrah «قُمِ ٱلَّيۡلَ», «وَقَالَتِ ٱخۡرُجۡ»; dammah for the plural meem «عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلذِّلَّةُ» and the plural waw «ٱشۡتَرَوُاْ ٱلضَّلَٰلَةَ»; and fathah for the noon of «مِنَ» before «ال», «مِنَ ٱللَّهِ».
idea.kidsLead: We cannot say two letters with sukun one after the other across two words. When they meet, we drop the madd letter in speech: «فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ» is read «fil-ard»; or we give the letter with sukun a vowel: «قُمۡ ٱلَّيۡلَ» is read «qumil-layl».

how.text: The madd letter is dropped in speech, not in writing: «وَقَالَا ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ», «فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ», «وَأَقِيمُواْ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ»; when you stop on the word, the madd is said.
The usual way out is kasrah: «قُمِ ٱلَّيۡلَ», «وَقَالَتِ ٱخۡرُجۡ», «لَمۡ يَكُنِ ٱلَّذِينَ».
For the plural meem «لَهُمُ ٱلۡبُشۡرَىٰ», «عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡقِتَالُ», and the plural waw after fathah «ٱشۡتَرَوُاْ ٱلضَّلَٰلَةَ», «وَلَا تَنسَوُاْ ٱلۡفَضۡلَ».
For the noon of «مِنَ» before the laam of «ال»: «مِنَ ٱللَّهِ», «مِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ».
Tanween takes kasrah before a connecting hamzah: «نُوحٌ ٱبۡنَهُۥ» is read «nuhunibnah».
Two letters with sukun may meet in one word when the first is a madd letter: madd lazim «ٱلۡحَآقَّةُ», and the madd for stopping «ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ» at a stop.

idea.note: When you stop on the first word, the meeting goes and the letter returns to its origin: the madd is said in «وَقَالَا», and the meem takes sukun in «قُمۡ». It is a mistake to stretch the yaa in «فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ» when joining.

quiz.why: At the stop nothing with sukun follows it, so the natural madd is said.

lessons.title: The connecting hamzah and where it comes
lessons.lede: The connecting hamzah lets you start on a letter with sukun: said when starting, dropped when joining. It is in «ال» and in certain nouns and verbs.

idea.lead: The connecting hamzah (hamzat al-wasl) is an extra hamzah at the start of a word, used to reach the letter with sukun after it, since Arabic does not start on a sukun. It is said when starting, and dropped in speech, though written, when joining, as in «ٱهۡدِنَا» and «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ». The Mushaf writes it as an alif with a small head of saad «ٱ». Among particles it is only in «ال»; among nouns, in seven nouns and the verbal nouns of five- and six-letter verbs; among verbs, in the past and command of five- and six-letter verbs, and the command of three-letter verbs.
idea.kidsLead: We say the connecting hamzah when we start with the word, and leave it out when we join the word to what comes before: we start «ihdina», and join «wahdina». Its sign in the Mushaf is a small saad head over the alif «ٱ».

how.text: Only the hamzah of «ال»: «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ», «ٱلشَّمۡسُ».

The hamzah of «ال», seven nouns in the Quran «ٱبۡن», «ٱبۡنَت», «ٱمۡرُؤٌ», «ٱمۡرَأَت», «ٱثۡنَانِ», «ٱثۡنَتَانِ», «ٱسۡم», and the verbal nouns of five- and six-letter verbs: «ٱنتِقَامٖ», «ٱسۡتِغۡفَارُ».
The past and command of five- and six-letter verbs, and the command of three-letter verbs: «ٱنطَلَقُواْ», «ٱسۡتَغۡفِرۡ», «ٱقۡرَأۡ».
There is no connecting hamzah in a present-tense verb, nor in a three- or four-letter past verb: the hamzah of «أَخَذَ» and «أَنۡعَمۡتَ» is cutting (lesson 82).

idea.note: When the hamzah of a question comes before a connecting hamzah, the connecting hamzah is dropped, as in «أَسۡتَغۡفَرۡتَ» (Al-Munafiqun 6), except with «ال», where it becomes an alif or is softened (lesson 83). How to start with it is in lesson 81.

lessons.title: How to start with a connecting hamzah
lessons.lede: You start with a connecting hamzah with fathah in «ال», with kasrah in nouns, and in verbs with dammah if the third letter has a fixed dammah, and with kasrah if it has fathah or kasrah.

formula.caption: When the third letter has dammah

idea.lead: The vowel of a connecting hamzah when starting depends on where it is. It takes fathah in «ال»: «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ» is read «alhamdu». It takes kasrah in nouns: «ٱبۡنَ» is read «ibna». In verbs, look at the third letter: if it has a fixed dammah, the hamzah takes dammah: «ٱدۡعُ» «ud'u», «ٱنظُرۡ» «unzur»; if it has fathah or kasrah, the hamzah takes kasrah: «ٱذۡهَبۡ» «idhhab», «ٱضۡرِب» «idrib». If the dammah of the third letter is passing, it takes kasrah.
idea.kidsLead: When we start with a word that has a connecting hamzah: with «ال» we give it fathah «alhamdu», with nouns kasrah «ibna», and with verbs we look at the third letter: if it has dammah, we give it dammah «ud'u»; otherwise kasrah «idhhab».

how.text: Fathah in «ال»; kasrah in nouns; in verbs, dammah if the third letter has a fixed dammah «ٱدۡعُ» read «اُدۡعُ», kasrah if it has a fathah or kasrah «ٱذۡهَبۡ», «ٱضۡرِب».
Kasrah in «ٱمۡشُواْ», «ٱقۡضُوٓاْ», «ٱبۡنُواْ» and «ٱئۡتُواْ», since the dammah on their third letter is temporary; it was a kasrah.
Starting on «ٱلِٱسۡمُ» in «بِئۡسَ ٱلِٱسۡمُ» (Al-Hujurat 11), Hafs has two ways: «أَلِسۡمُ» and «لِسۡمُ», and the first is preferred.
Their hamzah takes kasrah when starting: «إِبۡن», «إِبۡنَت», «إِمۡرُؤٌ», «إِمۡرَأَت», «إِثۡنَانِ», «إِثۡنَتَانِ», «إِسۡم».

idea.note: When you start with a connecting hamzah with kasrah and a raa with sukun follows, the raa is heavy because the kasrah is passing: «ٱرۡجِعِيٓ» (lesson 68). When a hamzah with sukun follows it, that hamzah becomes a madd letter matching the vowel of the connecting hamzah: «ٱئۡتُواْ» is read «ītū».

quiz.why: You start it «أَلِسۡمُ», with the joining hamzah, or «لِسۡمُ», without it.

lessons.title: The cutting hamzah
lessons.lede: The cutting hamzah is said both when starting and when joining; it comes at the start, middle or end of a word, in nouns, verbs and particles.

idea.lead: The cutting hamzah (hamzat al-qat') is said both when starting and when joining; it is called cutting because it cuts what is before it from what is after it in speech. It comes at the start of a word «أَنۡعَمۡتَ», in the middle «يُؤۡمِنُونَ» and at the end «جَآءَ». It is in all nouns except those with a connecting hamzah; in verbs, in the three-letter past «أَخَذَ», the four-letter past «أَنۡعَمَ», its command «أَنذِرۡ» and its verbal noun «إِسۡرَافٗا», and the present verb starting with the "I" hamzah «أَعُوذُ»; and in all particles except «ال»: «إِنَّ», «أَنۡ», «إِلَىٰ», «أَوۡ». Hafs says every hamzah in full, except the second in «ءَا۬عۡجَمِيّٞ» (lesson 83).
idea.kidsLead: We always say the cutting hamzah, at the start, middle and end of a word: «أَنۡعَمۡتَ», «يُؤۡمِنُونَ», «جَآءَ», whether we start with the word or join it.

how.text: Said when starting and joining; written on an alif, under it, or alone: «أَنۡعَمۡتَ», «إِنَّ», «ٱلسَّمَآءِ».
All nouns except the seven nouns and the verbal nouns of five- and six-letter verbs: «أَحَدٌ», «إِنسَٰنٞ», «أُمّ».
The three-letter past «أَخَذَ», the four-letter past «أَنۡعَمۡتَ» with its command «أَنذِرۡ» and verbal noun «إِسۡرَافٗا», and the present starting with the "I" hamzah «أَعُوذُ», «أَعۡبُدُ».
All of them except «ال»: «إِنَّ», «أَنۡ», «إِلَىٰ», «أَوۡ», «إِذَا».
In full, from the deepest throat, without softening or overdoing it, especially after a madd: «جَآءَ», «ٱلسَّمَآءِ».

idea.note: It is a mistake to drop a cutting hamzah or move its vowel to the letter with sukun before it, as in reading «قَدۡ أَفۡلَحَ» as «qadaflaha»; that moving is not in the riwayah of Hafs. It is also a mistake to drop the hamzah with sukun in «يُؤۡمِنُونَ» and «ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ».

ayat.findHint: Find the hamzahs in each ayah: which are said when joining? Then bring the colours back to check.

The hamzahs of «أَنۡ» and «أَنذِرۡ» are cutting

ayat.tip: A cutting hamzah has a small head of 'ayn over or under it: «أ», «إ».

quiz.why: The "I" hamzah of a present verb is cutting.

quiz.why: The hamzahs of particles are all cutting except «ال».

options: Moving the vowel of the hamzah to the dal

quiz.why: Hafs says the hamzah in full and does not move its vowel.

options: Connecting, since it is a command
Cutting, since it is the command of a four-letter verb

lessons.title: Two hamzahs in one word
lessons.lede: When two hamzahs meet in a word, Hafs says both in full, except in «ءَا۬عۡجَمِيّٞ», where he softens the second. A connecting hamzah after a question is dropped, except with «ال», where it becomes alif or is softened.

idea.lead: When two hamzahs meet in a word, the first is usually the hamzah of a question. If the second is a cutting hamzah, Hafs says both in full, «ءَأَنذَرۡتَهُمۡ», «ءَأَنتُمۡ», except in «ءَا۬عۡجَمِيّٞ» (Fussilat 44), where he softens the second between hamzah and alif. If the second is the connecting hamzah of a verb, it is dropped in speech and writing, and the question hamzah stays with fathah: «أَسۡتَغۡفَرۡتَ», «أَطَّلَعَ ٱلۡغَيۡبَ». If it is the connecting hamzah of «ال», it is not dropped, so the question is not mistaken for a statement, and Hafs has two ways: changing it to an alif stretched six counts, which is preferred, or softening it between hamzah and alif with no madd. This is in six places: «ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ» twice in Al-An'am, «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ» twice in Yunus, and «ءَآللَّهُ» in Yunus and An-Naml.
idea.kidsLead: In a few words two hamzahs come one after the other: in «ءَأَنذَرۡتَهُمۡ» we say both clearly, in «ءَا۬عۡجَمِيّٞ» we say the second between hamzah and alif, and in «ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ» we stretch the alif six counts.

how.text: When the second is a cutting hamzah: «ءَأَنذَرۡتَهُمۡ» (Al-Baqarah 6), «ءَأَنتُمۡ أَشَدُّ خَلۡقًا», «ءَأَلِدُ».
Only in «ءَا۬عۡجَمِيّٞ» (Fussilat 44): the second is said between hamzah and alif; its sign in the Mushaf is a filled dot.
In verbs: «أَسۡتَغۡفَرۡتَ» (Al-Munafiqun 6), «أَطَّلَعَ ٱلۡغَيۡبَ» (Maryam 78), «أَصۡطَفَى ٱلۡبَنَاتِ» (As-Saffat 153); you start with a hamzah with fathah.
The connecting hamzah becomes an alif stretched six counts, the madd of distinction (lesson 51), or is softened with no madd: «ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ», «ءَآلۡـَٰٔنَ», «ءَآللَّهُ».
When the second has sukun, it becomes a madd letter matching the vowel of the first: «ءَامَنُواْ», «إِيمَٰنٗا», «أُوتِيَ»; this is the badal madd (lesson 42).

idea.note: In «ءَآلذَّكَرَيۡنِ» and the like, changing to alif with six counts is preferred, and tas-hil is correct. The connecting hamzah is not dropped here, because if it were, the question would sound like a statement.

quiz.q: What is tas-hil?

options: It is dropped, and the question hamzah stays
quiz.why: The connecting hamzah of a verb is dropped after the question hamzah.

options: Changing to alif with six counts

lessons.title: Alifs said when stopping and dropped when joining
lessons.lede: Some alifs are written but dropped when joining and said when stopping, as in «أَنَا۠».

idea.lead: Some alifs are written in the Mushaf but not said when joining, and said when stopping; their sign is the upright zero above the alif «۠». For Hafs they are in: «أَنَا۠», the pronoun "I", wherever it comes, as in «فَقَالَ أَنَا۠ رَبُّكُمُ ٱلۡأَعۡلَىٰ»; «لَّٰكِنَّا۠ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ رَبِّي» (Al-Kahf 38); «ٱلظُّنُونَا۠» (Al-Ahzab 10); «ٱلرَّسُولَا۠» (Al-Ahzab 66); «ٱلسَّبِيلَا۠» (Al-Ahzab 67); and the first «قَوَارِيرَا۠» (Al-Insan 15). In «سَلَٰسِلَاْ» (Al-Insan 4) the alif is dropped when joining, and when stopping there are two ways: saying the alif, or dropping it with sukun on the laam.
idea.kidsLead: In some words we see an alif with a small upright mark «أَنَا۠»: we do not read it when joining, and we read it when we stop on the word: «ana rabbukum», and «anā».

how.text: The pronoun "I" wherever it comes: its alif is dropped when joining «أَنَا۠ رَبُّكُمُ» and said when stopping «أَنَا».
In Al-Kahf 38: originally «لَكِنۡ أَنَا»; the alif is dropped when joining and said when stopping.
«ٱلظُّنُونَا۠» (10), «ٱلرَّسُولَا۠» (66), «ٱلسَّبِيلَا۠» (67): ends of ayahs, the alif said when stopping and dropped when joining.
The first (Al-Insan 15) keeps its alif when stopping; the second «قَوَارِيرَاْ» (Al-Insan 16) is never said with alif, and you stop on it with sukun.
In Al-Insan 4: the alif is dropped when joining, and when stopping there are two ways: «سَلَٰسِلَا» with alif, and «سَلَٰسِلۡ» with sukun.
The upright zero above the alif means it is dropped when joining and said when stopping; the round zero means it is never said.

idea.note: These alifs are part of the writing: anyone who says them when joining adds a letter to the Quran, and anyone who drops them when stopping goes against the riwayah. The alif in words like «قَالُواْ» and «ءَامَنُواْ» is never said, joining or stopping.

lessons.title: Saktah in the riwayah of Hafs
lessons.lede: Saktah is stopping the sound briefly, without a breath, meaning to go on reading. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, has four required pauses when joining.

formula.caption: a brief stop of the sound

idea.lead: Saktah is stopping the sound briefly, for about two counts, without a breath, meaning to go on reading. It happens only where it has come down from the reciters, and the Mushaf marks it with a small seen «ۜ» over the letter. Hafs, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, has four required pauses when joining: on «عِوَجَاۜ» in Al-Kahf, «مَّرۡقَدِنَاۜ» in Ya-Sin, «مَنۡۜ» in Al-Qiyamah, and «بَلۡۜ» in Al-Mutaffifin.
idea.kidsLead: A saktah is a very short stop, without taking a breath; then we go on reading. Hafs has four places where we pause, such as «مَنْ ۜ رَاقٍ» and «بَلْ ۜ رَانَ». The sign is a small seen over the letter.

how.text: «وَلَمۡ يَجۡعَل لَّهُۥ عِوَجَاۜ ۝ قَيِّمٗا» (Al-Kahf 1 and 2), when the two ayahs are joined.
«مَنۢ بَعَثَنَا مِن مَّرۡقَدِنَاۜۗ هَٰذَا» (Ya-Sin 52).
«وَقِيلَ مَنۡۜ رَاقٖ» (Al-Qiyamah 27): the noon is said clearly and does not merge into the raa.
«كَلَّاۖ بَلۡۜ رَانَ» (Al-Mutaffifin 14): the laam is said clearly and does not merge into the raa.
«مَالِيَهۡۜ ۝ هَلَكَ» (Al-Haqqah 28 and 29): a pause with the letters clear, or merging. Between Al-Anfal and At-Tawbah: stop, pause or join (lesson 5).

idea.note: The pauses keep away a wrong meaning: in «عِوَجَا قَيِّمًا», so that «قَيِّمًا» (upright) is not taken to describe «عِوَجَا» (crookedness); in «مَرۡقَدِنَا هَٰذَا», so that «هَٰذَا» is not taken to describe the resting place. When you stop on the word itself, there is no saktah: the stop does its work.

ayat.findHint: Find the pause sign in each ayah, and listen to how the reciter stops the sound without a breath, then bring the colours back to check.

quiz.why: Saktah is stopping the sound briefly, without a breath, meaning to go on reading.

quiz.why: You pause on «عِوَجَاۜ» when joining it to «قَيِّمٗا».

quiz.q: How does the Mushaf mark a pause?
quiz.why: The pause sign is a small seen over the letter.

quiz.q: Why the pause in «مَنۡۜ رَاقٖ»?
options: So the noon does not merge into the raa and sound like one word
quiz.why: With the pause the noon is said clearly, so it does not become «مَرَّاق», as if one word.

quiz.q: What are the two ways for Hafs in «مَالِيَهۡۜ ۝ هَلَكَ»?
options: A pause with the letters clear, or merging
quiz.why: You may pause on the haa and say it clearly, or merge it into the haa after it.

lessons.title: Stopping and starting: the idea and the kinds
lessons.lede: Stopping (waqf) is cutting the sound on a word long enough to breathe, intending to go on reciting. It has four kinds: forced, waiting, testing and chosen.

formula.caption: starting where the meaning stands alone

idea.lead: Stopping (waqf) is cutting the sound on a word long enough to breathe, intending to go on reciting; saktah is cutting it briefly without breathing; and qat' is ending the recitation. Knowing where to stop and start is one of the most important parts of tajweed, because the meaning depends on it. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَبَعْدَ تَجْوِيدِكَ لِلْحُرُوفِ، لَا بُدَّ مِنْ مَعْرِفَةِ الوُقُوفِ، وَالِابْتِدَاءِ» (after perfecting the letters, you must know the stops and the starts). Stopping has four kinds by its cause: forced, waiting, testing and chosen; the chosen stop is complete, sufficient, good or bad.
idea.kidsLead: We stop in our reading to breathe, but we choose a place where the meaning is complete, like the end of an ayah. We do not stop in the middle of a phrase so the meaning changes, and we start again from a word where the meaning is right.

how.text: Because of running out of breath, a sneeze or forgetting: stop where you must, then start where the meaning is sound.
Waiting: stopping on a word with several readings to give them all, when combining riwayahs. Testing: in teaching, when asked about a stop.
The reciter chooses it with none of the causes above; it is complete, sufficient, good or bad (lessons 87 and 88).
Ending the recitation and turning away from it; it is only at the end of an ayah, and you seek refuge again when you come back.
Starting is always by choice, so start only on words whose meaning stands on its own and is complete.

idea.note: Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَلَيْسَ فِي القُرْآنِ مِنْ وَقْفٍ وَجَبْ، وَلَا حَرَامٌ غَيْرُ مَا لَهُ سَبَبْ» (no stop in the Quran is required, and none forbidden, except for a reason): the reciter is not at fault for a stop unless he intends a wrong meaning. The stop signs are in lesson 89, and how to stop on the ends of words in lessons 90 and 91.

options: Stopping the sound long enough to breathe, meaning to go on
quiz.why: Waqf is stopping the sound on a word long enough to breathe, meaning to go on reading.

quiz.q: How does waqf differ from saktah?
options: Saktah is a shorter stop without a breath
quiz.why: Saktah stops the sound briefly without a breath; waqf comes with a breath.

quiz.q: What is a forced stop?
options: A stop for lack of breath or a sneeze
A stop to give all the readings
A stop at the end of an ayah
quiz.why: You stop where you must, then start where the meaning is sound.

quiz.q: How many kinds of stop are there by cause?
quiz.why: Forced, waiting, testing and chosen.

quiz.q: What is the testing stop?
options: A stop when teaching or being asked
A stop for lack of breath
A stop at the end of an ayah
A stop to complete the readings
quiz.why: It is when a reciter is tested, or taught the rule of a word.

quiz.q: What is qat'?
options: Ending the recitation and turning away from it
Stopping in the middle of an ayah
quiz.why: Qat' is ending the recitation, and it is only at the end of an ayah.

quiz.q: With what do you start after a stop?
options: Always the start of the surah
Always the word you stopped on
Words whose meaning stands on its own and is complete
quiz.why: Starting is always by choice, so choose a place where the meaning is right.

lessons.title: The complete and sufficient stop
lessons.lede: The complete stop is on words whose meaning is complete and have no tie to what follows, in wording or meaning; the sufficient stop is on words whose meaning is complete but tied to what follows in meaning, not wording. You may stop on both and start after them.

formula.caption: No tie in wording or meaning

idea.lead: The chosen stop has four kinds, and the highest is the complete stop: stopping on words whose meaning is complete, with no tie to what follows in wording or meaning. It comes often at the end of stories, at the ends of ayahs and when a subject ends, as in «وَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡمُفۡلِحُونَ» (Al-Baqarah 5): what follows is about the disbelievers. Then the sufficient stop: stopping on words whose meaning is complete, tied to what follows in meaning but not wording, as in «أَمۡ لَمۡ تُنذِرۡهُمۡ لَا يُؤۡمِنُونَ» (Al-Baqarah 6): what follows is about the same people. You may stop on both and start with what follows.
idea.kidsLead: The best place to stop is where the words finish and new words begin, like the end of a story. We may also stop where the meaning is complete, even if what follows is on the same subject.

how.text: On a phrase whose meaning is finished, with no link to what follows in wording or meaning: «وَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡمُفۡلِحُونَ» (Al-Baqarah 5).
Linked to what follows in meaning but not in wording: «أَمۡ لَمۡ تُنذِرۡهُمۡ لَا يُؤۡمِنُونَ» (Al-Baqarah 6).

how.term: In the middle of an ayah
how.text: A complete stop can be in the middle of an ayah: «لَّقَدۡ أَضَلَّنِي عَنِ ٱلذِّكۡرِ بَعۡدَ إِذۡ جَآءَنِي» (Al-Furqan 29); the words of the wrongdoer end here, and what follows is the word of Allah.
A stop may be complete on one reading of the meaning and sufficient on another, and each varies, so scholars say complete and more complete, sufficient and more sufficient.
The Mushaf may mark them with «قلى» or «ج» (lesson 89), and stopping at the ends of ayahs is sunnah.

idea.note: Books on stopping and starting are the reference for knowing the stops, and the signs of the Mushaf come from them. Sometimes joining is better, to bring out a meaning in the ayah.

ayat.findHint: Think about the stop at the end of each ayah: is what follows tied to it in meaning? Then bring the colours back to check.

why: A complete stop: what follows is about the disbelievers
A sufficient stop: what follows is about the same people

ayat.tip: Read what follows each place: if a new subject begins, the stop is complete; if the subject goes on, it is sufficient.

One where no meaning is complete

quiz.why: A complete stop is on a finished phrase cut off from what follows, as at the end of a story.

Where it is tied to what follows in wording and meaning
A stop for lack of breath
quiz.why: The sufficient stop is complete in meaning, and what follows is tied to it in meaning only.

options: At the end of stories and ayahs
Between two words that belong together
quiz.why: The complete stop comes often where a subject ends.

options: You must go back to what comes before
Start from the beginning of the surah

quiz.why: The words about the believers end, and the words about the disbelievers begin.

quiz.q: Stopping on «لَا يُؤۡمِنُونَ» (Al-Baqarah 6) is:
quiz.why: The meaning is complete, and what follows is about the same people, tied in meaning but not wording.

quiz.why: The words of the wrongdoer end at «جَآءَنِي», and what follows is the word of Allah.

lessons.title: The good and the bad stop
lessons.lede: The good stop is on words whose meaning is complete in themselves but tied to what follows in wording and meaning: you may stop there, but not start with what follows. The bad stop is on words with no complete meaning, or that suggest a wrong one.

idea.lead: The good stop is on words whose meaning is complete in themselves but tied to what follows in wording and meaning, as in stopping on «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ»: it makes sense, but «رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ» describes the name Allah, so you do not start with it; you go back to what comes before so the words join up, unless it is the end of an ayah, where stopping is sunnah and you start with what follows. The bad stop is on words with no complete meaning, like stopping on a word that needs the next, «بِسۡمِ», or on words that suggest a wrong meaning, like stopping on «إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَسۡتَحۡيِۦٓ» (Al-Baqarah 26); you do not stop there unless you must, and then you go back to what comes before.
idea.kidsLead: If we stop where the meaning is a little complete but what follows is joined to it, we go back a step and join. We never stop where the meaning changes or cannot be understood.

how.text: Linked to what follows in wording and meaning: fine to stop on, but not to start after: «ٱلۡحَمۡدُ لِلَّهِ».
No meaning is complete, or it suggests a wrong meaning: stopping on «بِسۡمِ», or on «إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَسۡتَحۡيِۦٓ» (Al-Baqarah 26).
Stopping on them is sunnah even if what follows is tied to them: «رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ», and you start with what follows.
Stopping on words that suggest something unfitting about Allah, like stopping on «وَمَا مِنۡ إِلَٰهٍ» (Al Imran 62), must never be done on purpose.
A start can be bad even where the stop is fine, like starting with «يَدُ ٱللَّهِ مَغۡلُولَةٌ» (Al-Ma'idah 64) without «وَقَالَتِ ٱلۡيَهُودُ».

idea.note: If you make a good stop that is not at the end of an ayah, start again from what comes before so the meaning joins up; if you are forced into a bad stop, go back and join it to what follows.

quiz.why: It gives a sound meaning, but «رَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ» after it is linked in wording: a good stop.

quiz.why: It suggests a wrong meaning, so it is bad: join it to what follows.

quiz.q: What is the ruling on stopping at the end of each ayah?
quiz.why: Stopping at the end of each ayah is sunnah, even when what follows is linked to it.

quiz.why: The good stop makes sense in itself, but what follows is tied to it in wording.

quiz.why: You do not start with words tied to what came before, so you go back.

quiz.q: Stopping on «بِسۡمِ» in «بِسۡمِ ٱللَّهِ» is:
quiz.why: It has no complete meaning: the word needs the next one.

quiz.q: Why is it bad to start with «يَدُ ٱللَّهِ مَغۡلُولَةٌ»?
options: Because cut off from «وَقَالَتِ ٱلۡيَهُودُ» it suggests a wrong meaning
Because it is the end of an ayah
Because it is a complete stop
quiz.why: These are the words of the Jews, so you do not start with them cut off from who said them.

lessons.title: Stop signs in the Mushaf
lessons.lede: The Madinah Mushaf has six signs over the words, showing the reader where to stop and where to join.

idea.lead: Scholars put signs over the words in the Mushaf to guide the reader on stopping and joining, from their understanding of the meaning. The Madinah Mushaf has six: «مـ» for a required stop; «لا» for "do not stop"; «ج» for an allowed stop, stopping and joining being equal; «صلى» for an allowed stop where joining is better; «قلى» for an allowed stop where stopping is better; and «∴ ∴» for linked stops (ta'anuq).
idea.kidsLead: In the Mushaf, small signs over the words tell us where to stop: «مـ» means stop here, «لا» means do not stop, and «ج», «صلى» and «قلى» mean you may stop. The three dots come twice: stop at only one of them.

how.text: Required stop: stop here, since joining suggests a wrong meaning: «إِنَّمَا يَسۡتَجِيبُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَسۡمَعُونَۘ وَٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰ يَبۡعَثُهُمُ ٱللَّهُ».
Do not stop here; if you do, go back a little and read on. At the end of an ayah, stopping is allowed.
Stopping is allowed, stopping and joining being equal: «وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرۡهُۚ».
Stopping is allowed, but joining is better: «فَزَادَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ مَرَضٗاۖ».
Stopping is allowed, and stopping is better: «إِلَّا قَلِيلٞۗ».
Linked stops: if you stop at one of the two places, do not stop at the other: «لَا رَيۡبَۛ فِيهِۛ».

idea.note: These are the signs of the Madinah Mushaf; other Mushafs may differ. They come from scholars' understanding of the meaning: the required stop is kept, and the others are guidance. Stopping at the end of each ayah is sunnah.

«صلى» over «مَرَضٗا»: stopping is allowed, joining is better
«ج» over «وَٱسۡتَغۡفِرۡهُ»: stopping and joining are equal
The linked-stop dots over «رَيۡبَ» and «فِيهِ»: stop on only one

ayat.tip: The sign is written small over the last letter of the word, as you can see in the ayahs above.

quiz.why: «مـ» marks a required stop, since joining suggests a wrong meaning.

quiz.q: What does «لا» over a word mean?
quiz.why: «لا» means do not stop; if you do, go back a little, except at the end of an ayah.

quiz.q: What does «صلى» mean?
quiz.why: «صلى» means you may stop, but joining is better.

quiz.q: What does «قلى» mean?
quiz.why: «قلى» means you may stop, and stopping is better.

options: Stopping allowed, stopping and joining equal
quiz.why: «ج» means stopping and joining are equal.

quiz.why: With linked stops, if you stop at one place, you do not stop at the other.

options: Joining suggests the dead answer with those who hear
quiz.why: Allah raises the dead; they do not answer with those who hear. Joining would suggest a wrong meaning.

lessons.title: Stopping with sukun, rawm and ishmam
lessons.lede: You stop on the end of a word with a plain sukun; rawm is allowed with dammah and kasrah, and ishmam with dammah only.

formula.caption: part of the vowel: dammah, kasrah

idea.lead: The basic way to stop is a plain sukun, dropping the vowel completely. Rawm is saying part of the vowel in a faint voice that only someone near can hear; it is for dammah and kasrah, not fathah. Ishmam is rounding the lips after giving the last letter a sukun, silently, as a sign of the dammah: the seeing can see it and the blind cannot hear it; it is for dammah only. Ibn al-Jazari says: «وَحَاذِرِ الوَقْفَ بِكُلِّ الحَرَكَهْ، إِلَّا إِذَا رُمْتَ فَبَعْضُ الحَرَكَهْ، إِلَّا بِفَتْحٍ أَوْ بِنَصْبٍ وَأَشِمّْ، إِشَارَةً بِالضَّمِّ فِي رَفْعٍ وَضَمّْ» (beware of stopping with the whole vowel, except with rawm, which is part of it, but not with fathah; and use ishmam to point to the dammah).
idea.kidsLead: When we stop on the end of a word, we read it with sukun: «نَسْتَعِينْ». We may let a tiny bit of the dammah or kasrah be heard: this is rawm. Or we round our lips after the sukun, silently: this is ishmam, only with dammah.

how.text: Allowed on any word ending in a vowel: «نَسۡتَعِينۡ», «ٱلرَّحِيمۡ».
With dammah and kasrah: say the dammah of «نَسۡتَعِينُ» or the kasrah of «ٱلرَّحِيمِ» faintly, about a third of the vowel.
With dammah only: give the noon of «نَسۡتَعِينُ» a sukun, then round the lips silently.
Fathah; the feminine haa «رَحۡمَةۡ»; the plural meem «عَلَيۡهِمۡ»; or a temporary vowel, as when stopping on «قُمۡ» from «قُمِ ٱلَّيۡلَ».
With rawm, the madd for stopping is only two counts; with sukun and ishmam, two, four or six.

idea.note: In «لَا تَأۡمَ۬نَّا» (Yusuf 11), Hafs has two ways when joining: ishmam, merging the two noons, or rawm, keeping them apart. The word was «تَأۡمَنُنَا», with two noons. Learn rawm and ishmam from a teacher, by listening and repeating.

ayat.legendNoon: The place of ishmam or rawm
ayat.findHint: Listen to «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا» and look at the mark under the meem, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Ishmam at the doubled noon, or rawm with both noons clear

ayat.tip: The small diamond under the meem of «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا» in the Mushaf marks ishmam or rawm, in this word alone.

quiz.q: What is rawm?
options: Saying part of the vowel in a faint voice
quiz.why: Rawm is saying part of the vowel in a faint voice that only someone near can hear.

quiz.q: What is ishmam?
options: Rounding the lips after the sukun, silently
quiz.why: Ishmam is rounding the lips after the sukun, silently, as a sign of the dammah.

quiz.q: With which vowel is ishmam used?
quiz.why: Ishmam points to the dammah, so it is only for a dammah.

quiz.q: With which vowel is rawm not allowed?
quiz.why: Rawm is for dammah and kasrah, not fathah.

quiz.q: Is rawm allowed when stopping on «رَحۡمَةٞ»?
options: No: it is a feminine haa, stopped on with a haa
quiz.why: The feminine haa is stopped on with sukun, so it takes neither rawm nor ishmam.

quiz.q: With rawm on «نَسۡتَعِينُ», how long is the madd?
quiz.why: With rawm the sukun is not complete, so only two counts are allowed.

quiz.q: What are the two ways for Hafs in «تَأۡمَ۬نَّا»?
options: Ishmam with idgham, or rawm with izhar
quiz.why: Ishmam with the two noons merged, or rawm with both noons clear.

lessons.title: Stopping on taa marbutah and the feminine haa
lessons.lede: A closed feminine taa «ة» is stopped on as a haa with sukun; an open one «ت» is stopped on as a taa, following the writing of the Mushaf, as in «رَحۡمَتَ ٱللَّهِ».

formula.caption: Stopped on as a haa with sukun

idea.lead: The feminine haa is written in the Mushaf two ways: closed «ة» in most places, as in «رَحۡمَةٗ» and «جَنَّةٍ», stopped on as a haa with sukun «رَحۡمَهۡ»; and open «ت» in certain places, as in «رَحۡمَتَ ٱللَّهِ» (Al-A'raf 56), «فِطۡرَتَ ٱللَّهِ» (Ar-Rum 30), «شَجَرَتَ ٱلزَّقُّومِ» (Ad-Dukhan 43) and «ٱمۡرَأَتُ ٱلۡعَزِيزِ» (Yusuf 30), which Hafs stops on as a taa with sukun, following the writing. The rule is that stopping follows the writing of the Mushaf: what is written with haa is stopped on with haa, and what is written with taa is stopped on with taa.
idea.kidsLead: We stop on a closed taa «ة» as a haa with sukun: «رَحۡمَةٌ» is stopped on as «raḥmah». But the open taa «ت», as in «رَحۡمَتَ ٱللَّهِ», we stop on as a taa: «raḥmat».

how.text: Stopped on as a haa with sukun, with no rawm or ishmam: «وَرَحۡمَةٗ» «wa raḥmah», «ٱلۡقَارِعَةُ» «al-qāri'ah».
Stopped on as a taa with sukun: «رَحۡمَتَ» «raḥmat», «نِعۡمَتَ» «ni'mat», «ٱمۡرَأَتُ» «imra'at», «سُنَّتُ» «sunnat».

Among the best known: «رَحۡمَتَ», «نِعۡمَتَ», «ٱمۡرَأَتُ», «سُنَّتُ», «لَعۡنَتَ», «مَعۡصِيَتِ», «كَلِمَتُ», «شَجَرَتَ», «فِطۡرَتَ», «قُرَّتُ عَيۡنٖ», «جَنَّتُ نَعِيمٖ», «بَقِيَّتُ», «ٱبۡنَتَ», in certain places only.
Hafs also stops with taa on «يَٰٓأَبَتِ», «هَيۡهَاتَ», «ذَاتَ», «لَاتَ», «مَرۡضَاتِ» and «ٱللَّٰتَ», following the writing.
It is different from the feminine haa: you stop on it with sukun and drop its silah: «لَهُۥ» is stopped on as «lah» (lessons 43 and 44).

idea.note: The writing in each place is the reference: the same word may be written with taa in one place and haa elsewhere, like «رَحۡمَتَ», written with taa in seven places and with haa in the rest of the Quran.

ayat.findHint: Find the feminine taa in each ayah: open or closed? Then bring the colours back to check.

why: Open taa: stopped on as «raḥmat»
Open taa: stopped on as «shajarat»
Open taa: stopped on as «imra'at»
Closed taa: stopped on as «wa raḥmah»

ayat.tip: The same word, «رَحۡمَة», is written with taa in Al-A'raf and with haa in An-Nahl, and the stop follows the writing.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «رَحۡمَةٗ» with a closed taa?
quiz.why: A closed taa is stopped on as a haa with sukun.

quiz.q: How does Hafs stop on «رَحۡمَتَ ٱللَّهِ» (Al-A'raf 56)?
options: With a taa with sukun, following the writing
quiz.why: It is written with an open taa, so you stop on it with taa.

quiz.q: What is the reference for stopping on the feminine haa?
quiz.why: What is written with haa is stopped on with haa, and what is written with taa with taa.

quiz.q: Do rawm and ishmam come in a closed taa stopped on as haa?
quiz.why: You stop on it with a haa with sukun, so there is no rawm or ishmam.

quiz.q: How does Hafs stop on «يَٰٓأَبَتِ»?
quiz.why: Hafs stops on it with taa, following the writing.

quiz.q: How do you stop on «شَجَرَتَ ٱلزَّقُّومِ»?
quiz.why: It is written with an open taa in Ad-Dukhan 43, so you stop on it with taa.

quiz.q: In how many places is «رَحۡمَتَ» written with an open taa?
quiz.why: Seven places, and with haa in the rest of the Quran.

lessons.title: Words special to Hafs
lessons.lede: Words special to the riwayah of Hafs, learned as narrated, such as «يَبۡصُۜطُ» and «مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا».

formula.caption: Fathah or dammah on the daad

idea.lead: Hafs from 'Asim, by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, has words where he differs from his usual way or from the general rule, so the reciter should learn them as they were narrated. They are gathered in the table below: in the letters, between seen and saad; in the vowel of the daad of «ضَعۡفٖ»; and in imalah, ishmam, tas-hil and the pronoun haa. Most are marked by small signs in the Mushaf, like the seen above the saad in «يَبۡصُۜطُ».
idea.kidsLead: In the riwayah of Hafs a few words are read in a special way, and we learn them as they are: «يَبۡصُۜطُ» is read with seen, and in «مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا» the raa leans towards kasrah.

how.text: «يَبۡصُۜطُ» (Al-Baqarah 245) and «بَصۜۡطَةٗ» (Al-A'raf 69) with seen, «ٱلۡمُصَۜيۡطِرُونَ» (At-Tur 37) either way, and «بِمُصَيۡطِرٍ» (Al-Ghashiyah 22) with saad.
Three times in Ar-Rum 54: «مِّن ضَعۡفٖ», «مِنۢ بَعۡدِ ضَعۡفٖ», «ضَعۡفٗا»: fathah or dammah on the daad, and fathah is preferred.
«مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا» (Hud 41): the fathah leans towards kasrah and the alif towards yaa; it is the only imalah for Hafs.
In Yusuf 11: ishmam with idgham, or rawm with izhar (lesson 90).
«ءَا۬عۡجَمِيّٞ» (Fussilat 44): the second hamzah is softened between hamzah and alif (lesson 83).
Dammah in «عَلَيۡهُ ٱللَّهَ» and «أَنسَىٰنِيهُ», silah in «فِيهِۦ مُهَانًا», sukun in «أَرۡجِهۡ» and «فَأَلۡقِهۡ», and dammah without silah in «يَرۡضَهُ لَكُمۡ» (lesson 44).

idea.note: These readings are by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, and other ways may differ. Add to them the special rules already studied: the saktahs (lesson 85), the madd of distinction (lesson 51), «ٱلِٱسۡمُ» (lesson 81), the alifs said when stopping (lesson 84), and the two ways in «مَالِيَهۡۜ ۝ هَلَكَ» (lesson 76).

ayat.legendNoon: A letter or vowel special to Hafs
ayat.findHint: Find the word special to the riwayah of Hafs in each ayah, then bring the colours back to check.

why: Written with saad and read with seen
Fathah or dammah on the daad, and fathah is preferred
The only imalah for Hafs
Ishmam with idgham, or rawm with izhar

ayat.tip: The small signs in the Mushaf mark these words: the seen above the saad, and the diamond under the raa in «مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا».

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «يَبۡصُطُ» in Al-Baqarah?
quiz.why: It is written with saad, and Hafs reads it with seen; a small seen is written over the saad.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «بِمُصَيۡطِرٍ» in Al-Ghashiyah?
quiz.why: Hafs reads it with saad; «ٱلۡمُصَيۡطِرُونَ» in At-Tur has both ways.

quiz.q: What does Hafs prefer in «ضَعۡفٖ» in Surah Ar-Rum?
quiz.why: Hafs has fathah and dammah on the daad; fathah is preferred.

quiz.q: What is the imalah in «مَجۡر۪ىٰهَا»?
options: The fathah leaning towards kasrah and the alif towards yaa
quiz.why: The raa and the alif after it lean; it is the only imalah for Hafs.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read the haa in «عَلَيۡهُ ٱللَّهَ» (Al-Fath 10)?
quiz.why: Hafs gives the haa a dammah here, unlike his usual kasrah after yaa.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read the haa in «أَرۡجِهۡ» (Al-A'raf 111)?
quiz.why: Hafs gives the haa sukun in «أَرۡجِهۡ», in Al-A'raf and Ash-Shu'ara.

quiz.q: How does Hafs read «يَرۡضَهُ لَكُمۡ» (Az-Zumar 7)?
options: With dammah on the haa, no silah
quiz.why: The haa is between two vowels, yet Hafs does not join it.
